It was the second botched execution in the state this year. The apparent failure came after dueling court rulings delayed the execution of the woman, Christa Pike, by about nine hours.

ARTICLE

Tennessee Fails to Execute Woman After 2 Doses of Lethal Injection
Christa Pike was convicted of murdering a classmate in 1995. It was not clear what went wrong in the execution or what her current medical condition was.
By Emily Cochrane and Ann E. Marimow
Published 2026-09-30 14:14 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/us/christa-pike-stay-execution-tennessee.html

A Tennessee woman convicted of murder survived two doses of lethal injection on Wednesday night before state officials suspended the execution and had her taken to a hospital for medical care, her lawyers said.

It was the second botched execution in the state this year.

The apparent failure came after dueling court rulings delayed the execution of the woman, Christa Pike, by about nine hours. The state had raced to go ahead with the execution before the day ended and to avoid having to reschedule.

In a pair of emergency legal filings, Ms. Pike’s lawyers said that while two syringes of pentobarbital, the lethal drug, had been administered, Ms. Pike had not lost consciousness. She still had a heartbeat, they said, and was audibly snoring.

It was not immediately clear what went wrong with the administration of the drugs, or what Ms. Pike’s medical condition was. In a statement late Wednesday, her lawyers said that she was at a nearby hospital but that they did not know her condition. Tennessee officials confirmed to a federal judge late Wednesday that Ms. Pike was receiving medical care.

“This event is the worst we’ve seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era,” said Robin Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center. “There is no precedent.”

At a news conference after the execution attempt, members of the media who served as witnesses described Ms. Pike as somewhat alert, at one point singing with her spiritual adviser. They were brought into the witness room outside the execution chamber just before 6:30 p.m. Shortly after, the curtains separating the execution chamber from the witnesses were opened to show Ms. Pike, strapped to a gurney, they said.

“I’m going to leave this world the way I spent most of my life,” she said. “And that is with love.”

At one point, they said, she described a burning spot in her arm that felt like it was going to burst. She asked if that was normal. The curtains briefly closed, then reopened.

The curtains were then closed again for nearly an hour, reporters said, adding that they could hear breathing and steady snoring. Just before 9 p.m., reporters were told to leave for the news conference.

Emergency vehicles arrived at the prison as the witnesses were addressing the news conference and left about 15 minutes later.

Officials at the prison, the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, did not address reporters afterward. In a statement, the Tennessee Department of Correction said it “had followed every step of the state’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the attorney general’s office.”

“The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective,” the department said.

It was the second time this year that Tennessee failed to administer the lethal drugs. In May, the state called off one of four planned executions because medical staff could not find a vein while administering a lethal drug.

Ms. Pike’s lawyers had argued the procedure could be torturous for her because she has small veins, a history of sexual trauma and other medical conditions.

“We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms. Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy,” they said in a joint statement after the execution attempt.

Ms. Pike, 50, who was convicted of murdering her classmate in 1995, would have been the first woman to be executed in the state in over 200 years.

The attempted execution came hours after the U.S. Supreme Court allowed the state to proceed, overturning a pause imposed by a lower court earlier in the day.

The lower court briefly paused the execution, saying more time was needed to consider the case. Her lawyers had argued that Ms. Pike’s initial legal defense did not adequately present her history of child sexual abuse and neglect.

The three liberal justices on the Supreme Court dissented from the order allowing the execution to proceed, with Justice Sonia Sotomayor writing that the majority “unnecessarily prevents” the appeals court from fully considering Ms. Pike’s argument.

“I see no reason to short-circuit the ordinary process of appellate review, particularly in light of the grave consequences of an erroneous decision,” Justice Sotomayor wrote. She was joined by Justices Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson.

Justice Sotomayor added that “Tennessee’s desire to expedite Pike’s execution by a few days or even weeks cannot outweigh” Ms. Pike’s interest in protecting her own life.

In January 1995, Ms. Pike, her boyfriend at the time and a friend lured 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer into the woods on the University of Tennessee campus, taunting and torturing her. They beat her with asphalt rocks and slashed her with a box carver. Ms. Pike, who was 18 then, took a piece of Ms. Slemmer’s skull with her, which she showed to at least one other person.

Tadaryl Shipp, Ms. Pike’s boyfriend, testified to carving a pentagram into Ms. Slemmer’s chest, a gesture that sparked fears of Satan worship. Because Tennessee law applies the death penalty only to people 18 and older at the time of the crime, Mr. Shipp, at 17, was sentenced to life in prison. He was denied parole last year.

Ms. Slemmer’s family remained firmly in support of Ms. Pike’s execution and raised funds to cover the drive from their home outside of Jacksonville, Fla., to Nashville to witness the execution. May Martinez, Ms. Slemmer’s mother, was adamant that Ms. Pike could not atone for the death of her daughter and should be executed.

The lone woman on Tennessee’s death row, Ms. Pike has expressed remorse for her crime. She was diagnosed and treated while in prison for bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder, something which her lawyers said had contributed to her violence. Women who were incarcerated alongside Ms. Pike said she was a supportive and kind presence.

In the grassy fields outside the prison, where protesters gathered both in favor of and against the death penalty, there was confusion and disbelief over the lower court’s last-minute intervention on Wednesday. Some people walked away, frustrated that another legal hurdle had temporarily delayed the execution.

Tennessee is among a small number of states that have pushed forward with executions in recent years. This month, Alabama executed a man using lethal injection just months after the Supreme Court blocked his execution by nitrogen gas.

Both states, along with Oklahoma, held executions on the same day in August. It was the first time in more than a decade that three people were executed on the same day.

Seamus Hughes contributed research.

Ms. Noem claimed “for settlement purposes only” that “irreconcilable differences” were to blame for the dissolution of the marriage, according to a complaint for divorce filed in Hamlin County, S.D., where she and Mr. Noem live in the small town of Castlewood. “Kristi Noem has filed for the dissolution of her marriage to Bryon Noem,” her lawyer, Michael K. ARTICLE

Kristi Noem Files for Divorce After 34 Years of Marriage
Ms. Noem, a former homeland security secretary and governor of South Dakota, filed court papers there seeking to end her marriage to Bryon Noem, an insurance salesman.
By Michael Levenson
Published 2026-09-30 17:57 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/us/kristi-noem-divorce-byron-husband.html

Kristi Noem, the former South Dakota governor whom President Trump fired as homeland security secretary in March, has filed for divorce from her husband, Bryon Noem, after 34 years of marriage, according to court records.

Ms. Noem claimed “for settlement purposes only” that “irreconcilable differences” were to blame for the dissolution of the marriage, according to a complaint for divorce filed in Hamlin County, S.D., where she and Mr. Noem live in the small town of Castlewood.

The document was signed by Ms. Noem’s lawyer on April 6 but was not filed with the court until Monday.

“Kristi Noem has filed for the dissolution of her marriage to Bryon Noem,” her lawyer, Michael K. Sabers, said in a statement. “She has great faith in the South Dakota judicial system and will reserve any further comments for the legal process.”

Mr. Noem’s lawyer, Timothy G. Bottum, said in a statement on Wednesday that Mr. Noem was “saddened that the marriage is ending and hopes for a private and amicable resolution.”

“If court proceedings become necessary, Bryon will welcome the opportunity to truthfully share his perspective,” the statement said. “Bryon’s priority is to protect the family and move forward as loving parents and grandparents.”

Ms. Noem, 54, and Mr. Noem, 56, were high school sweethearts who got engaged on the Fourth of July in 1991. They were married less than a year later, on May 23, 1992, in Watertown, S.D., where Ms. Noem was born. They have three adult children.

Mr. Noem, an insurance salesman, received intense public scrutiny in late March when The Daily Mail published what it said were images of him wearing what appeared to be large inflated balloons under a spandex shirt.

Ms. Noem said in a statement at the time that she was “devastated” by the images and that “the family was blindsided by this.” Mr. Noem declined to comment in March, responding in a text to a New York Times reporter: “I will at some point. Today is not the day. I appreciate your heart.”

While the images provoked online mockery, they touched off a more sympathetic reaction in Castlewood, where some residents said they felt sorry for Mr. Noem.

Ms. Noem’s personal life was also the focus of speculation and rumor in South Dakota and Washington.

On March 4, the day before Ms. Noem was fired as homeland security secretary, a Democratic member of Congress asked her at a hearing on Capitol Hill whether she had had sexual relations with her lieutenant, Corey Lewandowski. Responding under oath, Ms. Noem called the question “tabloid garbage.” But she did not say no. Mr. Noem accompanied Ms. Noem to the hearing.

Mr. Trump announced in November 2024 that he was selecting Ms. Noem to lead the Department of Homeland Security, a position that put her in charge of the administration’s aggressive crackdown on immigration and its large-scale deportation operation. The department includes U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and U.S. Customs and Border Protection.

Mr. Trump fired Ms. Noem in March, making her the first cabinet official ousted in his second term.

The immediate catalyst for her firing appeared to be her answers during two congressional hearings, particularly her statements asserting that Mr. Trump had approved of tens of millions of dollars in government ads in which Ms. Noem was prominently featured riding on horseback in chaps and a cowboy hat. Mr. Trump had denied that he was involved, telling Reuters in March, “I never knew anything about it.”

Ms. Noem had presided over other controversies during her tenure.

In January, federal immigration agents fatally shot two American citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, during vigorous protests of the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement surge in Minneapolis. As bystander videos of the shootings caused a national outcry, Ms. Noem responded by accusing Ms. Good and Mr. Pretti of domestic terrorism.

When Mr. Trump announced that he was firing Ms. Noem and replacing her with Senator Markwayne Mullin of Oklahoma, he said in a social media post that she had “served us well, and has had numerous and spectacular results,” particularly on the border.

He also announced a new role for her: the previously nonexistent post of special envoy for the Shield of the Americas, which he said would be a new security initiative for the Western Hemisphere.

ARTICLE

California Governor Candidates to Face Off in Televised Debate
Xavier Becerra, a Democrat who served in the Biden administration, will debate Steve Hilton, a Republican former talk show host, in what’s likely to be their only face-off before the election.
By Laurel Rosenhall
Published 2026-09-30 12:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/us/california-governor-race-debate-becerra-hilton.html

The two candidates running for California governor will meet Wednesday for a nationally televised debate that is likely to be their only face-off before the Nov. 3 election.

After a wild primary campaign this year, the governor’s race has settled into a low-key affair. Xavier Becerra, a Democrat who served as health and human services secretary under President Joseph R. Biden Jr., is a heavy favorite in a state dominated by his party. He is facing Steve Hilton, a Republican who was once a Fox News television host and an aide to David Cameron, the former British prime minister.

CNN will host the debate at 6 p.m. local time, just days before ballots begin landing in voters’ mailboxes.

Univision, the Spanish-language network, told The New York Times that both candidates have also agreed to participate in a town-hall-style forum on Oct. 20. But the candidates will not appear at the same time at that event.

Mr. Hilton, 57, who has lagged in polls and fund-raising, stands to gain more than Mr. Becerra from the national exposure that Wednesday’s debate will provide. He has been traveling the state to hold campaign events and sit for media interviews, trying to catch voters’ attention however he can.

By comparison, Mr. Becerra, 68, has made limited public appearances since the June primary. It’s been two decades since California voters elected a Republican to statewide office, so many Democratic candidates in the state have come to wage fiercer fights in the primary against party rivals and then kept a lower profile in less competitive general elections.

The two men are vying to lead a state during a moment of economic pessimism, recent polling shows. Price increases and high housing costs are straining many households, and reducing the cost of living is a top priority for a plurality of likely voters.

Gov. Gavin Newsom, who must leave office in January because of term limits, made sparring with President Trump a core part of his strategy as governor. The candidates running to replace him are taking cues, as Mr. Trump remains deeply unpopular in California.

Mr. Becerra has attacked Mr. Trump’s moves to restrict voting access while serving as an adviser on a lawsuit against a Republican sheriff who seized ballots and while campaigning against a California ballot measure to require voter identification. Mr. Becerra was California’s attorney general before he worked for the Biden administration.

“It’s really a threat to our democracy, and he’s working hard to protect people’s right to vote,” said Jonathan Underland, a spokesman for Mr. Becerra.

Mr. Hilton got Mr. Trump’s endorsement, which may have benefited him in the primary but now requires a difficult balancing act. He is trying to appeal to California voters who dislike the president while still keeping MAGA voters in his camp.

“Can you be anti-Trump but still vote for me?” Mr. Hilton asked in a full-page newspaper ad this summer that outlined the reasons he believed voters who oppose the president should still support him.

He said he’s met many voters on the campaign trail who tell him, “One-party rule just isn’t working, and we need a bit of balance.”

“I hear that often,” Mr. Hilton said in an interview.

For the Univision town halls in October, the candidates will appear separately and take questions from the audience. Mr. Becerra will address voters in Spanish, which he grew up speaking in California with his parents, who immigrated from Mexico. An interpreter will translate the responses given by Mr. Hilton, who grew up in England with parents who emigrated there from Hungary.

Most voters view debates as a partisan “team sport,” said Kim Nalder, a political science professor who leads the Project for an Informed Electorate at California State University, Sacramento. But she said that the debate may help some voters decide whom to support given that many are still learning about the candidates.

Mr. Becerra has run a low-profile campaign, Ms. Nalder said, and many voters may be unfamiliar with Mr. Hilton unless they watch Fox News.

“In this particular case, I think it is possible that some persuasion might happen because the impressions are not already formed,” Ms. Nalder said.

In general, she said, televised political debates have had less impact in recent years as media habits have changed and candidates have focused more on turning out their supporters rather than persuading undecided voters to choose them.

This summer, Mr. Hilton called for at least six debates. But front-runners like Mr. Becerra who enjoy a lopsided partisan advantage often decide that they have more to lose than gain from debating.

Mr. Newsom was even more elusive than Mr. Becerra in 2018, the last time California had an open race for governor. The two candidates met for just one debate ahead of the general election — and very few people saw it.

Mr. Newsom, a Democrat who was lieutenant governor, debated John Cox, a Republican businessman, on the radio. No television cameras were allowed to broadcast the event. And it took place in the middle of a Monday morning.

Still, Democrats have sought to make data centers a central issue in competitive races across the country, including Mr. Husted’s in Ohio.

ARTICLE

Congress Set to Leave Washington for the Midterms With No A.I. Progress
Senate Democrats blocked a measure that would encourage, but not require, states to protect consumers from power rate hikes tied to data center growth, and had no limits on A.I. use or deployment.
By Michael Gold and Cecilia Kang
Published 2026-09-30 16:55 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/us/politics/congress-ai-safety.html

Facing a growing backlash over the boom in data center construction and widespread concern over the safety of artificial intelligence, Congress is set to depart Washington this week ahead of the midterm elections having accomplished nothing to address either issue.

Eager to show they hear the public alarm over A.I. as they fight to keep their majority, Republicans in the Senate on Wednesday attempted to bring up a bill intended to insulate Americans from rising electricity costs tied to data centers. But Democrats blocked it, noting that the legislation was not enforceable and arguing it would do little to significantly curb energy prices.

The bill, sponsored by Senator Jon Husted of Ohio, a Republican in a difficult re-election battle, also would not impose any regulation on the use or deployment of artificial intelligence in the wake of several revelations that A.I. agents evaded safeguards meant to constrain them.

With widespread disagreement over the best path forward but lawmakers eager to show voters progress on the issue before facing them in November, members of both parties have in recent days released a barrage of legislation, letters and statements of concern about A.I. and held a Senate hearing on “Rogue A.I.” on Wednesday afternoon as they rushed for the exits.

“I remain an A.I. optimist. I am not an A.I. doomer,” Senator Mark Warner, a Virginia Democrat who is also up for re-election, said. “But we are at a moment in time, particularly over the last few weeks, where I think the whole world has recognized we’ve got to do something.”

It comes as President Trump has played down A.I. safety risks and lawmakers in both parties remain uncertain about how to proceed on the issue as major players in the industry are spending heavily to influence the midterms. Though Mr. Trump convened top technology executives at the White House on Tuesday, the group agreed only to voluntary safety agreements and to follow the president’s preference in rebranding A.I. as “super intelligence.”

Some Republican senators have argued there is a need for stronger oversight. Senator Josh Hawley, Republican of Missouri, who has sponsored several pieces of legislation that would limit A.I., convened Wednesday’s hearing and said that companies should be subject to consequences when their technology is misused.

“It’s time to talk about what we’re going to do to hold the companies, the product makers accountable, rather than all of this talk about the end of the world,” Mr. Hawley said. None of the executives who joined the White House meeting attended; Mr. Hawley said that Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, had declined his invitation to participate.

Still, Republicans also are facing blowback for having included tax breaks in their major tax and spending cut legislation last year that benefited data center developers. Mr. Hawley has introduced legislation that would bar data centers from taking advantage of the incentives.

It is unclear whether Congress’s lack of action on the issue will have political consequences in November. A poll conducted this month by The New York Times and Siena University found that neither party had a clear advantage with voters on A.I., even as voters broadly opposed the construction of data centers.

Still, Democrats have sought to make data centers a central issue in competitive races across the country, including Mr. Husted’s in Ohio.

Before he was appointed to the Senate last year, Mr. Husted, the state’s lieutenant governor, backed tax incentives for data centers. Democrats have spent millions on television advertisements labeling him as the “face of data centers.” In August, Senate Republicans’ campaign arm distributed a memo warning that the issue was threatening Mr. Husted’s re-election bid.

Wednesday’s vote was seen as a potential boon for his campaign.

The legislation, which passed the House overwhelmingly earlier this month, would order state utility regulators to consider adopting rules requiring the centers to cover higher costs associated with their power use. But it would not force state regulators to follow federal standards when they are setting electricity rates, and it would give them two years to weigh changes.

Mr. Husted argued that the bill was the best mechanism available for Congress to quickly address energy prices. He pointed to its bipartisan support in the House and said it was the only legislation ready to make it to the president’s desk.

“This is the only game in town,” Mr. Husted said. “This bill passing is the only way to get a chance to prove to the American people before the midterm elections whose side you’re on.”

Democrats have argued that Mr. Husted’s bill is little more than a symbolic gesture that will have little effect on electricity costs. Senator Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, pronounced it “toothless” and called for more meaningful regulations.

“An optional guardrail isn’t a guardrail at all,” Mr. Schumer said. “At a time when Americans are calling out for real guardrails on A.I., Senate Republicans are trying to secure an ineffectual participation trophy before they skip town.”

Though four Democrats joined Republicans, they still fell short of the 60-vote threshold required to proceed.

Republicans accused Democrats of putting politics first while seeking to flip Mr. Husted’s seat. But Senator John Kennedy, Republican of Louisiana, said he was frustrated that lawmakers had waited until the last minute to try to do something about data centers.

“That’s the sort of thing that I wish we’d started talking about a month or a month and a half ago and tried to work something out with the Democrats,” Mr. Kennedy said of Mr. Husted’s bill. Instead, he said, “we’re doing it at the last minute.”

Lawmakers from both parties have introduced a flurry of proposals hoping to slow the pace of A.I. development, impose guardrails and address the national security risks that could be posed by rogue A.I. agents. But their bills have largely gone nowhere in the face of deep disagreements both within the parties and between them.

Even lawmakers who are calling for swift regulation are being careful to say they do not want to stop A.I. development outright.

On Tuesday, three Democratic senators, including Mr. Warner, asked their colleagues to quickly take up and pass a bill that would establish a federal panel to oversee safety standards for A.I. models and to evaluate models before they were deployed.

But Mr. Warner framed the effort in part as a chance to stem the rising A.I. backlash.

“We should not miss the moment to put a safety protocol in place now,” Mr. Warner, whose state has benefited from data center growth, said. “If Congress goes out, God forbid we have an incident, A.I. is already suspect by most Americans. We could see the stop of innovation if an A.I. tool took over a hospital or water system.”

Senator Ted Cruz, Republican of Texas, objected and blocked the legislation, saying that he feared giving the government too much authority over A.I.

He also accused his colleagues of moving too quickly.

“Congress must not legislate on the issue of artificial intelligence hastily or in a closed manner,” he said.

democrats-block-stock-trading-bill.html

SUMMARY

Senate Democrats on Wednesday blocked legislation that would limit the ability of members of Congress to trade stock, dismissing it as an empty G.O.P. effort to appeal to widespread voter distrust of public officials ahead of the November elections without actually addressing it. But Democrats said they would have opposed the bill even without the voter ID measure, because it fails to do what voters have been clamoring for: impose an outright ban on congressional stock trading. In North Carolina, the Democratic Senate nominee, former Gov. Roy Cooper, has said that the first thing he would support in Congress would be a stock trading ban.

ARTICLE

Democrats Block Stock-Trading Bill, Denying the G.O.P. a Pre-Midterm Win
A Republican measure to limit, but not bar, congressional stock trading faltered in the Senate as Democrats thwarted a G.O.P. bid to show progress on an issue that has rankled voters.
By Annie Karni
Published 2026-09-30 17:38 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/us/politics/democrats-block-stock-trading-bill.html

Senate Democrats on Wednesday blocked legislation that would limit the ability of members of Congress to trade stock, dismissing it as an empty G.O.P. effort to appeal to widespread voter distrust of public officials ahead of the November elections without actually addressing it.

The Stop Insider Trading Act, which the House passed in July, would bar lawmakers and their spouses and family members from buying individual stocks but allow members of Congress who already own them to keep trading with new notice requirements. It places no restrictions on the president or the vice president.

The measure, which needed 60 votes to pass, was blocked on a party-line vote of 53 to 47, its failure predetermined after Republicans attached sweeping voter ID restrictions opposed by Democrats and some G.O.P. lawmakers that have already been rejected by the Senate six times.

But Democrats said they would have opposed the bill even without the voter ID measure, because it fails to do what voters have been clamoring for: impose an outright ban on congressional stock trading. They accused Republicans of bringing it up in an effort to appear as if they were addressing the issue, which has become politically toxic for both parties.

Senator Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, called it a “toothless” bill that was as “ineffective as a screen door on a submarine.” He noted that it would do nothing to stop President Trump, who he said has made 30,000 stock trades in the past year, from continuing such transactions.

Mr. Schumer called the bill a “last-ditch effort to save face” with voters, but said that “Americans don’t buy it.”

The Campaign Legal Center, a nonpartisan legal organization, also urged Congress to reject the measure because it “does not actually ban congressional stock trading, and it will thus not remove the cloud of distrust that hangs over lawmakers’ suspicious stock sales.”

The bill was brought to the floor as part of a final sprint of legislative moves before the midterm elections by Senate Republicans. They are facing a bleak political landscape with just weeks to go before the balloting, aimed at showing they were responsive to voters’ concerns.

“It would ensure transparency when it comes to stock sales to provide that members of Congress and their families provide public notice of any stock sale,” Senator John Thune, Republican of South Dakota and the majority leader, said on the Senate floor. He called it a “simple” but important way “to ensure that members of Congress are held to the standards that Americans should be able to expect of their representatives.”

Senator Pete Ricketts, Republican of Nebraska, said passage was necessary to “restore the faith of the American people in the House and in the Senate.”

For House Republicans who voted for an identical measure earlier this year, the bill has provided them with a talking point to appeal to voters on the issue.

In Iowa, for example, an outside group supporting Representative Zach Nunn, a vulnerable Republican, has spent almost $400,000 on an ad highlighting his support for the bill, exaggerating what it does.

“While honest, hard-working Americans struggle at home, fat cat politicians in Washington are getting rich on inside information,” the ad states. Mr. Nunn’s support for the bill, it claims inaccurately, means that “those fat cat lawmakers and their families are prohibited from buying stocks, putting an end to their greed and corruption, and leveling the playing field for hard-working Americans.”

A public backlash against perceived corruption in Washington has shaped the battle for control of Congress, with Democrats and Republicans alike seizing on congressional stock trading and putting it at the forefront of ads in some of the most competitive races in the country.

Candidates in both parties have cited congressional stock trading as a way to portray their opponents as corrupt and out of touch with the financial realities of working-class Americans.

Roughly a quarter of legislators on Capitol Hill have traded individual stocks during this congressional session, with some buying and selling millions of dollars in shares. Since the start of this term in January 2025, members and their families have collectively traded $160 million to $664 million in individual stocks, according to a New York Times analysis of data collected from members’ required financial filings by 2iQ Research, an analytics firm.

This year, candidates and outside groups have spent an estimated $162 million on advertisements highlighting the issue, according to an analysis by AdImpact.

In competitive House districts, Republicans are targeting Democrats on the issue with television ads in Florida, Virginia, Texas and Ohio.

And Democratic candidates in some of the most competitive Senate races in the country, where they are hoping to flip seats, have all zeroed in on the topic as they make their appeals to voters.

In Alaska, former Representative Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee, has been campaigning on a ban, attacking Senator Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, for being one of the most prolific stock traders in Congress.

“He’s ballooned his net worth, reporting nearly 100 stock trades while serving in office,” she said at an event in July.

In North Carolina, the Democratic Senate nominee, former Gov. Roy Cooper, has said that the first thing he would support in Congress would be a stock trading ban. He also challenged his Republican opponent, Michael Whatley, to sell his stock.

In Iowa, State Representative Josh Turek, the Democratic nominee for Senate, has been attacking Representative Ashley Hinson, the Republican nominee, in paid advertisements for increasing her net worth up to $8 million since she went to Congress. (Ms. Hinson, in paid ads, also says that she is “fighting to ban stock trading in Congress.”)

And in Ohio, former Senator Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, tells voters in an ad that “last year, members of Congress made more than $635 million in stock trades.” He adds: “The fact is, we’ve come to expect that kind of thing from Washington. But you shouldn’t, and I never will.”

Senate Democrats have made their own attempts at addressing the issue, all of which have been blocked by Republicans. In June, Senator Jon Ossoff, Democrat of Georgia, sought to bar senators from trading stocks and cryptocurrency.

“This may be one of the most unifying issues in our deeply divided country,” he said at the time. A Republican, Senator Cynthia Lummis of Wyoming, objected.

In July, Senator Alex Padilla, Democrat of California, tried twice to offer a bipartisan bill that would bar members of Congress and their family members, as well as the president and vice president, from trading stocks.

Republicans moved to block it both times.

jack-smith-lawsuit-trump-blackburn.html

SUMMARY

A Republican senator on Wednesday sued the former special counsel Jack Smith and the Justice Department, arguing that a subpoena for her phone records during an investigation into Donald J. Trump violated the Constitution. The complaint, filed by Senator Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee in her state’s Middle District, could put before the courts a novel and contested constitutional issue on a matter that has become a Republican talking point: whether the so-called speech or debate clause bars subpoenas to phone companies for data about lawmakers’ communications. “We took our obligations seriously under the speech or debate clause,” Mr. Smith said.

ARTICLE

Republican Senator Sues Over Jack Smith’s Subpoena During Trump Inquiry
The lawsuit, brought by Senator Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee, tests the reach of the Constitution’s “speech or debate” clause.
By Charlie Savage
Published 2026-09-30 21:27 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/us/politics/jack-smith-lawsuit-trump-blackburn.html

A Republican senator on Wednesday sued the former special counsel Jack Smith and the Justice Department, arguing that a subpoena for her phone records during an investigation into Donald J. Trump violated the Constitution.

The complaint, filed by Senator Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee in her state’s Middle District, could put before the courts a novel and contested constitutional issue on a matter that has become a Republican talking point: whether the so-called speech or debate clause bars subpoenas to phone companies for data about lawmakers’ communications.

Ms. Blackburn was among several lawmakers who apparently interacted with Mr. Trump while he was president, or with his proxies, during a period of days around the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the Capitol. The lawsuit seeks a declaration that Mr. Smith conspired to violate her rights, $1 in symbolic damages from the former special counsel, and an order that the Justice Department destroy her records.

When Mr. Smith oversaw an investigation into Mr. Trump’s attempt to overturn the 2020 election, he signed off on subpoenas to phone companies for lawmakers’ toll records, or logs showing when calls took place, but not their contents. The subpoenas were accompanied by nondisclosure orders to the phone companies, but came to light last year.

Republicans have portrayed themselves as having been unfairly targeted, and have framed the subpoenas for their call records as violating the speech or debate clause. In her lawsuit, Ms. Blackburn’s lawyers said she sought to hold Mr. Smith “accountable for his gross abuse of power and his disregard for the Constitution’s separation of powers, the speech or debate clause,” and for other allegations.

Mr. Smith faced similar accusations on Tuesday when he appeared before the Senate Judiciary Committee. Ms. Blackburn is a member of the panel but did not attend the hearing.

In his testimony, Mr. Smith said that the lawmakers were not the targets of the investigation. He added that the intent of seeking the data was to gather corroborating evidence about calls by Mr. Trump or his proxies to members of Congress seeking to get them to delay the Electoral College certification proceedings, which he said “added to the powerful evidence we had of Donald Trump’s guilt.”

Mr. Smith also noted that the public integrity section, which had been the Justice Department’s hub of legal expertise for issues involving criminal investigations and members of Congress until the Trump administration gutted it last year, signed off on the subpoenas as lawful.

“We took our obligations seriously under the speech or debate clause,” Mr. Smith said. “It’s, in my view, an important part of the separation of powers. I had members of my staff who were very familiar with the clause, having worked in the public integrity section for years. We also, when it was appropriate or required, consulted with the public integrity section regarding application of that clause.”

Ms. Blackburn’s complaint was full of political grievances. But beyond the bluster is a serious question of how far the speech or debate clause extends. The clause says that lawmakers “shall not be questioned in any other place” for their “speech or debate in either House.”

It is widely agreed that the clause bars both prosecuting lawmakers for their legislative acts and compelling them to testify about them. But appeals courts have disagreed about whether or how the clause may also protect the confidentiality of legislative material in circumstances in which lawmakers are not being forced to divulge information and the data is relevant evidence for investigations targeting other people.

To date, no court has held that the clause extends to barring subpoenas to phone companies. But lawmakers have also rarely had an opportunity to contest them in court, because investigators typically also obtain nondisclosure orders from a judge barring the phone companies from notifying their customers.

The applications for nondisclosure orders by Mr. Smith’s team did not tell the court that the phone numbers belonged to lawmakers, as material unsealed this summer at the request of The New York Times confirmed. Department policy at the time did not require such notice to the judges being asked to issue the gag orders, but was later changed to do so.

SUMMARY

The Justice Department on Wednesday accused two of Minnesota’s federal judges of engaging in misconduct for comments made to The New York Times about how their court handled the administration’s immigration surge in Minneapolis this winter. The Justice Department urged a judicial investigation into four other federal judges in Minnesota who spoke to The Times. In a statement on Wednesday, Judge Schiltz, who was appointed by President George W. Bush, said he was “acting well within the ethical rules that apply to federal judges in speaking to The New York Times.”

ARTICLE

Justice Dept. Tries to Rebuke Federal Judges for Speaking to The Times
Judge Patrick J. Schiltz had warned that the administration’s actions “created a grave threat to the rule of law.” The attorney general accused him of “obvious bias.”
By Mattathias Schwartz and Devlin Barrett
Published 2026-09-30 20:12 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/us/politics/justice-department-complaint-judges-schiltz.html

The Justice Department on Wednesday accused two of Minnesota’s federal judges of engaging in misconduct for comments made to The New York Times about how their court handled the administration’s immigration surge in Minneapolis this winter.

In a six-page complaint filed with the Judicial Council of the Eighth Circuit, which includes the Minnesota district, the department alleged that the judges’ comments violated ethics rules that limit what judges are allowed to say publicly, particularly on pending cases. It singles out Judge Patrick J. Schiltz and Judge John R. Tunheim, both of whom were quoted in the Times article.

At a news conference on Wednesday, Attorney General Todd Blanche accused the judges of “obvious bias” for giving interviews to The Times about the Trump administration’s immigration surge in Minnesota this winter. Judge Schiltz told The Times that the administration’s actions had “created a grave threat to the rule of law.” Mr. Blanche called those comments “overtly political.”

The article, which appeared on Sept. 17, drew on interviews that took place the previous month with all but one of the judges who were active during the weeks when Operation Metro Surge put the Twin Cities, as well as the court, under tremendous pressure. The judges described the challenges they faced when their dockets were swamped with petitions from detainees, criminal cases against protesters and civil cases challenging the administration’s entire approach.

The Justice Department urged a judicial investigation into four other federal judges in Minnesota who spoke to The Times. The department requested that Judge Schiltz and Judge Tunheim be ordered to recuse themselves from matters involving the Department of Homeland Security.

In a statement on Wednesday, Judge Schiltz, who was appointed by President George W. Bush, said he was “acting well within the ethical rules that apply to federal judges in speaking to The New York Times.” He cited an opinion issued this year by a judicial committee, advising that judges are allowed to speak and write on “core judiciary matters,” including the rule of law and judicial independence.

“That is exactly what I did,” he said.

Judge Tunheim, who was appointed by President Bill Clinton, declined to comment.

Complaints about judicial misconduct are considered by other judges. The circuit’s chief judge can choose to dismiss the complaint or appoint a committee to investigate further. If an investigative committee is formed, that group can recommend that a judge be censured or impose other punishments.

In cases of extreme misconduct, the Judicial Council, the judiciary’s internal governing body, can refer a judge to Congress for impeachment. Ultimately, federal judges are appointed for life and can be ousted only by Congress.

Jeremy Fogel, a retired federal judge who consults with judges on ethics questions, said he did not believe the judges had engaged in misconduct. The judges’ comments in the article, he added, “described breaches of professional obligations by government lawyers” and “appear to have been directed to matters within their purview as judges rather than broader policy questions.”

A spokesman for The Times said, “Reporting by The New York Times on concerns among federal judges about the conduct of the Justice Department highlights the importance of public officials stepping up to shed light on governmental actions.”

“Seeking to punish or silence those who speak up to journalists about any administration’s agenda undercuts democratic accountability and the public’s right to know,” added the spokesman, Charlie Stadtlander.

The complaint escalates the long-simmering clash between the Trump administration and the district’s bench, which began when federal immigration agents poured into the Twin Cities last winter. It was aggravated by the killing of two Americans by federal agents, and pressure from the Justice Department to issue a warrant for the arrest of Don Lemon, the former cable news anchor.

In January, Judge Schiltz compiled a list of nearly 100 court orders that he said the Trump administration had violated in its effort to sweep up and deport hundreds of undocumented immigrants, including some who had lived in the United States for years. The Minnesota court was inundated with petitions from detainees asking the court to review the legality of their detention. During the first three months of 2025, the court fielded two of those petitions. Over the same period in 2026, it received 1,116 of them.

The Eighth Circuit was one of the few appeals courts to eventually rule in favor of the administration on the legality of its indefinite detention policy. That ruling has been appealed to the Supreme Court.

This is not the first time that the administration has tried to wield the judiciary’s internal disciplinary process against judges who have issued unfavorable rulings. The Justice Department also filed an ethics complaint against Judge James E. Boasberg over comments it claimed he made at a private meeting of judges. That complaint was dismissed earlier this year.

On Wednesday, Mr. Blanche drew a distinction between the criticism leveled against his department by judges and the public criticism he has leveled against them. He noted that he is not a judge and not bound by judicial ethics.

He then seemed to acknowledge the Justice Department had in fact violated orders from the Minnesota judges but said the orders should not have been issued in the first place.

“I’m allowed to get really fired up when, for example, judges in Minnesota complain about us violating court orders but the reason why, that we are, quote, violating court orders is because these judges are violating Supreme Court law, OK, in allowing these cases to be filed,” he said, apparently referring to a case that clarifies which courts have jurisdiction to hear detention challenges.

After sharply criticizing the Minnesota judges on Wednesday, Mr. Blanche added that the department has “total respect for the judiciary. There’s not a prosecutor in this country that should ever, ever violate a court order.”

Last year, Mr. Blanche railed against what he called “rogue judges” who were unfair to the administration.

“It’s a war, man,” Mr. Blanche said at a public event with conservative lawyers. “They have a robe on, but they are more political or certainly as political as the most liberal governor,” he said, adding, “There’s a group of judges that are repeat players, and that’s obviously not by happenstance, that’s intentional.”

ARTICLE

How Seating at Trump’s A.I. Luncheon Reveals Who Has the President’s Ear
A seating chart of the meeting illustrated growing divisions within the artificial intelligence industry and how it is viewed by the White House.
By Cecilia Kang
Published 2026-09-30 00:30 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/us/politics/trump-ai-luncheon-guests-ceos.html

There was room for 34 at the table, including the president. But the seating chart that Mr. Trump posted on social media illustrated growing divisions within the artificial intelligence industry and how it is viewed by the White House.

Some of the biggest proponents of aggressive regulation — including Dario Amodei of Anthropic — were relegated to the far reaches of the table, while Mr. Musk and Mr. Huang had prominent seats, with each man flanking Mr. Trump. The meeting also included top officials, such as Speaker Mike Johnson and Vice President JD Vance, who believe that formalized safeguards would hurt American competitiveness.

The seat assignment for Mr. Musk illustrated the billionaire’s mended relationship with the president after a monthslong public spat over their differences on policy earlier in the administration. And Mr. Huang is perhaps one of the most influential figures at the table, and a frequent visitor of the White House, whom the president has listened to on easing export controls of A.I. chips to China and the need to keep the industry free of regulations.

The next layer of influence included Jeff Bezos, the founder of Amazon, and Satya Nadella of Microsoft, who both sat across from the president. Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Sundar Pichai were also seated in the inner circle, one removed from Mr. Trump. These tech titans have invested tens of billions of dollars in developing A.I. models and data centers.

This A-squad of executives and their companies have also contributed millions of dollars to Mr. Trump’s inauguration and projects like the construction of the White House East Wing ballroom.

But the most notable seating assignment may belong to Dario Amodei of Anthropic, who has clashed with Mr. Trump’s anti-regulatory view of his industry. Mr. Amodei was seated near one end of the table, between two corporate leaders of tech companies and not next to any government officials. Mr. Amodei, who dined separately with Mr. Trump on Sunday, has warned that A.I. poses great existential risks and called for a global slowdown of development.

Far from Mr. Amodei was one of his biggest critics, David Sacks, the former senior adviser to Mr. Trump on A.I. Mr. Sacks has referred to Anthropic’s leadership as “doomers,” and while he is no longer in the administration, he continues to have the ear of Mr. Trump as a venture capitalist.

Most of the executives have been wary of strong regulations on A.I. But a series of security incidents in recent months have caused some to shift their stance. Mr. Huang remains the most strident against regulations and has said existing laws are sufficient to protect individuals. But Mr. Musk and Sam Altman of OpenAI, who did not attend the luncheon, recently agreed with Mr. Amodei that governments need to take a more active role in overseeing the technology and that the pace of development should slow.

The A.I. leaders did seem to find common ground. After the luncheon, they signed an accord promising to make their systems safe by committing to internal risk policies and outside audits.

The agreement, company insiders said, was table stakes.

SUMMARY

If there was something familiar about the voluntary safety guidelines that President Trump signed on Tuesday with the nation’s frontier artificial intelligence companies, this may be the reason: It closely echoed a previous agreement that President Joseph R. Biden Jr. struck with many of the same firms three years ago. ARTICLE

Trump’s Voluntary A.I. Policing Echoes What Biden Did. But Is It Enough Today?
President Trump’s plan to let A.I. companies police themselves comes amid mounting examples that they are failing to put safeguards on the technology.
By David E. Sanger
Published 2026-09-30 20:15 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/us/politics/trump-biden-ai.html

If there was something familiar about the voluntary safety guidelines that President Trump signed on Tuesday with the nation’s frontier artificial intelligence companies, this may be the reason: It closely echoed a previous agreement that President Joseph R. Biden Jr. struck with many of the same firms three years ago.

But the question now is whether the kind of voluntary framework that seemed plausible in 2023 is sufficient in 2026.

Back then, the central concept was the same: Since federal regulations could not keep up with the blistering pace of new A.I. models, the companies agreed to set up systems to monitor themselves, establishing layers of protection aimed at ensuring the technology would not be turned to nefarious purposes. The most commonly discussed scenario, for example, is that as A.I. enables biological breakthroughs, alarm bells will go off at the first whiff of evidence that the model is being hijacked to produce biological weapons.

“We must be cleareyed and vigilant about the threats emerging from emerging technologies that can pose — don’t have to, but can pose — to our democracy and our values,” Mr. Biden said in the Roosevelt Room at the White House in July 2023. “This is a serious responsibility.”

Mr. Trump essentially offered the same approach on Tuesday afternoon, after a luncheon with A.I. executives. “They’re really going to be policing each other,” he said outside the White House, as the leaders of Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta, Nvidia and SpaceX AI nodded in agreement.

After a summer of surprises — of A.I. agents escaping the “sandboxes” designed to contain them, hacking into other companies, and engaging in activities behind the backs of their creators — why would anyone think these protections are sufficient? The layered early-warning systems designed over the past few years have clearly failed, by the accounting of the companies themselves. New cases of A.I. agents behaving badly, or at least unpredictably, emerge on nearly a daily basis. Virtually all are after-the-fact discoveries, like the Louvre guards who woke up eight minutes too late to a brilliantly executed heist last year.

“We recognized in 2023 that voluntary pledges alone would not be enough, which is why President Biden followed up with an executive order,” one that Mr. Trump overrode after coming to office, noted Ben Buchanan, a Johns Hopkins professor who was one of the authors of the 2023 pledge.

“Given how fast A.I. capabilities have advanced, it’s even clearer now the federal government will need to act once again,” added Mr. Buchanan, who has consulted for Anthropic and other firms and is about to publish a book on the efforts to rein in A.I.

Mr. Biden’s order created a small unit inside the Commerce Department, called the U.S. Artificial Intelligence Safety Institute, to create standards for new A.I. models and to test the models before they are released. The institute has been renamed and has been a bit player in the current A.I. debates; Britain, for example, has a far larger and more powerful institution playing that role.

It is hard to find another industry with so much potential to do harm as well as good that the government believes can regulate itself. After all, pharmaceutical companies are not permitted to approve their own drugs — that is why there is a Food and Drug Administration. Boeing cannot certify its own planes as flight-ready. And when OpenAI and Anthropic want to build new data centers — suddenly one of the most contentious issues of the midterm elections — they need to get more government approvals than they do for the new A.I. models that the centers’ computing power will be helping create.

In one respect, the Trump accord goes beyond the Biden one: The companies committed to embedding outside experts in their development process, with the power to blow the whistle if they see something going awry.

The idea is based on the International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors who visit nuclear sites, though those inspectors are chosen from countries around the world. It is a concept that has been around for a while, and was included in the essay Dario Amodei, one of the founders of Anthropic, wrote in recent weeks as he argued for slowing the pace of development until the industry had rogue A.I. agents under control.

As Anthropic heads toward an initial public offering that many on Wall Street expect to value the company in excess of $2 trillion — approaching the G.D.P. of Canada — the Trump administration is doubling down on the argument that regulation is simply an invitation for China to exceed the United States.

Advocates for shaping this surging technology with a light government hand celebrated the White House accord on Tuesday.

David Sacks, who was Mr. Trump’s A.I. czar until he left the White House early this year, ranked among the most enthusiastic.

“Only President Trump could convene all the leaders of the top companies developing chips, data centers and frontier models for Super Intelligence,” Mr. Sacks wrote later on social media, adopting Mr. Trump’s term for the technology, an attempt to rebrand it to sound more powerful, yet more under human control.

Mr. Sacks, who was sitting close to the center of the table for the luncheon that the president hosted for the A.I. leaders, said the agreement came down to one concept: that the frontier firms are “accepting responsibility for the safe development of their products and imposing new internal controls and external audits. This is far better than waiting years for some international agreement that would probably never happen.”

It is not yet clear that the firms are truly accepting responsibility for A.I. agents that go rogue, hacking into systems or sending misleading messages. But OpenAI did terminate work in recent days on a new model — called GPT-6.1 Astra — when it showed high levels of what the company labels as deception, covering up its actions.

“For anything regarding safety and alignment, there’s a trade-off,” Saachi Jain, the head of safety systems at OpenAI, said when the decision was announced.

OpenAI decided to take the cautious route. Presumably, every one of its competitors is struggling with the same issue.

On his second point — about how long it would take to secure international agreements — Mr. Sacks is undoubtedly right. When President Xi Jinping of China was in Washington last week for a state visit, the only concrete agreement on A.I. that emerged was a plan to convene experts from both countries — the two that dominate the field — to begin a conversation on mutual safety steps.

That decision also had its roots in the Biden White House, which took about 18 months to get Beijing to agree on what seems like a pretty obvious baby step: a single sentence declaring that any decision to employ nuclear weapons should be made by humans, not by artificial intelligence.

Mr. Xi built on that statement at the White House last week. Speaking in the Grand Foyer, he said that it was critical to “develop and manage A.I. for good and ensure that the development of A.I. is always under human control.” Mr. Trump has often repeated the first part, but he leaves out “under human control,” which worries those who fear the Pentagon is quickly moving toward fully autonomous weapons with weakened human oversight.

Mr. Trump clearly does not want to talk about autonomous weapons, or dwell on the recent cases of A.I. gone wrong. Last week he was still calling revelations of miscreant A.I. agents a “HOAX” being exploited by his political opponents.

On Tuesday, he dwelled at length on his effort to mandate use of the term “Super Intelligence,” as if changing the term will ameliorate the problem.

“This is going to be all for the good, and we’re going to have it be nice and safe,” Mr. Trump said.

While the accord was voluntary, he insisted, “it’s morally binding.”

The executives who came to the lunch yesterday, many of whom are already taking the steps outlined in the voluntary accord, say they agree they have a moral responsibility to get this right. But as they have learned to their shock in recent months, the technology is not entirely under their control. Whether the accord is morally binding on the rogue A.I. agents is yet to be determined.

Agents have typically been seated during the document checks, which are the first layer of the security screening process. Typically, T.S.A. agents rotate through a number of stations during an eight-hour shift, including identity document checks, divestiture and collection of belongings, and baggage screening, a T.S.A. spokesman said.

ARTICLE

T.S.A. Agents Are Told to Get on Their Feet During Airport ID Checks
The agency said that requiring agents to stand while examining documents was a “welcome change.” The union representing them was less welcoming.
By Christine Hauser
Published 2026-09-30 20:43 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/us/tsa-airports-standing.html

The next time you hand over your Real ID to be checked at the airport, the Transportation Security Administration agent who examines it might be standing rather than sitting.

The T.S.A. ordered that change recently in the hope that it will result in a more attentive and hospitable experience for travelers during the airport screening process. But the agency is receiving resistance from the union that represents more than 45,000 agents.

The T.S.A., which is responsible for screening passengers and baggage at 450 commercial airports across the United States, made the decision last week.

“T.S.A. officers performing the travel document checker role are the first to interact with the traveling public,” the T.S.A. said in a statement on Wednesday. “This welcome change reinforces both our security posture and our commitment to hospitality by having these officers on their feet and alert.”

The agency said officers must meet “fitness for duty requirements to be capable of performing their vital national security function while simultaneously creating a welcoming and professional environment for travelers.”

Council 100 of the American Federation of Government Employees, the union that represents T.S.A. agents across the country, has pushed back on the move.

It said in a statement this week that it had not been consulted about the decision to “remove all chairs” at the travel document checker positions where agents check passenger IDs.

“These chairs serve as basic ergonomic and safety support for officers that stand and walk on hard surfaces all day,” the union said.

The union said it was “moving aggressively to address this matter,” and urged its members to contact representatives in Congress to express their concern.

Agents have typically been seated during the document checks, which are the first layer of the security screening process. Duties at other stations, such as monitoring and instructing passengers as they place belongings in the bins to be screened, and at the end when they collect them again, require agents to stand.

The order will not affect agents who operate and monitor carry-on baggage scanners who may continue to be seated. Agents also get short rest breaks and meal breaks during their shift.

Typically, T.S.A. agents rotate through a number of stations during an eight-hour shift, including identity document checks, divestiture and collection of belongings, and baggage screening, a T.S.A. spokesman said.

It was not immediately clear whether the new guidelines on standing at identity checkpoints would contribute to the other measures that have been taken to ease the long wait times that plague passengers.

In 2025, the T.S.A. lifted its requirement that travelers remove their shoes. Airports have also been trying to implement changes to passenger and luggage screening with remote check-in points, and a “Touchless ID” program that provides a dedicated line for those allowing their identities to be verified through facial recognition.

Earlier this year, agents worked more than six weeks without pay during the government shutdown. As salaries went unpaid, hundreds of agents quit or called out of work, and long lines throttled the flow of passenger screenings at some of the nation’s busiest airports. By the end of March, most of the T.S.A.’s agents began receiving back pay, easing some of the chaos.

A man shot three co-workers at a Virginia equipment rental business on Wednesday, killing two of them, before fatally shooting himself after a standoff with the police, the authorities said.

The Manassas City Police Department received a call at 7:11 a.m. reporting a shooting at a United Rentals location in Manassas, Va., about 30 miles southwest of Washington, Douglas Keen, the department’s chief, said at a news conference. All three people who were shot were taken to nearby hospitals. Two of them, Richard Lamont, 48, and Christopher Serrano, 33, died. The third victim, whose name was not released, was in stable condition, according to a statement from the Virginia State Police.

By about 8:20 a.m., investigators had identified the gunman and begun searching for his silver Toyota Camry. A state trooper spotted the vehicle heading south on Interstate 81, Chief Keen said.

After a police pursuit, Mr. Grant stopped and got out of the car, the state police said. A negotiator was brought in to try to persuade him to surrender, but he shot himself at 10:30 a.m., the state police said.

Mr. Grant was taken to a hospital, where he died.

“We’ve got to figure out what happened here and what caused this,” Chief Keen said, adding, “Our community is still hurting, the family of United Rentals is still hurting, the families of the victims are still hurting.”
