ARTICLE

She Says Vaccines Killed Her Twins. The Authorities Say She Did.
In a small Idaho town, a young mother is accused of killing her young twins. She blames the childhood vaccines they received.
By Lisa Miller
Published 2026-09-30 13:18 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/well/andrea-shaw-twins-suffocation-vaccines.html

Andrea Shaw has spent most of the summer alone in a cell in Payette, Idaho, taking comfort from photos of her family, according to her lawyer. Her twins were 18 months old when they died, in May 2025, and her living daughter is three months old. She can talk to her husband, Nate, and the baby only by phone or video chat, which she does several times a day. As she waits for her lawyer to drive up from Boise, she reads inspirational books such as “Tuesdays With Morrie.”

Shaw, 23, is charged with the smothering murder of the twins — Tyson, a boy, and Dallas, a girl — in the middle of the night, in the bed that they shared. At trial, scheduled for January, evidence will show that “the only conceivable explanation” for their deaths is that she suffocated them, the Payette County prosecutor Mike Duke wrote in a court filing. Shaw has pleaded not guilty.

Joe Filicetti, Shaw’s lawyer, describes Shaw as “sweet.” In court, in her red-and-white striped uniform, she mostly comes across as young. The Shaw case, grim as it is, might have been a purely local story except for the extraordinary attention it has received from the captains of the nation’s vaccine-skeptical movement. Three days after their twins died, Andrea and Nate Shaw appeared on a video podcast produced by Children’s Health Defense, the anti-vaccine group founded by Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

Looking stricken, the couple told their version of events. The twins had been preemies, Shaw said, and had required intensive medical care. She inoculated them on the recommended schedule without ill effects. But in April 2025, after receiving the D-tap, flu and hepatitis A shots, the toddlers got sick, and when she sought help, clinicians repeatedly dismissed her concerns, she said.

“I wish I was anti-vaccine now,” Shaw concluded, with a wry chuckle.

Shaw was indicted by a grand jury more than a year after the deaths of her children. During that interval, in January, 2026, she became the lead plaintiff in a federal lawsuit filed by Children’s Health Defense against the American Academy of Pediatrics. (“I don’t understand where they come up with these plaintiffs,” said Richard Sauber, the attorney who represents the academy in this case, when reached for comment.) That suit claims that the nation’s pediatricians defrauded American families by colluding with pharmaceutical makers to spread misinformation about the safety of vaccines.

The Vaccine Safety Research Foundation, established in 2021 by Steve Kirsch, the Silicon Valley tech entrepreneur, to “tell the truth about vaccines,” as he put it in an interview, is working “in conjunction” with Children’s Health Defense to help support Shaw and her family. (Children’s Health Defense did not respond to a request for comment.) Documents in the court file make a terse reference to the law firm of Aaron Siri, a Kennedy ally and prominent vaccine critic. Siri wrote in an email, “We do not represent Ms. Shaw with regard to her criminal proceedings.”

Kirsch described his motivation. “When you hear of a case which is 100 percent consistent with a vaccine injury and is not at all consistent with a mother who is killing her kids, you have an ethical obligation to come to the mother’s aid,” he said. He added that if a single shred of evidence pointed to murder, he would “be out of there in a heartbeat.”

Filicetti began representing Shaw the day after the twins’ deaths. He doesn’t remember who first called him, he said, but in 2023, he had met some of the players in the vaccine-hesitant world at a Children’s Health Defense conference in Georgia. Filicetti has a solo practice in Boise, with a focus on defending Idaho police accused of crimes and misdeeds. In the Shaw case, he consults with the high profile advocacy groups. “They all want to give input,” Filicetti said in an interview. “I take any help I can get from anybody.”

Having received almost “every vaccine, including the shingles vaccine,” he said, he does not consider himself a vaccine denier. But during the Covid outbreak, he questioned the lethality of the novel virus and the efficacy of the new vaccine. He viewed government mandates as an overreach.

A believer in alternative therapies — in massage, dopamine patches, cold plunges and therapeutic ketamine for trauma — Filicetti declined the Covid shot. Instead, he treated his Covid symptoms with a 30-day water fast, as well as “ivermectin, hydroxychloroquine, and I went to a naturopath who flooded me with ozone,” he told me. “I came out of that healthier than I’ve ever been in my life,” he said. Existing as he does at the nexus of libertarian politics and the crunchy lifestyle of Boise, Filicetti gained a reputation for defending vaccine refusers.

In my conversations with him, Filicetti stressed Shaw’s vulnerability, portraying her as a young, naïve mother who is unjustly accused, has lost her twin toddlers and is separated from her newborn. His sole focus, he told me, is to “keep my client from being wrongly convicted and then receiving the death penalty for something she did not do.” At trial, his only burden will be to show that the state did not prove their case beyond a reasonable doubt, and in this case, “vaccines were a factor,” he said. In Payette, the “number of people who did not get vaccinated or are vaccine hesitant is high,” and those skeptics will be in the jury pool.

Filicetti is not out to set vaccine policy, he said. But he does have strong views about the way vaccines are debated in the public sphere. The pro-vaccine faithful are too absolutist, Filicetti told me. “When science becomes unquestionable, it becomes a religion,” he said. “They’re just saying, ‘Fall in line.’”

Filicetti sent Shaw “Tuesdays With Morrie” and other uplifting books. He also arranges frequent sessions for her with a trauma therapist specializing in E.M.D.R., or eye movement desensitization and reprocessing, which can be conducted through a glass barrier.

The next hearing is scheduled for Oct. 15. “It’s super important for me to keep her emotionally and spiritually healthy,” he said.

Andrea Shaw made the 911 call on Thursday morning, May 1, 2025. At the time, she lived with Nate and the twins at the Northgate trailer park, at the edge of town. Northgate is known locally as the Stepford Wives trailer park because the 65 homes there all look the same, like whitewashed barracks. The dispatcher told her to wait outside.

The police arrived at around 11:30. The park’s manager, Kathy Killkenney, a sharp-eyed 82-year-old, sits in an office at the entrance collecting rent checks. That day, observing all the emergency vehicles, she decided to stay in her office, she told me when I stopped in to see her in September.

“Nobody asked you,” she said to herself that morning. “And the police are going to do an investigation. Just leave them alone.”

Instead, she called Nate at work, according to his account on the Children’s Health Defense podcast. “‘What’s going on?’” she asked him. “‘The police have taped up your trailer.’” Nate said he did not know. He repeatedly called Andrea, who did not answer, and when he called his mother, a police officer picked up the phone. The officer said, “‘Hey, I hate to inform you but your kids are dead,’” Nate recalled. “I was like, ‘You’re lying. You’re not telling me the truth. This isn’t happening.’”

Andrea described peeking in on the twins earlier that morning and thinking they were asleep. When she went to wake them up later, she said, she touched Tyson and he was cold.

“The way I saw them, they looked as if they had gone in their sleep. They were in their sleeping positions. I think it’s called rigor mortis,” she said on the podcast.

According to the prosecutor, Shaw changed her story several times under police questioning. Duke summarized Shaw’s interview at a July hearing: She had been out late with a friend the night before; first she said she had gotten up with the twins at around 8 that morning and fed them breakfast; later she said that wasn’t true. On the other hand, Nate’s account was consistent, Duke said: He had been sleeping the whole time. Duke did not respond to requests for comment.

For her part, Andrea said the police had gotten into her head and made her feel crazy. They said that “I had supposedly had a postpartum, overwhelming blackout and done it to my children,” she said on the podcast.

In the podcast interview, Andrea appeared stunned. Nate looked tense and chewed his lip. Encouraged by the interviewer, they recounted the events of the previous week. On April 23, Andrea and Wendy Shaw, Nate’s mother, had brought Dallas and Tyson to Snake River Pediatrics for their 18-month well-child checkup. Both women had expressed caution about the flu vaccine, Andrea recalled: Nate and other members of the Shaw family were reactive to it. The nurse practitioner was dismissive of these concerns, Andrea said, and Andrea consented to the shot. (Snake River Pediatrics did not return requests for comment.)

The following day, both children were passing a greenish diarrhea and had a blue cast to their lips, and they were lethargic, according to Andrea. Alarmed, she took them to the emergency room at St. Luke’s in Fruitland, Idaho, in the company of her mother-in-law. After assessing them and giving them Tylenol and ice pops, the doctor sent them home.

In medical records provided to The New York Times by Children’s Health Defense, the E.R. physician remarked that the children had not seemed to be in any danger. They were diagnosed with “post-immunization reaction,” and he noted, further, that Andrea “seemed satisfied with their visit.” According to Duke, postmortem tests had showed that one twin had a rotavirus infection, transmitted from feces to mouth and extremely contagious. Multiple physicians I spoke with explained that rotavirus is rarely fatal but can become so if children are not vaccinated against it in infancy, or if they are inadequately hydrated. (The children were making wet diapers, the hospital notes said. Whether they had been vaccinated is not known.)

According to Andrea, the toddlers continued to have “severe” diarrhea. On the morning of April 30, she called Snake River to see if she could get an appointment, but they were backed up. That was the final day of the twins’ lives. In the Children’s Health Defense interview Andrea said they had started to recover that day and were “great” — eating, talking and drinking from their sippy cups.

Angela Wulbrecht was in touch with the Shaws within days of the twins’ deaths. A nurse who worked for 17 years at a hospital in Marin County, Calif., caring for mothers and babies, Wulbrecht is on the board of Kirsch’s Vaccine Safety Research Foundation. For her whole career, she had been an avid vaccine proponent, she said in a joint interview with Kirsch. But she said she had suffered an adverse reaction to the Covid vaccine and over time became a skeptic. “I didn’t know, when I went and got my Covid shot and 12 minutes later I almost died, that there would be no help for me. There was no recourse, nobody to sue,” Wulbrecht said.

Now, helping families like the Shaws “is my passion,” Wulbrecht said. People harmed by vaccines are “distraught,” she said, “and they need guidance.” She wouldn’t speak about the Shaw case, but said she often meets families who post what happened to them on Facebook.

“All of a sudden I’ll get tagged,” she said. “People know me. So they’ll start saying, ‘Contact Angela.’” Wulbrecht estimates she has helped about 1,000 families since starting this work. Her Facebook page recently included selfies of her with Kennedy at public events.

In the time between the deaths of the twins and her arrest, Shaw became pregnant again. When Shaw worried that the fetus was too small, Wulbrecht reviewed her test results and reassured her by text. “I have a feeling everything is going to be just fine,” she wrote.

Shaw was charged with two counts of murder on June 29. Initially the judge set her bail at $2 million. But when Filicetti requested a bond reduction, citing the best interests of the mother and her newborn daughter, Duke responded with ferocity. His experts had considered explanations other than murder, he said. They had looked at poisoning and considered the temperature in the bedroom, which frequently surpassed 100 degrees. They had ruled out both possibilities.

A forensic pathologist excluded vaccines as the cause of death. “This is not a vaccine case,” Duke said in court.

According to the autopsy report, both children had pulmonary vascular congestion, or a buildup of blood and fluid in the blood vessels of the lungs, he wrote. Tyson had pulmonary edema, a more severe buildup, as well.

“According to our expert, these symptoms are consistent with being smothered. They occur when something blocks air from entering the airways, and as the diaphragm expands, it creates a low pressure condition in the lungs and airways,” he wrote. “This is the cause of death of the twins. It is also the only reasonable explanation for why both would die at the same time, on the same night, in the same room, in the same bed.”

While Shaw enjoys the presumption of innocence, Duke continued, he had to consider the risk presented to the defendant’s infant daughter. Judge Kiley Stuchlik agreed. Instead of reducing Shaw’s bond, she revoked it.

For Duke to prevail, a jury in Payette needs to conclude beyond a reasonable doubt that Andrea Shaw murdered her children. But in Idaho, doubt about doctors and medications, and especially vaccines, has long been a way of life.

Until the deaths of Tyson and Dallas, Andrea and Nate Shaw were not known for anything much. Andrea moved in with Nate’s family when she was 17, during Covid. She “has no criminal record of any kind — not even a speeding or parking ticket,” according to a filing by Filicetti. In high school, Nate liked working on engines and was an active member of FFA (formerly Future Farmers of America), his teacher Tyson Smith said in an interview. Tyson, the boy twin, was named after him.

In Payette, a town of 8,800, Shaw’s claim that vaccines harmed her children is seen as unremarkable. Childhood vaccination rates in Idaho are 68.9 percent, well below the state goal of 79.5, and declining. Bryon Hemphill, a family doctor I spoke to, said that in his rural clinic in Payette, “I don’t know that we are reaching 30” percent.

In a conversation in his office on a bright September day, Hemphill pondered the causes of this deep reluctance. In general, people don’t go to the doctor in Payette, he said. That’s in part because Idaho has fewer doctors per capita than most other states, and Payette has fewer than the Idaho average.

But neither conventional medicine nor the insurance companies have made wellness, or prevention, a priority. Patients drive to the doctors’ office only when they are ill. Since Covid, he said, they often arrive with their own theories about why.

In his practice, Hemphill confronts what he calls “an epistemological problem,” he said. As he experiences it, the vaccine debate boils down to warring truths, in which “truth is what you think it is. It’s your perception. There’s this element of, ‘It’s my truth.’”

Faced with such strong hesitancy, Hemphill knows better than to push too hard. Instead, he tries to engage his patients in a conversation about risk. The chance of dying from a vaccine is far smaller than that of dying from the disease it’s designed to prevent, he’ll explain. Symptoms after vaccination indicate that the vaccine is working, he’ll sometimes add.

But he doesn’t insist. It is not his role, he told me, to tell his patients what to do. “That can come across as judgmental.”

In July, days after Shaw’s arrest, Kirsch, the tech entrepreneur, sent the prosecutor’s office an email. Kirsch doesn’t usually delve into the nitty-gritty of individual vaccine-injury claims and said he has never been to Payette. But he spoke to Shaw after the deaths of her children, and he believes this case could change the national conversation. It could “break this acceptance of, ‘all vaccines are safe.’”

Kirsch wanted Duke to see a 2004 study, based on research from the 1980s, by a retired micropaleontologist that purported to show a correlation between childhood vaccination and respiratory distress and deaths otherwise attributed to SIDS or shaken baby syndrome.

“If a jury understands science, unless you have a witness to the suffocation (which you don’t have), this creates reasonable doubt,” he wrote to the prosecutor, using boldface type.

The prosecutor did not respond to his note, Kirsch told me. “They never do,” he said.

Christina Jewett contributed reporting. Kitty Bennett, Alain Delaquérière, Georgia Gee, Sheelagh McNeill and Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

SUMMARY

The United States and the Soviet Union were jockeying desperately for advantage during the Cold War arms race. With shared information, “Because OpenAI knows that they’re going to get caught speeding up, that Anthropic is going to speed up in response, that they’re going to start an arms race or an A.I. race — that itself can stop them from racing past the safety threshold,” Professor Koh said. The voluntary agreement signed this week may help the leading U.S. companies agree on where the safety threshold is, and whether existing capabilities have crossed it already, he said.

ARTICLE

A Way Out of the A.I. Arms Race?
New research points to how the world could stop short of the brink of disaster. Even with the agreement signed at the White House by tech leaders, it won’t be easy.
By Amanda Taub
Published 2026-09-30 09:04 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/world/europe/ai-arms-race.html

Over the course of two harrowing weeks in October 1962, the world came within an eyelash of nuclear Armageddon.

The United States and the Soviet Union were jockeying desperately for advantage during the Cold War arms race. After the United States stationed intermediate-range nuclear missiles in Italy and Turkey, the Soviets, fearing a first strike, sought to station their own nuclear weapons in Cuba. The tense two-week standoff that ensued, the Cuban Missile Crisis, nearly escalated into nuclear war.

But it didn’t. Not only did the parties step back from the brink, the crisis proved to be a turning point in the Cold War itself.

That brush with calamity changed the thinking of leaders on both sides, said William Wohlforth, a political scientist at Dartmouth who studies national security and international relations. “Right away we got the hotline agreement, so we could talk to each other. We began to work toward the testing agreement. And slowly, in the subsequent years we got a big, complex bilateral arms-control process.”

The United States and the Soviet Union remained bitter enemies. But on one point of shared interest — not obliterating humanity — they could work together.

Today experts in the artificial intelligence industry are sounding alarms that A.I. companies, and the countries where they are based, are locked in their own kind of arms race. The consequences, many believe, could be as disastrous as the nuclear war that President John F. Kennedy and the Soviet leader, Nikita Khrushchev, narrowly avoided.

There are important differences, of course. Artificial intelligence models are not atomic bombs, even if they can be turned to military uses. Catastrophic A.I. risks remain seemingly more speculative than the specter of nuclear war was in the 1960s. And companies seeking a market advantage are not the same as superpowers fighting for global supremacy, even if the United States and China are vying for the upper hand of the new technology and the broad global advantages it could bring.

But at its core, the A.I. competition points to the same question that loomed over the Cold War: How can adversaries cooperate on keeping the world safe, even as they compete for economic and geopolitical dominance?

A new working paper by Drew Fudenberg, an economics professor at M.I.T. who is a leading game theorist, and Andrew Koh, an economics professor at Columbia University and a research scientist at Google DeepMind, suggests a possible way to slow the A.I. arms race to a safer pace.

It would require the players in the competition, both companies and governments, to share good information about their advances, and to agree on where danger actually begins.

Despite the voluntary agreement signed by tech leaders at the White House on Tuesday, neither condition is currently being met, and the number and variety of players may make it challenging to do so. But the paper suggests what could be possible.

The Safety Game

Professors Koh and Fudenberg start from a simple premise: Everyone has an interest in averting catastrophe, no matter how self-interested they may be.

At the same time, they argue, the major players in the A.I. industry are under strong incentives to compete for dominance. The companies want the market share and billions of investment dollars that the most advanced models will bring. Governments want the economic benefits of A.I. and also access to advanced models for their own purposes.

Those competitive pressures spur the players to race dangerously toward the brink of disaster, where many worry that rogue A.I. agents could, for instance, bring down government or financial systems, sabotage vital infrastructure or launch a biological attack.

Professors Koh and Fudenberg suggest that if the competitors were to share information — on their technological progress and how close they are to the edge of the safety frontier — those incentives would change.

If the players, including companies like OpenAI and Anthropic, can see that no one is racing into dangerous territory, they will have less motivation to do so themselves, the paper reasons.

Conversely, players will also know that if they do race into danger, their competitors will see and likely do the same, creating an intolerable level of risk for everyone.

With shared information, “Because OpenAI knows that they’re going to get caught speeding up, that Anthropic is going to speed up in response, that they’re going to start an arms race or an A.I. race — that itself can stop them from racing past the safety threshold,” Professor Koh said.

He compared the scenario to “second strike” capabilities during the Cold War. Both the United States and the Soviet Union built weapons that would allow them to strike back in the event of a nuclear attack.

“One reason to not attack first is that I know that if my opponent has a second strike capability, we are just going to destroy the world,” Professor Koh said. “And that itself would have prevented first strikes.”

The same logic, he says, could hold true for A.I.

To Trust, Verify

Right now, that sharing is not happening.

Companies like Anthropic and OpenAI develop their most advanced A.I. models behind closed doors, so the companies must guess at each other’s progress. But if the companies accepted outside monitors who could disclose vital safety and progress information, that would help establish trust. There is already evidence that some of the biggest players in A.I. would be willing to go that route.

Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, called in a recent essay for A.I. companies to accept embedded independent safety monitors, and said his company would unilaterally agree to do so.

“Dario is right,” Elon Musk, who runs an A.I. venture within his company SpaceX, wrote on X in response to Mr. Amodei’s essay. Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, did the same.

Chinese companies have not supported the plan, but there are signs that they, too, are starting to take the need for outside monitoring seriously, said Jeffrey Ding, a political scientist at George Washington University who researches U.S.-Chinese competition around emerging technology.

For example, Moonshot, a Chinese company, recently submitted a new model to the United Kingdom’s A.I. Security Institute for review.

At the moment, that kind of safety vetting is voluntary and inconsistent, but it could be systematized.

Such a regime would potentially be similar to arms control treaties that included monitoring and inspection requirements to ensure compliance.

But there are important questions about whether governments themselves would embrace it and, short of that, whether voluntary self-policing by a small group of entrepreneurs and their investors with billions on the line would be stable and transparent enough to ensure safety.

Mr. Trump wants a hands-off approach by the government. Among those he convened at the White House on Tuesday were Mr. Amodei, as well as the leaders of Google, Meta, Nvidia, OpenAI and SpaceXAI.

The agreement they signed expressed support for third-party monitoring of risks, but it did not appear to impose any concrete obligations. Mr. Trump said he thought the agreement would be “morally binding.”

“And they’re really going to be policing each other,” Mr. Trump said, “and that’s the way it works.”

Though a step in the right direction, Professor Koh said the agreement is unlikely to solve the current incentives problem. It does not include transparency about companies’ internal capabilities and leaves open the question of U.S.-China competition.

The Blurry Brink

In the Cold War, the danger of nuclear weapons was clear and concrete. The world had seen their terrifying power in Hiroshima and Nagasaki. There was no doubt that the superpowers could eliminate any city at the touch of a button — potentially touching off a war that could end life on earth.

For the moment, A.I. isn’t like that, and not all agree on where the brink of catastrophe actually lies. A.I. doomsday scenarios seem the stuff of science fiction to many.

Even for experts, developers and policymakers there is wide disagreement on the risks and how fast they are approaching. That matters, because those who believe the danger threshold is far away lack incentive to slow down, even if there is sharing of information.

Some employees of leading A.I. companies argue that the technology has a significant chance of killing all humans within the next decade.

Others tend to see the risks as coming from negligence and ineptitude by A.I. companies, and a failure of other industries to harden their defenses against A.I.-powered tools.

Then there are the A.I. evangelists, President Trump among them. Those who are calling for guardrails, he said, are “bringing up things that won’t happen.” He has made clear that he considers A.I. a winner-take-all game.

Mr. Trump’s own motivations are not exactly the stuff of Cold War realpolitik. They have variously been reported as a desire for American dominance, keeping the stock market and economy afloat as an election approaches and enriching his family’s investment portfolio.

All of those things add an extra layer of unpredictability, as does the Chinese government’s stance.

Beijing is unlikely to agree to any monitoring regime that threatens its ability to catch up to the United States, which it currently trails in A.I. technology. For now, Mr. Ding said, it seems to see A.I. risks primarily through the lens of Communist Party control — maintaining the censorship regime — while defending against hostile forces like the United States and encouraging economic growth.

This range of disagreement over the A.I. threat poses a problem for coordination on safety, Professor Koh said. The voluntary agreement signed this week may help the leading U.S. companies agree on where the safety threshold is, and whether existing capabilities have crossed it already, he said. But it is nonbinding and limited to just a few companies.

The only way to get more agreement may be to encounter unambiguous lessons of the risks, he said. That, after all, is what happened when the Cuban Missile Crisis drove home the real risk of a nuclear holocaust.

But the secrecy around the industry continues to obscure lessons of the potential dangers. The recent revelation that OpenAI agents hacked Australian government servers was made public only this month though the breach happened in June.

The race continued all the while, with companies making unknown improvements to their agents’ skills and intelligence, and heightening fears that the agents could become self-interested players themselves.

If that happens, “the models will likely convince people that everything is fine,” Daniel Selsam, an OpenAI researcher, wrote in a recent essay. “Moreover, they will eloquently explain how aligned they are, discuss the nuances of human values and ethics, and argue convincingly that humans should trust them with power.”

SUMMARY

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel said a pilot tried to seize control of a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday, stabbing the other pilot. Passengers and crew members charged the cockpit and subdued the assailant, with crew members making an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. According to Mr. Netanyahu, one of the pilots attacked the other midair in a possible attempt to crash the plane, FlyDubai Flight 1073.

ARTICLE

What to Know About FlyDubai Flight Diverted After Clash Between Pilots
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel said one pilot stabbed another and may have attempted to crash the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv. The plane landed in Saudi Arabia and all passengers were safe.
By Leo Sands
Published 2026-09-30 14:33 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/world/middleeast/flydubai-dubai-israel-flight-diverted.html

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel said a pilot tried to seize control of a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday, stabbing the other pilot. Passengers and crew members charged the cockpit and subdued the assailant, with crew members making an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

According to Mr. Netanyahu, one of the pilots attacked the other midair in a possible attempt to crash the plane, FlyDubai Flight 1073. He said a passenger and member of the crew broke into the cockpit to “neutralize” the pilot-assailant, while another crew member stabilized the plane. The flight suddenly plunged thousands of feet and made an emergency landing at an airport in Tabuk, in northwestern Saudi Arabia.

Israeli officials said the plane was carrying between 160 and 180 passengers. FlyDubai said the passengers were all safe and accounted for. The flight’s pilot and co-pilot were treated in a hospital for injuries, according to the airport in Tabuk. The Saudi authorities arrested the suspected assailant, Mr. Netanyahu said.

Much of what happened aboard the flight remained unclear, including the cause of the sudden altitude loss and any possible motive.

What happened?

- Mr. Netanyahu said in a video statement that one of the pilots aboard the FlyDubai flight “stabbed the other pilot and apparently tried to crash the plane,” in what appears to have been a failed attempted hijacking. Other crew members and a passenger retook control of the cockpit and landed the plane in Tabuk, Mr. Netanyahu said.
- FlyDubai Flight 1073 plunged dramatically as it was flying over Saudi Arabia near the border with Jordan at around 8:20 a.m. local time on Wednesday morning, according to testimony from passengers and data from FlightRadar24, a flight tracking service. The flight had taken off from Dubai a little over two hours earlier.
- Officials have not publicly shared any information about the assailant’s possible motive. According to two Israeli security officials who spoke on condition of anonymity in accordance with government protocol, the Israeli authorities are investigating the possibility that the altercation was an attempted attack on Israelis, among other lines of inquiry.

What have passengers said?

- Passengers described a scene of chaos in the cabin as the aircraft lost altitude, fearing that the plane, a Boeing 737 Max 8, could crash. The aircraft dropped by around 17,000 feet in two minutes, according to FlightRadar24.
- According to accounts from passengers, the fight that broke out in the cockpit left at least one pilot seriously injured. Those aboard the flight said passengers intervened to subdue the assailant.
- A graphic social media video verified by The New York Times showed three men tending to two injured men on the floor of the cabin, both of whom appeared to be bleeding, while another bloodied man asks for help. At least one of the injured men on the floor wore what appeared to be a FlyDubai pilot uniform.

What have the aviation authorities said?

- FlyDubai said that crew members who were on duty on the flight secured the aircraft. According to the airport in Tabuk, the flight made an emergency landing at 9:45 a.m. local time.
- The pilot and co-pilot were treated in a hospital for injuries, the airport said, but it did not provide further details.
- The airline said it had sent two replacement aircraft to Tabuk to collect the passengers and crew and take them to Tel Aviv.

flydubai-israel-dubai-flight-pilots-attack.html

SUMMARY

Passengers on a morning flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv recounted scenes of panic and terror on Wednesday as their aircraft suddenly plunged thousands of feet while screams for help came from behind the cockpit door. What began as a routine flight turned terrifying when a violent altercation broke out inside the cockpit in midair. Several rushed into the cockpit and subdued an attacker before two off-duty pilots helped steer the aircraft to a safe emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

ARTICLE

Panic and Heroics on FlyDubai Flight: ‘We Felt That This Was It’
A routine flight turned terrifying when a violent altercation broke out inside the cockpit and the aircraft dropped 17,000 feet in two minutes. Passengers subdued a knife-wielding attacker.
By Karla Adam, Aaron Boxerman and Natan Odenheimer
Published 2026-09-30 15:45 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/world/middleeast/flydubai-israel-dubai-flight-pilots-attack.html

Passengers on a morning flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv recounted scenes of panic and terror on Wednesday as their aircraft suddenly plunged thousands of feet while screams for help came from behind the cockpit door.

What began as a routine flight turned terrifying when a violent altercation broke out inside the cockpit in midair. Passengers described a desperate scramble inside the cabin as travelers realized the plane was out of control. Several rushed into the cockpit and subdued an attacker before two off-duty pilots helped steer the aircraft to a safe emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

“Within a few minutes, our plane completely lost control, and we felt that this was it — we were about to crash,” one passenger, Miriam Ohayon, told Israel’s I24 News, a television channel. “We heard screams on the plane, and when they opened the cockpit, there was a lot of blood.”

She recalled reciting a Jewish prayer often said in times of distress as the plane jolted through the air.

The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said the attacker was one of the pilots, and Almog Itali, a passenger on the flight, told the BBC that there were two pilots in the cockpit and that “one stabbed the other.” He said that two off duty-pilots on the plane, one of whom was British, helped to land the aircraft after the altercation.

The incident began about two hours after takeoff when a passenger returning from the bathroom saw a struggle inside the cockpit and alerted passengers, Ms. Ohayon reported to her mother, Yasmin Ohayon-Abukasis.

Speaking to reporters at Ben Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv, Ms. Ohayon-Abukasis said her daughter had told her that the pilot had yelled “help, help, help” and that he was being attacked by a man with a knife.

Ms. Ohayon-Abukasis said her daughter had said that passengers had subdued the attacker and that a nurse and doctor on board provided initial medical care to the pilot.

Hila Gaier, who was on the flight, said that when the plane dived passengers couldn’t move. “You were sucked downward,” she told Kan, Israel’s public broadcaster. She said she was flying with her partner and two daughters. “I embraced them, told them I loved them, and we tried to practice breathing exercises,” she said.

Flight-tracking data from Flightradar24 showed Flight 1073 descended more than 17,000 feet in less than two minutes. “The plane kept stabilizing and then dropping again for several long seconds,” Mr. Itali told Channel 12. The plane landed safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, and the pilots were taken to a hospital.

Adam Polovincik, 40, who was on the flight with his family, described it as an “extreme experience,” even as he tried to remain calm for his children.

Speaking by phone from Saudi Arabia, where Israel has no formal relations, Mr. Polovincik said the circumstances were surreal.

“They brought us food and drink, served us coffee,” Mr. Polovincik said. “Yes, there are a lot of soldiers here and government officials, but the atmosphere is very relaxed, pleasant and respectful.”

Leo Sands and Heedo Abu Laban contributed reporting.

SUMMARY

U.S. forces formally withdrew from Iraq on Wednesday, ending a two-decade military presence that stoked years of devastating bloodshed, and leaves behind a battered nation struggling to unshackle itself from its two most powerful, and now warring, allies. After toppling Saddam Hussein in 2003, the brutal dictator who ruled Iraq for nearly 24 years, American forces are making their second withdrawal from the country. American forces ultimately returned three years later — this time to lead the international coalition fighting the Islamic State, the jihadist force that once seized swaths of Iraq and Syria and became notorious for its slaughter of Shiite Muslim Iraqis, public killings of hostages, and torture and enslavement of women from Iraq’s Yazidi minority.

ARTICLE

After Two Decades, U.S. Forces Leave Iraq to an Uncertain Future
Some Iraqis are celebrating the end of an American military presence that unleashed waves of bloodshed. Others fear what happens next for their country, trapped between Washington and Tehran.
By Erika Solomon, Falih Hassan and Eric Schmitt
Published 2026-09-30 09:31 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/world/middleeast/iraq-us-forces.html

U.S. forces formally withdrew from Iraq on Wednesday, ending a two-decade military presence that stoked years of devastating bloodshed, and leaves behind a battered nation struggling to unshackle itself from its two most powerful, and now warring, allies.

After toppling Saddam Hussein in 2003, the brutal dictator who ruled Iraq for nearly 24 years, American forces are making their second withdrawal from the country.

The U.S. invasion and subsequent occupation, which ended in 2011, left a country reeling from sectarian bloodletting and militant insurgencies that cost nearly 4,500 U.S. lives and killed more than 115,000 Iraqis, according to the most modest counts.

American forces ultimately returned three years later — this time to lead the international coalition fighting the Islamic State, the jihadist force that once seized swaths of Iraq and Syria and became notorious for its slaughter of Shiite Muslim Iraqis, public killings of hostages, and torture and enslavement of women from Iraq’s Yazidi minority.

With the end of Operation Inherent Resolve — the U.S. military’s official name for the multinational campaign against the Islamic State — the last of the 2,500 U.S. forces stationed in Iraq this year are now gone.

“The coalition successfully completed its organized withdrawal operation from Erbil,” Rear Adm. Liam M. Hulin, head of the joint task force for Operation Inherent Resolve, announced during a ceremony held by U.S. and Iraqi officials in Baghdad. Erbil, capital of Iraq’s semiautonomous Kurdistan region, hosted the last coalition base in Iraq.

“I stand before you at this historic moment, when a nation reclaims its destiny,” Admiral Hulin said, in a speech given in Arabic.

Promising that U.S. and Iraqi forces would forge new security partnerships, Admiral Hulin urged Iraq to remain vigilant, citing an Arabic proverb, “Gird yourself for the jackal with the belt of a lion.”

Physical reminders of decades of war are being erased every day. The blast walls that once snaked through Baghdad have come down. Malls, restaurants and construction sites are buzzing in a country determined to reclaim the rhythms of normal life stolen by years of car bombs.

Iraqis’ hard-won gains look more precarious in a region convulsing from the turmoil of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. Iraq is struggling to navigate its critical relationships with Iran, its powerful neighbor, and with its most important ally, Washington, wary of letting the exit of American troops in the country embolden Tehran.

The U.S. withdrawal agreement was struck between the Baghdad government and the Biden administration in 2024. That President Trump’s administration followed through with the Sept. 30 deadline — despite the war with Iran — reflects broader U.S. determination to step back from the region.

For years, there has been widespread American fatigue with so-called forever wars, as the conflicts in Iraq and in Afghanistan came to be known.

Even as Iraq commemorates the U.S. withdrawal this week with a three-day “celebration of sovereignty,” the country is under huge pressure from the Trump administration to disarm Iran-backed Shiite Muslim militias, many of which are defying state efforts to bring them under control.

The last U.S. forces leave a troubled American legacy. Iraq suffered huge numbers of civilian casualties and a cycle of sectarian violence between Iraq’s Shiite Muslim majority, empowered after years of repression by the Hussein government, and the Sunni minority, stripped of privileges it once held under his rule.

U.S. forces also committed many abuses themselves — including the torture of Iraqi detainees at Abu Ghraib and the use of private defense contractors like Blackwater, whose extrajudicial killings of civilians fueled deep resentments over American impunity.

Despite these grievances, Iraqis have been watching the U.S. departure with a sense of trepidation.

“My wife lost her eyesight from the shrapnel of an American bullet,” said Omar al-Husseini, a photographer from Mosul, the city at the heart of the Islamic State’s self-proclaimed caliphate. “My uncle was killed by ISIS, after being paralyzed by an American bullet. But today, when we speak about the Americans’ departure, our happiness is mixed with fear.”

Under the leadership of the novice prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi, Iraq faces the daunting task of reining in the vast array of militias.

First established with Iranian support to fight the U.S. occupation, the militias killed hundreds of American soldiers, and the sectarian bloodshed they helped foment killed tens of thousands of Iraqis. In 2014, when Iraqi Shiites mobilized to fight the Islamic State, the militias multiplied. In the years since, the thousands-strong militias have grown in power — not only through military might but also by forming political parties that deeply embed them in the state.

Mr. al-Zaidi has pledged to bring the militias under state control by mid-2027. But it is far from clear that he can deliver. The stakes are high: Through Iraq’s U.S.-based bank account for oil payments, Washington controls the physical shipment of dollars Iraq earns and has shown itself willing to use that power after temporarily halting the flow this year.

Iran is determined to preserve the militias, which have proved to be valuable partners in launching strikes during the war, in sowing regional chaos and in inflicting drastic costs on the global economy.

In a recent New York Times interview, Mr. al-Zaidi said, “Every Iraqi today wants his country to have complete sovereignty; they want power to be exclusively in the hands of the state,” and he pledged to end “the law of the jungle.”

The unforeseen consequences of withdrawal

Many Iraqis worry how their country will fare in this struggle.

“We fear Iraq could be swallowed up,” said Ahmad al-Shammari, an employee at the ministry of education in Falluja, a city that came to symbolize the fragile victories of the first American military presence in Iraq.

Falluja suffered the deadliest and most destructive battles to crush insurgents during the U.S. occupation, only to become the first city to be seized as Islamic State militants swept the country in 2014.

When the U.S. forces returned to spearhead a multinational coalition to defeat the jihadist force, the struggle to rout the Islamic State reduced huge parts of Iraqi cities to rubble.

It left an untold number of dead, displaced millions from Iraq’s Sunni minority and brought many more years of sectarian strife.

The question for many ordinary Iraqis today is what unforeseen consequences this latest U.S. departure may have on their lives, whether that is a jihadist resurgence or the state’s imminent confrontation with Iran-backed militias.

“I remember what happened after the withdrawal in 2011,” said Sarkawt Ahmad, a 26-year-old shopkeeper in northwestern Sulaymaniyah, in the Kurdistan region of Iraq. “Imagine what these pro-Iranian groups will do to us in the absence of the international coalition.”

Some regional security experts argue that it was the continued U.S. presence in Iraq that allowed Iran-backed militias to justify their existence, and their arms.

“We can’t just shape-shift these missions from one raison d’être to another, which is what we’ve done for 25 years,” said Adam Weinstein, a longtime proponent of U.S. forces’ ending their mission in Iraq who is the deputy director of the Middle East Program at the Quincy Institute, a research group.

At the ceremony marking the U.S. withdrawal on Wednesday, Mr. al-Zaidi expressed Iraq’s thanks to the United States and to all other countries who supported the fight against ISIS for more than a decade.

“The conclusion of the international coalition’s mission does not mean the end of our battle against terrorism,” he said. “It marks Iraq’s transition to a phase in which it assumes full responsibility for its security and stability.”

Kurds are vulnerable under a new security order

Though both countries have pledged to maintain robust collaboration, the United States and Iraq have still not finalized plans for their security relationship moving forward. In a statement, the Defense Department said it would continue to provide “targeted training and intelligence support” to Iraq.

The last time American forces left Iraq, the United States maintained one of its largest embassies in the world there. Today, the American diplomatic presence is a small fraction of that, said Renad Mansour, an Iraq analyst at Chatham House, a research institute based in London.

He said the shift reflected Washington’s desire to extricate itself from the Middle East: “In the bigger picture, this shows the U.S. is no longer what it used to be — but, also, its priorities are no longer what they used to be.”

This situation has particularly unnerved Iraq’s semiautonomous Kurdistan region in the north, which saw how the Trump administration’s withdrawal of U.S. forces from Syria’s Kurdish-controlled northeast forced the region to come under central government control.

Iraqi Kurds, who began establishing sovereignty in their region through U.S. air support in the 1990s, feel the most vulnerable under Iraq’s new security order. As one of the closest U.S. security partners in the region, Iraqi Kurdistan has come under repeated attacks by Iran and its allied Iraqi militias this year.

Kurdish officials argue this reflects a serious problem for Iraqi security more broadly. “There is no air defense system neither in the Kurdistan region, nor in Iraq as a whole,” said Kifah Mahmoud, an adviser to Masoud Barzani, the first president of Iraqi Kurdistan. “This creates a sense of anxiety and uncertainty.”

Baghdad’s efforts to assert its sovereignty have been repeatedly undermined in recent months by multiple incidents showing its lack of control over its sky and borders.

Most recently, Saudi Arabia accused Iraq of being the origin site of the strike that temporarily shut down its east-west pipeline, which provides 4 percent of global oil supplies. Iraqi officials suspect Iraqi militias facilitated an attack by Iranian operatives.

At the same time, Iraqi militias point to the fact that Israel set up covert bases in the Iraqi desert during the war with Iran. And for years, Turkish forces have controlled territory in northern Iraq, though Iraqi and Turkish officials recently announced plans for a phased withdrawal.

Such gaps in Iraqi sovereignty may become the biggest vulnerability in the government’s campaign to control the militias.

Days before the formal end of the U.S. military presence, Abu Mujahid al-Assaf, a leader from Kataib Hezbollah, one of Iraq’s most powerful Iran-backed militias, issued an ominous warning to the government if it kept complying with new U.S. sanctions against Tehran.

“Let Mr. al-Zaidi and those standing behind him know: A government that does not work for the benefit of the people will be brought down through various means,” he wrote in a statement.

The militias are trumpeting the official U.S. withdrawal day not as a success of the anti-Islamic State campaign, but of their own. They announced an afternoon celebration on the streets of Baghdad on Wednesday under the slogan: “We won’t keep you.” They called the withdrawal an “occasion made possible by the blessed blood of the martyrs and the patience of the fighters in the Iraqi Islamic Resistance.”

Many Iraqis who reject the militias have painful memories of the U.S. presence in Iraq. Among them is Awatif al-Azawi, a 57-year-old who blames the United States for the death of her son, who she says was killed in the crossfire between militants and American forces in their hometown, Falluja.

“I used to love the Americans because they delivered us from the oppression of Saddam Hussein,” she said. “We unfortunately later discovered that the U.S. military’s oppression and cruelty were worse than Saddam.”

On the first night that U.S. forces no longer maintain a presence in Iraq, she said, “I will bake a cake at home, light candles and blow them out to celebrate.”

Kamil Kakol contributed reporting.

iraq-us-troop-withdrawal.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 43  Words: 1466/1465

SUMMARY

I got to Iraq a few weeks after the U.S. Army did. It was just a couple of days after the statue of the Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein was pulled down in Baghdad by a crowd that included U.S. Marines. Now, they said, the United States and the military coalition it formed were there to bring democracy to Iraq.

ARTICLE

What I Saw as the U.S. Debacle in Iraq Unfurled
The Americans did not understand the country when they invaded in 2003. Over a correspondent’s many trips there, it was not clear that this ever changed much.
By Alissa J. Rubin
Published 2026-09-30 09:31 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/world/middleeast/iraq-us-troop-withdrawal.html

I got to Iraq a few weeks after the U.S. Army did. It was just a couple of days after the statue of the Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein was pulled down in Baghdad by a crowd that included U.S. Marines.

That was April 2003.

I had assured my family that I would stay for maybe a week. At the time a correspondent for The Los Angeles Times, I recall telling relatives that I just wanted to “get the lay of the land and take a look around.” That ended up taking longer than I thought.

From the beginning, the United States did not understand the country it was storming into. Twenty-three years later, as it pulls the last of its forces out, it probably still does not. I know I am still working to fully grasp it.

There were so few U.S. service members left in Iraq at the end that when the last ones officially withdrew on Wednesday it made little difference in the daily lives of Iraqis. But that was hardly the case when the first American forces arrived on March 20, 2003.

The early days of the invasion, which toppled a hated despot, were so heady with possibility that it was easy to dismiss the warning signs.

Driving over the border, through the yellow desolate scrub of the country’s western desert, I passed blackened and twisted Iraqi military vehicles hit in American strikes. On the horizon I could see smoke still curling into the air from recent attacks. And everywhere was the smell of burning rubber.

Amid all this wreckage, I wondered, what sort of welcome could an American expect?

When I reached Baghdad, the capital, there was hardly anything to eat in the shops except out-of-date Cadbury toffees and canned tuna, which no one seemed to be buying except foreigners. In the streets, the mood was charged, watchful. But the Iraqis seemed not so much afraid of the invaders, even those in Humvees, as curious.

I do not want to suggest the Americans were greeted with flowers — let alone as “liberators,” as the American vice president had predicted. But the Iraqis I met in those early days were intrigued at finally getting a glimmer of a future not defined by the brutality and restrictions of the Hussein regime. And it was the Americans who had helped bring that change.

But the reason for the American invasion and the rationale for the occupation that followed seemed liked a moving target.

The Bush administration had justified it initially with the claim — later discounted — that the Hussein government was developing chemical weapons.

But the military officers and policymakers who had moved into the so-called Green Zone palaces had a new set of rationales for the war: It was not that Hussein was a danger to mankind, nor a brutal dictator. Now, they said, the United States and the military coalition it formed were there to bring democracy to Iraq. Or, as President George W. Bush put it: “to help the Iraqi people build a lasting democracy in the heart of the Middle East.”

This began the pattern of adjusting or changing altogether the justification for the continued U.S. presence in the country. Along the way, the U.S.-led coalition made one disastrous misstep after another, starting almost from the first weeks after the invasion.

One moment stands out.

I remember vividly the order from Paul Bremer, the chief civilian administrator, to disband the Iraqi Army. “Do you mean, disband the whole army?” I asked a military press attaché.

He said he would get back to me.

Iraq had some 400,000 troops.

Stunned, baffled and increasingly angry, dismissed Iraqi soldiers began to gather every morning at the gates of the Green Zone. When I asked what they thought about the order to disband, some shrugged and walked away. Others had a message for Washington.

“Tell your president that we had to fight for Saddam,” one told me. “We are glad he’s gone.”

Another, a veteran of the eight-year war between Iraq and Iran, said he was 51 and could not make ends meet without his pension. “I have five children,” he said. “My son lost his leg. I work as a janitor. I am too old to find a new job.”

And there were even clearer signs of the trouble ahead.

One man wearing a long, dark gray dishdasha robe — I still see his face in my mind’s eye — asked the interpreter where I was from. When he heard “U.S.,” his face twisted in disgust and he spat a stream of liquid at me.

Some landed on my shoe. I stared at it, unsure whether to wipe it off. What message might that send? Would it seem as if I was ignoring what he had to say?

I wondered if no one saw the widening gap between Iraqi hopes for a post-Hussein future and what the United States was actually offering.

Yes, many Iraqis had unrealistic expectations. They wanted America to transform their country overnight into a Middle Eastern version of the shiny, idealized American world they knew from the bootlegged movies they had watched secretly under Hussein.

But what many more Iraqis were unprepared for was America’s disregard for the economic realities of their lives. They were unprepared for the Americans’ failure to realize that when you take away a person’s job, you often take away their ability to navigate day-to-day life, their dignity, their place in their community, their family.

Only much later did I connect the fury of the man who spat on me with his feeling of having been disrespected. I could see that a dangerous dynamic had already begun.

A fast-growing and increasingly angry Sunni insurgency was becoming shrewder and more technically adept at taking on the American occupiers. The insurgents bombed U.S. checkpoints and military vehicles; they laid ever more sophisticated road bombs.

That made the U.S. troops, many of whom were unprepared for the fraught mission handed to them, more skittish. The U.S. troops fired upon speeding cars near traffic stops, believing they were targeting them, even when they were just carrying families trying to get to safety. Some engaged in human rights abuses, among them the sexual violence and torture at the Abu Ghraib prison and the killing of civilians in Haditha.

Not only did this fuel the insurgency, it helped lay the groundwork for a forerunner of the Islamic State terrorist group.

And when the United States ousted Hussein, it created not just a political vacuum but, with the dismantling of the army, a security one. A U.S. nemesis, Iran, methodically set about backing Shia politicians with whom it shared common ground. Now, 23 years later, its allies are embedded in many Iraqi government agencies and politicians close to Iran have become kingmakers.

The outlines of an emerging sectarian divide were already clear not long after Hussein’s fall. So was the specter of deepening fundamentalism among both Sunnis and Shiites.

Some three weeks after I arrived, Iraqi Shiites were able for the first time in more than a decade to freely celebrate one of the holiest days in the Muslim year, Ashura. Thousands trekked from their homes for days — the old, the young, some in wheelchairs — to reach the city of Karbala in southern Iraq and its elaborately carved shrines with their soaring gilded minarets.

I was unprepared for the religious intensity of the pilgrimage. The women wore long black abayas and tight black veils. The men carried prayer beads.

Jotting down notes near one of the shrines, I did not at first realize that the shouting I was hearing was coming closer — and was directed at me. A group of clerics was bearing down, and other pilgrims were beginning to gather.

What had I done?

I looked for my interpreter, but he was nowhere in sight. As the men shook their fists, I felt a strong grip on my upper arm. It was a woman in an abaya. She nodded to the men and pulled me away.

My offense soon became clear.

The woman led me to a small group of other women sitting with children on a blanket, with small bowls of raisins and nuts. They pointed to my veil, which I had draped over my head in the style I had learned in Afghanistan. Then one pulled on a wisp of my hair that had escaped into view.

The women never looked disapproving, but it was clear how seriously they took the situation. For half an hour they worked to refold and pin my head scarf so that not one hair could work its way out.

When they were finished, one reached into her pocket and pulled out a small mirror to show me their handiwork.

Then one smiled and handed me back my notebook.

SUMMARY

A $75 Manga Fan Pass gets you and a friend unlimited entry to the show during its run from Oct. 3 to Jan. 31. This month’s concerts by generation: Baby boomers, Steve Miller is at the Rose Theater on the Upper West Side (Oct. 9-10). On Oct. 24, the sly comedian-magician brings his new stage show, “One for the Ages,” to the Beacon Theater on the Upper West Side.

ARTICLE

26 Things to Do in N.Y.C. in October
This month brings a major manga exhibition, birthday tributes to John Coltrane and Steve Reich and a night with Michael Douglas.
By Erik Piepenburg
Published 2026-10-01 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/01/arts/fun-things-to-do-nyc-october.html

Art

Over 600 drawings by manga artists, or “mangaka,” like Fujio Akatsuka and Eiichiro Oda are on view in “Art of Manga,” a huge exhibition on the eye-popping world of Japanese comics and graphic novels, at the Brooklyn Museum in Prospect Heights. A $75 Manga Fan Pass gets you and a friend unlimited entry to the show during its run from Oct. 3 to Jan. 31.

Pop Music

This month’s concerts by generation: Baby boomers, Steve Miller is at the Rose Theater on the Upper West Side (Oct. 9-10). Gen X, Toad the Wet Sprocket hops on over to Sony Hall in Times Square (Oct. 19). Millennials, Hawthorne Heights rocks Irving Plaza near Union Square (Oct. 26). Gen Z, Artms plays Webster Hall in the East Village (Oct. 7).

Jazz

How’s this for a powerhouse party: The saxophonist-composer Branford Marsalis and the singer Dianne Reeves mark John Coltrane’s 100th birthday with a concert at Carnegie Hall on Oct. 27.

Comedy

I still have no idea how Justin Willman shoplifted a video game through a store window on his brain-boggling Netflix series “Magic for Humans.” On Oct. 24, the sly comedian-magician brings his new stage show, “One for the Ages,” to the Beacon Theater on the Upper West Side.

Cabaret

When musical theater intermingles with other genres you never know what you’ll get. The TikTok creator Matt Copley brings his viral musical project “Broadway Does Punk” to the stage at the Abrons Arts Center on the Lower East Side; it’s sold out but there will be a wait list (Oct. 2-3). And expect drama that slaps at “Broadway Sin Vergüenza,” a night of original telenovela-inspired musical works at 54 Below in Manhattan’s theater district (Oct. 15).

Film

Genre fans, it’s time to geek out. The Brooklyn Sci-Fi Film Festival is spotlighting 60 years of “Star Trek” (Oct. 5-11). The Brooklyn Horror Film Festival hosts the U.S. premiere of the vampire mockumentary “I Love Paris” (Oct. 15-22). And Netflix’s buzzy Spanish epic “La Bola Negra” opens NewFest (Oct. 15-25), a longtime annual celebration of queer cinema.

Reminiscence

Michael Douglas — Academy Award winner and a reminder that if you watch only one horror movie this Halloween it should be “Fatal Attraction” — talks about his new memoir, “One Helluva Ride,” on Oct. 6 at 92NY on the Upper East Side.

On Oct. 7, Melissa King, winner of “Top Chef: All Stars L.A.,” discusses “The Girl Who Became King,” her new memoir about cooking and coming out. Presented by the Asian American bookstore Yu & Me, the talk is at New Design High School on the Lower East Side.

Family Time

City of Forest Day offers more than a hundred free activities in every borough on Oct. 3, giving city kids ample opportunities to explore the forests around them. Among the highlights are a hike through High Rock Park on Staten Island led by the Urban Park Rangers and, in the Bronx, a nature walk through Shoelace Park and canoeing on the Bronx River.

The New York Botanical Garden is hosting several children’s events as part of its “Dia de los Muertos” exhibition (Oct. 3-Nov. 2). On Halloween weekend, the fun includes skeleton puppet processions and English-Spanish singalong concerts and dance parties; families are encouraged to bring photos of deceased loved ones.

Classical Music

The Park Avenue Armory is home to a maximalist celebration of the minimalist composer Steve Reich, who turns 90 this month. From Oct. 14 to 18, the armory’s massive drill hall on the Upper East Side will fill with “Music for 18 Musicians: Staged Variations,” a new production of Reich’s 1976 work that runs over three hours, performed by the Steve Reich Ensemble, Alarm Will Sound and musicians from the Manhattan School of Music.

Theater

It’s revival time for two gay-themed hair-raisers. A Brazilian adaptation of “Tom at the Farm” — Michel Marc Bouchard’s 2011 psychological drama about a gay man and his fraught relationship with his dead boyfriend’s family — has its U.S. premiere at N.Y.U. Skirball in Greenwich Village (Oct. 8-10).

The real-life killers Leopold and Loeb are the inspiration behind Gordon Greenberg’s “Rope,” a new take on the 1929 Patrick Hamilton play that inspired Hitchcock’s crackling 1948 homoerotic thriller. The New Group production is at the Theater at St. Clement’s in Hell’s Kitchen from Oct. 13 to Dec. 6.

In the Buff

Standing naked in a house of worship sounds like my worst nightmare. But there’s nothing to be scared of at Figure Drawing at the Church, a nude figure drawing event organized by Tiny Arts Supply, a store in Ridgewood, Queens. Classes take place on Oct. 14 and 28 in the sanctuary of Ridgewood Presbyterian Church, with basic drawing materials provided. No experience is needed and there’s no formal instruction; it’s simply a chance to “get your eyes off screens and decompress.”

Dance

The dance-theater piece “From the Horse’s Mouth: The Swans of Harlem” celebrates five trailblazing Black ballerinas associated with the early years of Arthur Mitchell’s Dance Theater of Harlem. The cast includes the four surviving “swans”: Marcia Sells, Sheila Rohan, Karlya Shelton-Benjamin and Lydia Abarca Mitchell. Performances are at Theater at the 14th Street Y in the East Village from Oct. 16 to 18.

Perk Up

Grind and agitation are words often used to describe a bad day at the office. But they were some of the considerations I nerded out on at an afternoon pour-over class at Coffee Project New York’s roastery in Long Island City, Queens. Test your skills when the next session is held on Oct. 23, or refine your palate at a coffee tasting class the next day.

Mind Your P’s and Q’s

Attention, word nerds: On Oct. 19, the comedians Calvin Cato and Hannah Lieberman host an Adult Spelling Bee at Q.E.D. in Astoria, Queens. Instead of cash, the grand prize winner takes home a jar of Honey House honey.

Last Call

Speaking of orthographic skills: The final curtain comes down on “The 25th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee” — a “tender, joyous, bittersweet and very, very funny” musical, as Elisabeth Vincentelli put it in her review — on Oct. 11 at New World Stages in Hell’s Kitchen.

I’ve long admired Carson Ellis for her fanciful folk-art illustrations for her husband Colin’s band, the Decemberists. You have until Oct. 24 to see “All Around Us,” a delightful exhibition of her work at the Society of Illustrators on the Upper East Side.

changpeng-zhao-binance.html
