SUMMARY

This event occurred on Oct. 1, but appeared in the Oct. 2 issue of The New York Times. “Four hundred and forty students have been admitted to the various classes” of the newly established Stanford University, The Times reported from Palo Alto, Calif. A military junta named General Francisco Franco dictator of Spain, The Times reported, as Nationalist forces under his command fought to overthrow the Spanish government in the civil war.

ARTICLE

On This Day | Oct. 1
In 1949, Mao Zedong proclaimed the founding of the People’s Republic of China in Beijing.
By The Learning Network
Published 2026-10-01 04:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/01/learning/on-this-day-oct-1.html

On This Day spotlights a historic New York Times front-page article. For teaching ideas, visit this resource.

Reds Proclaim a Republic In China; Chou Is Premier

SHANGHAI, Oct. 1—Chou En-lai was today named in Peiping as Premier and concurrently Foreign Minister of China’s new People’s (Communist) Republic. At the same time the new regime declared itself the sole legal Government of China and invited recognition by other nations. This was announced in a proclamation read by Mao Tze-tung, head of the Chinese Communist party, before a crowd officially estimated at 200,000 that gathered in the newly cleared Square of the Gate of Heavenly Peace, Peking’s equivalent of Red Square in Moscow.

This event occurred on Oct. 1, but appeared in the Oct. 2 issue of The New York Times. Read the entire article or explore this issue in full in TimesMachine.

What else happened on Oct. 1?

“Stanford University Opened”

“Four hundred and forty students have been admitted to the various classes” of the newly established Stanford University, The Times reported from Palo Alto, Calif.

“Fire Kills 19; Unions Accused; Two Bombs Found After Explosion Wrecks Los Angeles Times Building.”

A dynamite bomb planted beneath The Los Angeles Times building triggered an explosion and fire that killed 21 workers. The bomber, James B. McNamara, a union ironworker, later pleaded guilty. The bombing became a watershed moment in the era’s violent conflicts between employers and organized labor.

“Insurgents Name Franco Dictator in an Army Regime”

A military junta named General Francisco Franco dictator of Spain, The Times reported, as Nationalist forces under his command fought to overthrow the Spanish government in the civil war. Franco would go on to win the war in 1939 and rule Spain as an authoritarian dictator until his death in 1975.

“12 Nazi War Leaders Sentenced to Be Hanged”

After 10 months of testimony on “the unprecedented horrors precipitated upon the world through the Nazi hierarchy,” 19 defendants were found guilty of war crimes at the Nuremberg trials, The Times reported.

“New Dollar Bill Makes Its Debut”

“The apparent big change is the words ‘In God We Trust’ printed on the back,” The Times reported.

“Civil Space Group Starts Operation.”

The National Aeronautics and Space Administration, or NASA, came into being, taking over civilian space projects at the height of the space race. The Times reported that the new agency was given responsibility for projects “ranging from earth satellites to the development of nuclear rockets.”

“Nigerians Achieve Their Independence”

Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country, gained independence from Britain as a member of the Commonwealth. It was one of 17 African nations to become independent that year.

“Maris Hits 61st in Final Game”

Roger Maris of the New York Yankees “became the first major league player in history to hit more than sixty home runs in a season,” The Times reported. He broke Babe Ruth’s record of 60 set in 1927.

“Now It’s Johnny Carson vs. Sleep”

Johnny Carson took over as host of “The Tonight Show,” succeeding Jack Paar. Carson would host the program for nearly 30 years and more than 4,500 episodes. “Heeeere’s Johnny!” — Ed McMahon’s introduction as Carson came onstage — became an iconic television catchphrase.

“3,000 Troops Put Down Mississippi Rioting and Seize 200 as Negro Attends Classes”

After a deadly riot and federal intervention, James H. Meredith enrolled as the first Black student at the University of Mississippi. The Times reported that his enrollment “ends segregation in state schools.”

“Disney World Opens Without Expected Crush”

Only 10,000 customers materialized out of the 30,000 that officials had expected on Disney World’s opening day. But with short lines and flawless weather, patrons had few complaints. “We need a place like this because of the world situation,” one guest told The Times, “a place where we can come and relax and forget about all the bad things.”

“Panama Takes Control of Canal Zone.”

Under the Panama Canal treaties, Panama assumed control of the Canal Zone, ending decades of exclusive American administration there. The Times reported that Panama took control “amid fireworks, bands and blaring car horns.”

“Multiple Weapons Found in Las Vegas Gunman’s Hotel Room.”

A gunman firing from the Mandalay Bay Resort attacked a country music festival, killing dozens and injuring hundreds in the deadliest mass shooting in modern U.S. history.

“Mexico’s First Female President Takes Office.”

Claudia Sheinbaum took office as the first woman, and first Jewish person, to lead Mexico. “For the first time, we women have arrived,” she said at her inauguration.

SUMMARY

When a woman sued Cornell University last month over an alleged sexual assault at a fraternity, the case reverberated across the nation, igniting shock and anger about the persistent phenomenon of sexual misconduct on campuses. They also include the original six-page statement that the Cornell Police Department submitted to the Tompkins County, N.Y., district attorney; investigatory interviews with six of the seven men whom the woman accused of being involved in the sexual assault; and interviews with 20 additional witnesses. Jane Doe considered two of the men friends.

ARTICLE

The Cornell Rape Investigation: Five Takeaways
The New York Times obtained more than 1,000 pages from the university’s internal inquiry into accusations by “Jane Doe.” Here are the revelations so far.
By Sharon Otterman
Published 2026-10-01 04:30 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/01/nyregion/cornell-jane-doe-rape-investigation-documents.html

When a woman sued Cornell University last month over an alleged sexual assault at a fraternity, the case reverberated across the nation, igniting shock and anger about the persistent phenomenon of sexual misconduct on campuses.

Those involved have fought for control of the narrative, with the woman’s lawyer, lawyers for the accused men and a district attorney making assertions that often appeared at odds.

Now, The New York Times has obtained more than 1,000 pages of material from Cornell’s internal investigation into the 2024 rape allegations that are at the center of the bombshell lawsuit against the university.

The files, compiled for Cornell’s Title IX administrative hearing process and distributed in early 2025, include an extensive transcript of the original police interviews with the 20-year-old undergraduate, who accused the men of sexually assaulting her at the Chi Phi fraternity on Oct. 19, 2024.

They also include the original six-page statement that the Cornell Police Department submitted to the Tompkins County, N.Y., district attorney; investigatory interviews with six of the seven men whom the woman accused of being involved in the sexual assault; and interviews with 20 additional witnesses. A trove of emails, text messages and screenshots of message boards are included, some showing how rumors about what had happened that night raced around campus.

While it will take reporters several days to fully comb through the material, here are some of the main early takeaways.

Jane Doe’s statement sent to the district attorney left out key context.

On Nov. 14, 2024, about three weeks after the incident, the woman who filed the suit, known as Jane Doe, spoke for hours to a Cornell police investigator and an investigator from Cornell’s Title IX office, which makes sure the university complies with federal regulations related to sex discrimination. She had with her a support person — someone who provides emotional support during the hearing process — and an adviser to explain her rights.

The transcript of their conversation stretches about 120 pages. It was condensed by the police investigator into a six-page official statement that the woman signed.

This statement was crucial because the Tompkins County district attorney says it was the main piece of evidence he considered when deciding not to bring a criminal case.

But the official statement omits much of the context about Jane Doe’s state of mind, her history as a sexual assault survivor and her thoughts as she was processing what was happening to her. It is these details, in addition to the actions she alleges, that help explain how a series of sexual encounters that started off “pretty OK” had devolved into a situation that was “just raping,” in her words.

“I can say with 100 percent confidence I was raped,” she told the police investigator about what happened by the end of that night, in a statement that did not make it into the six-page summary report.

The omissions may help explain why the district attorney did not think he could bring a criminal case based on her allegations.

The summary made clear, however, that she felt that some of what was happening to her was a crime, and had thought about taking the drug ketamine to escape it.

“I had become extremely uncomfortable with how this night was turning out, so my thought was, if I do ketamine again, maybe I will pass out,” it quotes her saying. “My thought was that if I passed out and these men had sex with me, then they could be charged with rape.”

Her thinking about the incident evolved.

Jane Doe considered two of the men friends. She and the men involved that night had taken ketamine. Things had started off consensual — though she was drunk — and some of her memories were hazy, the transcript shows. She had lost control. Her initial impulse was to keep quiet about what had happened.

But within a day or two, “everyone involved in sorority and fraternity life knew what had happened,” she told investigators. Most of the gossip blamed her, calling her “a whore that had an eightsome with the Chi Phi guys.”

She had not known how or why so many men had showed up in the room that night. But then she heard that a Snapchat message had been sent to the fraternity, inviting members to join what was happening. And when she saw on a message board that someone had said that Chi Phi members were “gang banging,” the pieces started coming together.

She told investigators that she had a revelation when reading an online comment that called Chi Phi brothers “terrible people, they gang raped a sophomore.”

“And that’s kind of when I came to the realization that I had been gang raped, gang assaulted, whatever you want to call it; that’s what happened,” she said.

The accounts of the men emerge.

Transcripts of Title IX interviews that were conducted with six of the seven men provide the first glimpse of the defendants’ accounts of the assault. In interviews with the school’s investigators, the men almost universally denied the accusations against them and said any sex that took place was consensual. Several of the men suggested that Jane Doe had not only initiated the sexual encounters, but in some cases, had done so without asking.

Many of the men paused their interrogations repeatedly to seek legal guidance from advisers who accompanied them, including law students and lawyers. At least one of the accused men appeared with a “support person” in the form of his father.

Despite their insistence that they were innocent, the men in some of their comments appeared to acknowledge the unsettling nature of the interaction that they had witnessed and joined.

“I was genuinely concerned and wanted to investigate what’s going on,” one of the men, identified by his initials S.N., said of entering the room where Jane Doe said the assault occurred. When the man was pressed later by the investigator on what he thought would happen after leaving the room, he said: “I thought they were just going to continue conversating.”

She documented her injuries and evidence.

The woman’s main source of pain after the incident was from what she thought was a urinary tract infection. In her account to investigators, she said that when she went to a Cornell health clinic two days after the incident to get medication, she told the doctor that she had contracted the infection in “a traumatic way.” They advised her to seek therapy.

Before Jane Doe decided that she would go to the campus police department, she gathered additional documentation.

She took a photograph of a hickey on her neck. More than a week after the incident, she took a picture of fading bruises on her buttocks that she alleged were caused by one of the men hitting her. She didn’t wash the dress she had been wearing that night, to save potential evidence. Two weeks after the incident, and the day before she went to police, she went to an emergency room for a pelvic exam, the documents state.

Her view on whether she consented to sex appears to shift.

The allegations found in Jane Doe’s September lawsuit recount the same events as those described in her original statements to police investigators. But what is different is how she characterizes her ability to consent at different moments in the encounter, particularly at its start.

In the November 2024 account, she had told investigators that she was “pretty OK” with the initial sexual encounter she had with the two men whom she considered friends. But she said that as more men showed up seeking sex, she had felt that she could not stop them and came to clearly regard what was happening as rape.

She had told investigators in November 2024 that she didn’t remember exactly when she first took ketamine that night, though she remembers that, in general, she felt coerced to do it. “I felt like they were just kind of giving me substances until I said ‘yes,’ ” she said. In the 2026 lawsuit, she states that the two men with whom she first had sex that night “pressured” her into snorting ketamine with them.

In 2024, she put her initial level of inebriation at about a “5 or 6” out of 10 when that first encounter began. By the end of the night, she said, it was near a 10 and that she was practically hallucinating, feeling like her eyes were going in different directions. She told investigators that she had never taken ketamine before.

In her lawsuit, she said that she was “incapable of consenting” to even that initial sexual encounter because of severe inebriation. She asserted that the two men had forced sex on her and called it an assault.

In the transcript of the police interview, she had a more complicated reaction. She said that she was upset and hurt that a man she liked was using her.

She added: “I was a sex doll for all intents and purposes, which is sad.”

Maia Coleman contributed reporting.

cornell-rape-accusation-reporting.html

SUMMARY

In October 2024, about a week after a Chi Phi fraternity party at Cornell University, the sophomore who would come to be known as Jane Doe was milling around an online forum about Greek life when she encountered a post that stopped her cold. Jane Doe replied and reassured him. On Oct. 23, Jane Doe texted Mr. Ingalls.

ARTICLE

How a Cornell Student Went From Shame to Seeking Justice
The woman known as “Jane Doe” was initially embarrassed about what happened at a fraternity party in 2024, but soon concluded: “I was assaulted.”
By Debra Kamin, Matt Flegenheimer and Amy Julia Harris
Published 2026-10-01 04:15 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/01/nyregion/cornell-rape-accusation-reporting.html

In October 2024, about a week after a Chi Phi fraternity party at Cornell University, the sophomore who would come to be known as Jane Doe was milling around an online forum about Greek life when she encountered a post that stopped her cold.

“Are Chi Phi brothers Crips or Bloods because I hear they have been doing hell Gang Banging?” someone had written.

“They do drugs and gang r*ped a sophomore,” another user said. “Report them.”

Since the evening that began on Oct. 19, 2024, Jane Doe had recounted the night’s events to her roommates without identifying herself as a rape victim. She had exchanged friendly text messages with men she would later accuse of assault. She had heard uncharitable appraisals of herself from undergraduate gossips.

Then she read the words.

“That’s the first time I had ever heard the narrative change that I wasn’t a whore and that I was assaulted,” Jane Doe told investigators, according to documents from a university review of the accusations obtained by The New York Times.

Those records, which have not been previously reported, help illuminate a case that has horrified the nation and plunged one of its elite institutions into crisis. They shed light on the crucial three-week period between the fraternity party and Jane Doe’s decision to take her story to the campus police, accusing multiple fraternity brothers of sexual assault and alleging that she was coerced into taking ketamine.

The bare facts of what happened after she made her accusations are by now well known: The Tompkins County, N.Y., district attorney, Matthew Van Houten, reviewed her complaint and declined to bring criminal charges, saying there was not sufficient evidence to do so. Jane Doe filed a complaint that prompted at least a dozen hearings by the school’s Title IX committee, which is supposed to ensure compliance with federal civil rights laws.

On Sept. 16, Jane Doe also filed a lawsuit against seven men, accusing them of sexual assault. Lawyers for at least three of the accused men have broadly denied criminal wrongdoing; others have not yet made public statements.

What had not been known publicly, until now, were the detailed filings collected during the private Title IX proceedings — hundreds of pages of emails, text messages, photographs and interviews with Jane Doe, her friends and those she accused.

Taken together, the raw materials sketch Jane Doe’s journey from an unknown sophomore to the embodiment of another searing national dialogue about sexual assault and consent. (Although Jane Doe is identified in the documents, The Times is withholding her name.)

Some women around her, the documents show, were quick to say they viewed the events of the evening of Oct. 19 as sexual assault. But Jane Doe, the interviews and text messages reveal, first appeared to grapple with shame, humiliation and concerns about her reputation before she began to consider herself an assault victim.

“I don’t really remember her ever kind of citing that she had said yes to anything that occurred,” one of her roommates had said of the first hours after Jane Doe returned home the morning of Oct. 20, according to the Title IX files, which were compiled as part of the school’s formal process for investigating allegations of sexual harassment and assault.

On page upon page, the documents make for difficult reading, vacillating between the merry shorthand of college students — asides about the gym, Snapchat, Greek life — and the blunt-force details of an alleged gang assault that the victim appeared to be processing in real time.

From the beginning, the case has seemed to double as a referendum on so many vexing questions about what it means to be a young woman on a college campus, even a campus as nominally esteemed as Cornell’s: Who is believed, and who is coddled? How much good can Title IX do? Has anything changed, really?

For Jane Doe, the records suggest, the first task was to make sense of what had happened to her.

‘A traumatic way’

At 3:05 a.m. on Oct. 20, 2024, one of Jane Doe’s roommates sent her a text.

“Are you coming home tonight?” she asked.

Four minutes later, Jane Doe texted back that she didn’t know.

The roommate went to sleep, she would tell investigators. When she woke up at 11 a.m., she uploaded a photo of her empty room to Snapchat. “Only I made it back home,” she wrote on the post.

Around 11:15 a.m., she said, Jane Doe arrived home, still in her “big boots and small dress” from the night before, according to the roommate. She had consumed ketamine and had sex with multiple men, she told her two roommates. One roommate told investigators that Jane Doe did not use the word “rape” or “assault” yet.

It seemed like she was “in shock,” her other roommate later told investigators, “not really understanding the gravity of what she was saying.”

The next day, on Oct. 21, Jane Doe went to her “big sister” — a woman designated as a mentor — at Cornell’s Tri Delta sorority and told her there were rumors circulating that she was a “slut.” The big sister, a junior at Cornell, told investigators that Jane Doe added with a laugh that “unfortunately they are true.”

“I could tell that — just from personal experiences — that what she was going through is that she had not yet processed what had happened,” the big sister told investigators.

That same day, Jane Doe received a text message from Jonathan Newell, one of the men she would go on to accuse of sexual assault.

“I just wanted to apologize for how things went down the other night,” Mr. Newell wrote. He then said that both he and Matthew Ingalls, another of the men she would later accuse of assault, both felt terrible for being too under the influence of drugs and alcohol to “shut it down and kick people out before it got way out of hand.”

Jane Doe replied and reassured him.

“At the end of the day non of the sexual stuff was illegal and honestly i really liked being w u and matt,” she wrote.

A lawyer for Mr. Newell did not respond to requests for comment. A lawyer for Mr. Ingalls declined to comment.

The next day, on Oct. 22, Jane Doe made an appointment at Cornell Health to see a doctor because she had contracted a urinary tract infection and wanted to be tested for sexually transmitted diseases. She told the doctor she contracted the U.T.I. “in a traumatic way,” according to a transcript of her conversation with investigators.

“She didn’t really follow up on that,” Jane Doe said of the doctor. “She just suggested I go to therapy.”

‘Say it didn’t happen’

On Oct. 23, Jane Doe texted Mr. Ingalls.

“Bro,” she wrote, “everyone knows.”

She said the episode was “RUINING my life temporarily” and that her reputation had been destroyed. She said all she could do was “sleep and cry all day.”

According to the documents, Mr. Ingalls assured her that it would all blow over soon, noting “how fast nonsense spreads at this school,” and said she did not have “anything to be ashamed of.”

“You’re right,” Jane Doe wrote. “It’ll get better.”

Jane Doe’s sorority big sister received a text that week: “Have you heard the rumor about your little?”

In the meantime, Jane Doe had delivered strict instructions to one of her roommates: “If anyone asks about this,” she said, according to the roommate’s testimony, “say it didn’t happen.”

The roommate was plainly concerned. Initially, she said, Jane Doe was “kind of recounting it as this sort of crazy thing that she had done.”

“As the days went on,” the roommate continued, “I think she kind of came to realize that it was something bad. And that she didn’t really enjoy her time there.”

On Oct. 25, Mr. Ingalls texted Jane Doe: “U good?”

Jane Doe replied that Mr. Newell had “def told people.”

Days later, she sent Mr. Ingalls an image of the forum post accusing Chi Phi of gang rape.

“???” she wrote.

“Ridiculous,” Mr. Ingalls wrote. “I’m gonna report that.”

Uninvited from the party

As Halloween approached, Jane Doe’s roommates told investigators, her understanding of what had happened to her appeared to have shifted.

Around Oct. 28, Mr. Ingalls was on the phone with Jane Doe and, according to one of her roommates who said she overheard the conversation, he apologized to her. But rather than assure him everything was OK, Jane Doe took a different tone.

“How could you let this happen?” the roommate recalled her saying.

“I think she wanted it to be consensual,” the roommate told investigators, looking back on how Jane Doe had processed the alleged assault. The roommate told investigators that Jane Doe had been sexually assaulted before, which made it particularly hard for her to talk openly about what had happened.

“I’d have conversations and she would describe a part of what happened and I would tell her that that is what could be classified as rape,” the roommate said.

At Chi Phi, the fraternity was preparing for a Halloween party, and Jane Doe was eager to attend. Text messages included in the investigation show Mr. Ingalls assuring Jane Doe that he and other fraternity members wanted her to be there.

“chi phi is your house and you are welcome here,” he wrote, relaying the views of the fraternity’s president, who was not among those accused of sexual assault.

“thank u i really appreciate that,” Jane Doe responded. “<3 i’ll bring my cigs tomorrow”

But then Jane Doe received a phone call from the fraternity’s president, according to the text messages.

She was disinvited from the party. It was for her own good, he said.

Jane Doe sent a biting text to Mr. Ingalls.

“I knew this was going to happen,” she wrote. “The woman will always get the short end of the stick. Yall aren’t my friends. Yall are covering your asses.”

By Nov. 3, Jane Doe appears to have concluded that she was assaulted at the October party. She sent a text to Mr. Newell.

“let’s be clear that 90% of what happened that night was not consensual. i was given more key than i can remember,” she said, using a shorthand for ketamine, “and i know that i told u i felt uncomfortable and i didn’t know anyone in the room.”

The text continued with her telling him that one of her only memories was doing ketamine off of his penis “in front of everyone like a sex doll/worker.”

Four days later, on Nov. 7, according to the documents, Jane Doe went to an emergency room in Ithaca and requested a rape kit.

Sharon Otterman, Hurubie Meko and Claire Fahy contributed reporting.

SUMMARY

In the weeks after a Cornell University student reported being raped at a fraternity party on campus, most of the men she accused were questioned by university officials about their actions that night. Since the woman, identified in her lawsuit as Jane Doe, sued the fraternity members, the men have largely remained silent. The other men involved that night said that Jane Doe and those around her did not seem overly inebriated and that they themselves had not had too much to drink.

ARTICLE

Men Accused in Cornell Sex Assault Suit Give Varying Accounts of Night
Their accounts, detailed in hundreds of pages of investigative files obtained by The New York Times, were disjointed and sometimes contradictory. All the men denied any wrongdoing.
By Maia Coleman, Claire Fahy and Michael C. Bender
Published 2026-10-01 16:38 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/01/nyregion/cornell-rape-fraternity-chi-phi-men.html

In the weeks after a Cornell University student reported being raped at a fraternity party on campus, most of the men she accused were questioned by university officials about their actions that night.

Their answers, which have not been previously reported, were detailed in hundreds of pages of confidential investigative files obtained by The New York Times.

The woman, who left Cornell and last month filed a lawsuit against the university, the fraternity and seven of its members, and her sorority, said she was plied with drugs in October 2024 after a night of heavy drinking and sexually assaulted multiple times at the Chi Phi fraternity house.

But in hours of interviews and a statement collected during Cornell’s administrative investigation over the winter of 2024, all the men denied any wrongdoing. Four acknowledged having sexual contact with the woman but said that their interactions had been consensual. The others denied participating in sexual encounters.

One said that he, in fact, was “a victim of sexual misconduct” because the woman had given him oral sex when he was “too incapacitated” to consent.

All their accounts differed, frequently contradicted each other and generally ran counter to the statements given by the woman to the Cornell police in 2024. The majority said they did not think the woman appeared intoxicated.

Most of the interviews, which were conducted by the university’s Title IX office, focused not on asking explicitly whether the men had raped the woman but rather on more quotidian questions: where they had been that night, what they had said and why they had found themselves in the bedroom to begin with.

None of the men has been charged with a crime — the local district attorney declined to pursue a criminal case after reviewing the Cornell police report about her complaint in 2024. But each was identified by name in her lawsuit filed on Sept. 16 and accused of sexually assaulting her, and the district attorney, Matthew Van Houten of Tompkins County, has since said that his office would again consider whether charges were warranted.

Since the woman, identified in her lawsuit as Jane Doe, sued the fraternity members, the men have largely remained silent. Lawyers for at least three of them have issued statements denying criminal wrongdoing.

Lawyers for six of the men did not respond to requests for comment.

Jeremy Saland, who represents the seventh, Scott Kretzschmar, acknowledged that his client had participated in a group chat that described the sexual encounters in lewd terms but had otherwise done nothing wrong.

“Taking part in an offensive conversation is not the same as taking part in a rape,” Mr. Saland said, adding that he had reached out to the district attorney and was confident Mr. Kretzschmar would be exonerated. “Please let the process work before recklessly proliferating or coming to a wrongful conclusion about him.”

In the statements detailed in the investigative records, Mr. Kretzschmar and the other men described their recollections of the night of the party in their own words.

They said their interactions with Jane Doe began when one of the men, Matthew Ingalls, asked if she wanted to have a threesome with him and another fraternity member, Jonathan Newell.

That request later spiraled into a series of sexual encounters, they said. It was Mr. Newell who, not long into their encounter, fired off a Snapchat message to dozens of other members advertising “free pussy” in the bedroom, according to Jane Doe’s lawsuit.

Mr. Newell told investigators that he was invited by Mr. Ingalls to participate in the threesome, saying he assumed Mr. Ingalls had asked for permission, the records show. Mr. Newell said that he and Mr. Ingalls had drunk a lot and consumed marijuana and ketamine, causing both to throw up.

The other men involved that night said that Jane Doe and those around her did not seem overly inebriated and that they themselves had not had too much to drink.

“They weren’t slurring their speech,” said Winston Lee, one of the accused men. “They seem perfectly normal.”

Another fraternity brother, Gillio Lopes, who, along with Mr. Newell lived in the room where the sexual encounters took place, said that he had “a pretty solid recollection” of the night because in his view he had not drunk that much — roughly six beverages, he estimated, in the form of three Keystone beers and three vodka-and-Hawaiian Punch mixed drinks.

When asked about his involvement with Jane Doe, Mr. Lopes said that she initiated their sexual contact and did not ask for his consent — a statement flatly at odds with her account of the night.

Mr. Lopes left around 2 a.m., he said, after he said he became “uncomfortable,” and went with three friends to McDonald’s. He said he did not tell them about what had transpired, in part because he was “admittedly a bit embarrassed about what happened,” according to the interview records.

Mr. Lee also said that Jane Doe initiated sexual activity without asking. He said he snorted a line of ketamine off her body and she tried to initiate sex.

“I kind of took a step back because I didn’t want to engage in anything like sex,” Mr. Lee said. “I thought it wasn’t the time for that.”

But later that night, Mr. Lee said he asked for Jane Doe’s consent before engaging in a threesome with her. He recalled telling Jane Doe that “if you’re uncomfortable with any of this or you won’t want to do this, that’s perfectly fine. We can call it a night.” He said Jane Doe replied: “We’re all consenting adults here.”

Another of the men, Mr. Kretzschmar, told interviewers that he and his friend Scott Norris entered the room after reading Mr. Newell’s Snapchat message, which he said had left him “befuddled.”

He said Jane Doe was not slurring her words when they arrived and that she did not appear drunk. He said he asked her “if she was all right just because the nature of the text, and there was one female in the room with a couple dudes.”

“We were just checking out to see if everything was OK, and it was,” he said, later adding of Ms. Doe: “And if she wasn’t, I’d like to think that I would have helped out and did something about it.”

Mr. Norris, in his interview, said he had been “somewhat concerned” when he received Mr. Newell’s Snapchat message, but assumed it was “crude humor.” He said he did not do any drugs in the room and did not have sex with Jane Doe.

“She was conversational with people, and that alleviated whatever concerns I had from the text before,” Mr. Norris said, adding that he stayed in the room for only five minutes and that all the men in the room were completely or partially clothed for the duration.

In her interview with the police, Jane Doe said that Mr. Kretzschmar and Mr. Norris were “more like voyeurs than anything,” the records show.

Diego Sarabia said he entered the room after 2:30 a.m. and was shocked by the scene before him: Several fraternity brothers were there, and one was standing behind Jane Doe, although Mr. Sarabia refused to say whether the person was naked or dressed.

“I was immensely concerned since I’ve never seen anything like this in my four years at the house,” he said, according to the records.

But he said his concerns were allayed when “all the people in the room” told him to come in.

“I remember the girl in specific saying something along the lines of, ‘This was normal in the medieval times,’” he said. Jane Doe said at one point he insulted her before grabbing her and kissing her.

Jane Doe, a sophomore at the time, was also interviewed at length by Cornell’s Title IX investigators, as were about 20 other people, including her friends and other witnesses to the night and its aftermath.

She described a horrific night in the fraternity room where she could not reach her phone. She said she was given large amounts of drugs and alcohol and repeatedly raped by men she barely knew or had never met, the files show.

“I was super drunk,” she said.

Still, she said, she came to understand what had happened to her. When she gave her account to a police investigator three weeks after the party, she was unequivocal: “I can say with 100 percent confidence I was raped,” she said.

Cornell said on Monday that it gave the men “a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions.” Thomas Giuffra, Jane Doe’s lawyer, has said that only two of the men were expelled, which his client does not consider justice.

Jay Root and Hurubie Meko contributed reporting.

ARTICLE

Cornell Students Question Greek Life Culture After Sexual Assault Claim
With their university under fire in the wake of a sexual assault lawsuit, students are having difficult conversations about Greek life, campus rituals and the possibility for lasting changes.
By Emma Goldberg
Published 2026-09-30 22:19 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/nyregion/cornell-university-students-jane-doe-case.html

Homework, lectures and exams press on, but many students at Cornell are consumed by emotional conversations about an alleged assault that has put their campus under a microscope.

Cornell — an elite, high-pressure and, for some, hard-partying school — has become the subject of nationwide scrutiny, after a woman sued the university, a fraternity, a sorority and seven men for what she says was a failure to properly handle her 2024 sexual assault complaint.

The case has created a swirl of outrage, grief and confusion on the school’s Ithaca campus. Some students are shaken that men they’ve sat alongside in lectures or waved at walking through Ho Plaza were named in the shocking lawsuit. Some are defensive about fraternities. And others, particularly those with their own experiences of campus sexual misconduct, are wondering if this is a moment for enduring change.

“There’s a little bit of shock,” said Olympia Hall, 20, a sorority member who leads an anti-sexual assault group on campus. “People are like, Oh, my God, I can’t believe I was in a club with them, or I can’t believe I met them at O-week,” meaning campus orientation.

Ms. Hall’s organization convened three dozen Cornell fraternity and sorority members on Tuesday afternoon to talk about the alleged assault.

Gathered in a classroom, the students tried to process the screenshot of sexually explicit messages sent by members of Chi Phi, the fraternity at the center of the controversy. Fraternity members in the room asked: How was it possible that nobody in the chat had done more to stop what was unfolding over hours?

“If someone in one of the group chats had stood up and said something,” Ms. Hall said, “then it would have created a lot of change.”

Plenty of students interviewed said it is hard for them to imagine challenging the social influence of Greek life on campus, to which roughly one-third of Cornell students belong. Some said Greek life has only grown more socially powerful since the isolation of the Covid pandemic, which left people hungrier for tight social bonds. Still more said they recognize that many of Cornell’s donors have close and nostalgic ties to Greek life.

Others said they hope this will be a moment to reassess social rituals, especially in Cornell’s fraternities and sororities. There’s “Champagne and Shackles,” in which a female and male student are zip-tied together and told to finish a bottle of champagne before being freed. There’s “Thursday Night Dinner” (TnD), in which female sorority members are invited to serve dinner to certain fraternity brothers, who ply them with alcohol.

Claire Ting, who graduated last year and served on student government, said she has long worried about the practice of fraternity brothers putting away the phones of inebriated women attending their parties.

“Part of me had become jaded to seeing this over and over again,” Ms. Ting said of her time on campus, adding that she heard reports about alleged sexual assaults every year of her undergraduate career. “It’s like, ‘Oh, my God, my existence here is going to become a statistic.”

For some freshmen who just arrived at Cornell, hearing about Jane Doe’s case has been a gut punch. Iona Macdonald, 18, was relieved that in her first days at Cornell, administrators required her and every classmate to show up at the enormous Bailey Hall for a lecture on consent and how to report assaults. So she was shaken when news of the alleged campus rape case broke weeks later, with a shocking front-page story in the Cornell Daily Sun.

“I got the feeling that if something bad happened, I would be protected,” Ms. Macdonald said. “I just feel like I got the wrong impression.”

For its part, Cornell has denied that the alleged perpetrators weren’t properly disciplined in its own investigation. “A continuation of the false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case is irresponsible, will make survivors feel less safe and supported, and will perpetuate the underreporting of sexual assault,” said Kyle Kimball, the vice president for university relations, in a statement.

Shoshanna Witchel, 18, understands that many other colleges around the country have experienced similar reckonings, often with little long-term impact on campus culture. She, like other students, can rattle off a list of colleges known for highly public rape cases.

“My prediction is it will put a temporary damper on Greek life, and then it will spring back up,” she said.

There have been some changes already, like the mayor of Ithaca’s decision this week to pause all permits for social events. But students wondered whether anybody would obey, or whether parties would forge on illicitly. Even in the days after news of the lawsuit broke, parties continued, rolling through parents’ weekend as families poured into Ithaca to visit. Some students sensed a tension in the air as classmates tried to let loose.

“I went out this weekend and was offered an open drink,” Ms. Witchell recalled, adding she was at a fraternity house at the time. “Me and my entire friend group were freaked out.”

The lawsuit has attracted attention on social media from celebrities and influencers, creating an uncanny experience for Cornell students who are both trying to process their own emotions and react to a controversy that has become national in scope.

Earlier this week, Hannah Shvets, a senior who also serves on the Ithaca Common Council, a citywide board, sat with her unfinished statistics homework scrolling through Sidechat, a social media app many Cornell students use, in which students post anonymously about campus news. When she opened her feed, nearly every post was about the accuser, identified as Jane Doe. Some posts expressed fury about the university’s handling of the case and compassion for Ms. Doe. Other posts were skeptical. Some were defensive of fraternities, and argued that these fraternity men were an outlier and not representative of Greek life.

“The question is whether any of this changes anything for the victims or perpetrators,” Ms. Shvets, 21, said. “I’m not sure it does.”

She added that some of her friends, disappointed in Cornell administrators, have felt as though solutions must come from students, whether that means creating alternatives to Greek life or shaming the perpetrators on social media.

“At first people were reacting emotionally,” she said, “but now they’re talking in terms of solutions.”

SUMMARY

Cornell University plans to hire outside lawyers to investigate a woman’s claim that she was raped at a fraternity house near campus in 2024, amid growing pressure from students and politicians to explain how the case was handled. The agreement to begin an independent investigation came Wednesday during a conversation between Gov. Kathy Hochul and Michael I. Kotlikoff, the university’s president, the governor said. Political leaders, including Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a Democrat from New York City, have joined many social media commenters in strongly worded critiques of the university and law enforcement officials, arguing that lax penalties for the accused men reinforce a culture of rape and violence at the Ivy League school.

ARTICLE

Cornell Will Hire Outside Lawyers to Investigate 2024 Rape Claim
The university and law enforcement officials are under growing pressure to explain how they handled a woman’s initial claims of being assaulted by a group of students.
By Christopher Maag
Published 2026-10-01 01:25 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/nyregion/hochul-cornell-rape-investigation-lawyers.html

Cornell University plans to hire outside lawyers to investigate a woman’s claim that she was raped at a fraternity house near campus in 2024, amid growing pressure from students and politicians to explain how the case was handled.

The agreement to begin an independent investigation came Wednesday during a conversation between Gov. Kathy Hochul and Michael I. Kotlikoff, the university’s president, the governor said.

“I want answers,” Ms. Hochul said in posts on social media on Wednesday. “I want to know what happened.”

The woman, identified in court papers as Jane Doe, said in a lawsuit filed this month that seven men plied her with drugs and alcohol until she was unconscious, then raped her for hours inside the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024.

Ms. Doe said in court filings that she had never heard back from the campus police or prosecutors after giving her initial statement about the encounter to police. Some of the men involved were expelled and others were suspended, according to the university, which has not disclosed the punishments that each man received, citing privacy rules.

The student newspaper, The Cornell Daily Sun, published an editorial this month naming the seven accused men and criticizing the university’s leaders for their handling of the situation.

Political leaders, including Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a Democrat from New York City, have joined many social media commenters in strongly worded critiques of the university and law enforcement officials, arguing that lax penalties for the accused men reinforce a culture of rape and violence at the Ivy League school.

Rebecca Valli, a spokeswoman for Cornell, confirmed the decision to begin an independent investigation. Ms. Hochul automatically became a member of Cornell’s board of trustees when she became governor in 2021. In her brief comments on Wednesday, Ms. Hochul appeared to acknowledge the widely held view that the university was in need of change.

“This culture has to stop,” she said.

SUMMARY

Gov. In a post on X on Thursday night, Ms. Hochul said that she would be assigning Ms. James, who had already begun a review of the way law enforcement handled the matter, to oversee the investigation in Tompkins County. “New information has raised serious questions about how this case was handled, and I’ve lost faith in the Tompkins County D.A.’s ability to fairly oversee it,” Ms. Hochul said.

ARTICLE

Hochul Names Letitia James as Special Prosecutor in Cornell Case
Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed the state attorney general to investigate a former Cornell University student’s allegation of rape. The woman has sued seven men in connection with the alleged assault.
By Santul Nerkar, Benjamin Oreskes and Hurubie Meko
Published 2026-10-02 00:15 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/01/nyregion/letitia-james-cornell-rape-prosecutor.html

Gov. Kathy Hochul has named Letitia James, the New York State attorney general, to serve as special prosecutor to investigate a woman’s allegation that she was raped in a fraternity house near Cornell University’s campus in October 2024.

In a post on X on Thursday night, Ms. Hochul said that she would be assigning Ms. James, who had already begun a review of the way law enforcement handled the matter, to oversee the investigation in Tompkins County.

“New information has raised serious questions about how this case was handled, and I’ve lost faith in the Tompkins County D.A.’s ability to fairly oversee it,” Ms. Hochul said.

She added, “The young woman at the center of this case deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued.”

The announcement marked a dramatic development in a case that has horrified many Americans and renewed a long-running national conversation about sexual assault on college campuses.

The authorities in Ithaca, N.Y., have faced intense backlash over how they investigated the Oct. 19, 2024, encounter between a woman known as Jane Doe and a number of men at the Chi Phi fraternity house. Facing a public outcry, Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins County district attorney, said on Monday that his office would reopen the investigation into Jane Doe’s allegations.

In a lawsuit filed last month, the woman said that when she was a 20-year-old sophomore, she was plied with alcohol and drugs and then raped by several men at the fraternity house. She reported the incident to the Cornell University Police Department several weeks later, but no criminal charges were filed.

At the heart of the criticism has been the revelation that the woman, in her statements to the police, said that she could say “with 100 percent confidence I was raped.” Mr. Van Houten has said that his office primarily reviewed a six-page report provided by Cornell police, which omitted the definitive language detailed in a transcription of her interview with investigators.

Lawyers for at least three of the seven men named in Jane Doe’s lawsuit have issued statements denying criminal wrongdoing. In hours of interviews during a university investigation in the winter of 2024, the seven men denied wrongdoing. Four said they had consensual sexual interactions with Jane Doe; three denied participating in sexual encounters altogether.

On Thursday morning, The New York Times, after obtaining more than 1,000 pages from the university’s internal inquiry, published a detailed account of the woman’s weeks of struggle before she reported the episode.

Ms. Hochul had previously struck an agreement with Michael I. Kotlikoff, Cornell’s president, that the university would hire outside lawyers to begin an independent investigation.

In a statement on Thursday, Ms. James said that the case would be investigated “fully and fairly." Mr. Van Houten did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

With her appointment, Ms. James may “prosecute any offenses arising from that investigation” and present evidence to a grand jury, Ms. Hochul said in a statement.

Thomas Giuffra, the woman’s lawyer, said the announcement was “wonderful news” during an interview on NewsNation’s “Cuomo” late Thursday.

“My intention tomorrow, first thing, was to write a letter requesting that Governor Hochul appoint a special prosecutor because my client and I had zero confidence in this district attorney’s ability to prosecute,” Mr. Giuffra said.

Mr. Van Houten has defended his office’s work. In a statement this week, he said that the original statement the woman gave to police did not seem to warrant criminal charges.

“Jane Doe’s sworn statement in November of 2024 did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped,” he said.

Stefanos Chen and Caitlyn Freeman contributed reporting.

mamdani-rent-freeze-lawsuit-nyc.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 30  Words: 1214/1216

SUMMARY

A “rent freeze” on nearly one million rent-stabilized apartments in New York City went into effect on Thursday, prompting cries of victory from tenant advocates. At the same time, a group of landlords seeking to overturn the freeze made public dozens of pages of internal communications between city officials and members of the panel that approved it, claiming they showed improper efforts to influence an independent process. The city turned over the documents as part of a lawsuit arguing that the administration of Mayor Zohran Mamdani pressured the panel, the Rent Guidelines Board, to prioritize tenants’ concerns and disregard landlords’ financial challenges in its decision-making.

ARTICLE

Landlords Release Emails and Texts in Lawsuit Over Mamdani’s Rent Freeze
The communications were revealed as part of a lawsuit challenging the rent freeze on rent-stabilized units in New York City, which went into effect on Thursday.
By Mihir Zaveri and Dana Rubinstein
Published 2026-10-01 16:55 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/01/nyregion/mamdani-rent-freeze-lawsuit-nyc.html

A “rent freeze” on nearly one million rent-stabilized apartments in New York City went into effect on Thursday, prompting cries of victory from tenant advocates. At the same time, a group of landlords seeking to overturn the freeze made public dozens of pages of internal communications between city officials and members of the panel that approved it, claiming they showed improper efforts to influence an independent process.

The city turned over the documents as part of a lawsuit arguing that the administration of Mayor Zohran Mamdani pressured the panel, the Rent Guidelines Board, to prioritize tenants’ concerns and disregard landlords’ financial challenges in its decision-making.

The communications made public on Thursday are mostly mundane exchanges about the logistics of when and where to hold public meetings and make announcements, and the schedules of board members and the organizations and people invited to testify before the board. They do not show Mr. Mamdani or a member of his team explicitly directing members of the board to approve a rent freeze.

Still, they provide a rarely seen view of the board’s process, which is typically opaque. And lawyers for the landlords claimed that the documents showed “coordination and collaboration” between the city and the board — enough for the court to invalidate the policy.

At an unrelated news conference on Thursday, Mr. Mamdani said he was confident in the board’s “independent decision,” adding that it had been made “on the basis of all the information that they had in front of them.”

It is unclear when the judge in the case, Brendan T. Lantry of State Supreme Court in Manhattan, will make a decision. Any leases starting on or after Thursday will be subject to the freeze, at least until he issues a ruling.

If Justice Lantry sides with the landlords, the freeze will be nullified and will not apply to lease terms that begin after the ruling. And the board will have to start its process over again, which could result in members’ approving rent increases rather than a freeze, imperiling one of Mr. Mamdani’s key campaign promises.

The nine members of the Rent Guidelines Board are appointed by the mayor, and often align with the ideology and priorities of City Hall. But in deciding each year whether and how much rents should go up in rent-stabilized housing, they are supposed to consider a voluminous amount of data, taking into account the economic pressures facing the real estate industry as well as renters.

During the mayoral campaign, Mr. Mamdani promised to “freeze the rent,” drawing complaints that he was trying to inappropriately influence the board’s process. Earlier this year, he appointed a majority of members to the board, and in June, the board delivered a freeze on both one-year and two-year leases for the first time in city history.

Within weeks, landlords filed their lawsuit. In a rare step last month, Justice Lantry sided with the landlords in their request that the city turn over communications between City Hall officials and members of the board.

“The question naturally arises: How would the mayor comply with his ‘guarantee’ to the voters to ‘freeze the rent’ unless he, or his staff, communicated with the board to ensure that the board refrained from imposing any rental increase?” Justice Lantry wrote in his Sept. 16 order.

It is not illegal for the mayor’s office to communicate with members of the board, and mayors commonly appoint members who are likely to be sympathetic to their priorities. But landlords claim that given Mr. Mamdani’s clear stance on the issue, the outcome of this year’s vote was “predetermined.”

“The City has now produced documents from no less than eight different top City Hall officials who communicated directly with R.G.B. members and staff during the first six months of this year,” Randy Mastro, a lawyer representing landlords and a critic of the mayor, wrote in a letter to the court on Thursday. He asked the judge to schedule a hearing to allow the landlords’ lawyers to question city officials and board members.

In a letter filed with the court on Tuesday, Steven Banks, the city’s top lawyer, said that the communications showed that the board acted “with the utmost honesty, integrity and independence, reflecting a genuine desire of the board members to serve the public and meaningfully participate in this quasi-legislative process.”

Brandon Mancilla, one of the members appointed by Mr. Mamdani, said in an email on Thursday that he was “never influenced by any city official, before or during the process, to vote in one way or another on what the rent adjustment should be.”

Mr. Mamdani on Thursday also cited reporting by the news publication Gothamist indicating that Randy Mastro, a lawyer representing the landlords, had himself tried to influence the board last year when he was first deputy mayor under Eric Adams.

In a statement, Mr. Mastro acknowledged that he had communicated with the board’s chairman at the time, but said he had merely conveyed Mr. Adams’s disagreement with the board’s anticipated decision shortly before its vote. Mr. Mastro said there was “a world of difference” between his efforts and “orchestrating a sham process with a preordained outcome to do exactly what the mayor dictated and promised in his campaign.”

Vicki Been, a former deputy mayor for housing and economic development under Mayor Bill de Blasio who is not involved in the lawsuit, said it was typical for City Hall to be in touch with the board about logistical matters.

Asked about the communications revealed on Thursday, Ms. Been said, “I don’t see anything concerning.”

According to the documents, at least one City Hall staff member was in regular contact with the board’s chairwoman.

They include a March text message exchange between the chairwoman, Chantella Mitchell, and Arvind Sindhwani, a deputy chief of staff under the deputy mayor of housing and planning, in which Ms. Mitchell agrees to push back the date of a preliminary vote on rent increases to May 7 from April 30.

Another exchange between Mr. Sindhwani and Ms. Mitchell took place in April, a few days before a hearing where the board was set to discuss research about how much costs had gone up for landlords.

Mr. Sindhwani said that he had “notes” related to the subject matter, and asked Ms. Mitchell to set up a call to discuss them. “Please take a look before we chat,” Mr. Sindhwani wrote.

It is not clear what the two discussed.

Ms. Mitchell also agreed to share with Mr. Sindhwani a list of groups invited to testify before the board, the communications show.

Ms. Mitchell declined to comment on Thursday.

The communications also show that the mayor’s staff, including Cea Weaver, the director of his Office to Protect Tenants, and Leila Bozorg, the deputy mayor for housing and planning, set up meetings with board members before and after their appointments, though no details were included about what transpired during those meetings.

The only messages included in the documents from Mr. Mamdani himself are a brief exchange in which he shared his cellphone number with Mr. Mancilla on Feb. 10, days before Mr. Mancilla’s appointment was made public.

Mr. Mancilla then asked if he should call the mayor.

“No need my man but thank you! Hope you’re well,” Mr. Mamdani replied.

Sally Goldenberg contributed reporting.

================================================================================
nyc-affordable-housing-neighborhoods.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 29  Words: 1130/1131
================================================================================

SUMMARY

Geographically and culturally distant, these New York City neighborhoods have something in common: They are among the 12 community districts that have allowed the least affordable housing to be built over the past five years, according to an analysis released on Thursday by the Department of City Planning. Starting Jan. 1, the City Council will lose its authority to reject many types of new housing in those places. One of those measures created a “fast track” for development by giving the City Planning Commission, instead of the City Council, the authority to approve or reject housing projects that include affordable housing in the 12 community districts that have allowed the least affordable housing to be built, relative to their size.

ARTICLE

The New York City Neighborhoods Where It’s Hardest to Build Housing
Some City Council members are losing an informal veto power over new projects in their districts after voters approved a measure aimed at eliminating roadblocks to development.
By Mihir Zaveri
Published 2026-10-01 04:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/01/nyregion/nyc-affordable-housing-neighborhoods.html

On the South Shore of Staten Island, single-family homes are interspersed with woods and wetlands. In Bay Ridge, Brooklyn, small apartment buildings and houses line streets near the Verrazano Bridge. On Manhattan’s Upper East Side, majestic prewar co-op buildings rise alongside Central Park.

Geographically and culturally distant, these New York City neighborhoods have something in common: They are among the 12 community districts that have allowed the least affordable housing to be built over the past five years, according to an analysis released on Thursday by the Department of City Planning. That distinction will soon carry consequences.

Starting Jan. 1, the City Council will lose its authority to reject many types of new housing in those places.

“For far too long, our city has lagged in terms of housing production relative to our growth,” said Sideya Sherman, the director of the department, “but particularly the area of affordable housing production, where we see some communities that are creating a lot of housing and some communities that are creating little to none.”

The districts identified on Wednesday are clustered in parts of eastern Queens, southern Brooklyn, Staten Island and Manhattan’s Upper West and Upper East Sides.

They include:

- Brooklyn Community District 10: Bay Ridge, Dyker Heights
- Brooklyn C.D. 12: Borough Park, Kensington
- Brooklyn C.D. 18: Canarsie, Flatlands
-  Manhattan C.D. 7: Upper West Side
- Manhattan C.D. 8: Upper East Side, Roosevelt Island
- Queens C.D. 4: Corona, Elmhurst
- Queens C.D. 5: Ridgewood, Maspeth, Middle Village
- Queens C.D. 10: South Ozone Park, Howard Beach
- Queens C.D. 11: Auburndale, Bayside, Douglaston
- Queens C.D. 13: Queens Village, Bellerose, Rosedale
- Staten Island C.D. 2: Mid-Island
- Staten Island C.D. 3: South Shore

The effort to spur development in these areas is the latest step in New York’s continuing struggle with a housing shortage that has helped make the city one of the most expensive places to live in the world.

Nearly everybody agrees that the city needs more housing. But there have long been tensions over who gets to decide where it is built: City Hall, which has a broad view of the problem, or the City Council, whose members represent neighborhood interests.

In particular, City Hall officials and council members are at odds over members’ unofficial veto power over projects in their district. While many developments must be approved by the whole Council, it has typically allowed the decision to rest with the member representing the district where the project would be built.

But in November, voters approved several ballot measures that would threaten that veto, and make it easier to build homes.

One of those measures created a “fast track” for development by giving the City Planning Commission, instead of the City Council, the authority to approve or reject housing projects that include affordable housing in the 12 community districts that have allowed the least affordable housing to be built, relative to their size. A majority of the planning commission’s members are appointed by the mayor.

The City Council had opposed the measures, which were written by an independent commission and supported by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, asserting that its members needed the threat of the veto to push for the inclusion of amenities like parks and schools. Council members had also used it to pressure developers to make their projects even more affordable than initially proposed.

Phil Wong, a Democrat who represents parts of Queens, said the city was moving in the “wrong direction” by taking land-use decisions away from neighborhoods.

“New Yorkers voted for these charter changes, whether everyone fully understood what they were voting for or not, and unfortunately this is one of the consequences,” he said.

The low-development districts were identified using a formula: The number of affordable homes permitted to be built in each community district between 2021 and 2026 was divided by the total number of housing units that district contained in 2021. The result was an approximate rate of affordable housing production.

In the community district including Bay Ridge, for example, which had more than 55,000 homes in 2021, only three affordable homes were added over the past five years. In the Queens community district that includes neighborhoods like Rosedale and Cambria Heights, which had more than 66,000 homes in 2021, only nine affordable homes were added.

More than 150 affordable homes were added over the past five years on the Upper West Side. But because the area was already relatively dense — it had more than 126,000 homes in 2021 — its rate of affordable housing development was relatively low.

In each of the 12 community districts identified on Wednesday, the rate was 0.2 percent or less.

By contrast, the community districts that allowed the most affordable housing to be built are almost all in the Bronx. Each of the top five districts added more than 2,500 affordable homes over five years, a rate of more than seven percent.

The ballot measure that created the “fast track” also gave the mayor powers to more quickly build affordable housing financed by the city, which Mr. Mamdani has already used.

Voters also approved two other measures intended to encourage development.

One made it easier to build “modest” developments, such as those that would be up to 30 percent bigger than current rules allow. Those changes would also be subject to approval from the planning commission, and not the City Council.

Another created an appeals board that could overrule a decision by the Council to reject or modify an affordable housing development. The board would need agreement between two of its three members: the mayor, the Council speaker and the president of the borough where the development was proposed.

The effects of the changes may become clear only in the coming years, as developers assess the demand for new homes.

But the new paradigm is sure to upset some Council members and local activists who are loath to cede control over development in their neighborhoods.

Frank Morano, a Republican representing the South Shore of Staten Island, said that his district was “not an empty space on a planner’s map” and that the changes removed a layer of “local accountability.”

“I support creating housing, including affordable housing, but it has to make sense for the neighborhood, the infrastructure and the people who already call it home,” Mr. Morano said. “The answer to the housing crisis can’t be stripping communities of their voice and then calling that progress.”

Julie Menin, a Democrat and speaker of the Council, represents a dense district on the Upper East Side. She said it was “critical” that the city plan for the growth that might follow in the affected areas.

“That means working with communities to identify where new housing makes sense and ensuring that growth is accompanied by the transit, infrastructure, public space and other investments neighborhoods need,” she said.

ai-huang-gates-superintelligence.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 26  Words: 1826/1882
================================================================================

SUMMARY

Bret Stephens: Americans are growing hostile to artificial intelligence. Bret: So far the best economic research doesn’t back up the idea that A.I. is eliminating jobs, even in industries that have been early A.I. adopters. Bret: To me, the data center angst is a reminder that Americans of all political stripes always seem to want contrary things: We bemoan the loss of our manufacturing base — and the jobs and communities those manufacturers once supported — then wring our hands over the environmental or aesthetic costs of reacquiring that base.

ARTICLE

Behold the Paragons of Rank Incompetence
Behold the paragons of rank incompetence.
By Frank Bruni and Bret Stephens
Published 2026-10-01 09:07 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/01/opinion/ai-huang-gates-superintelligence.html

Bret Stephens: Americans are growing hostile to artificial intelligence. I’ve warned that letting A.I. write for you can be brain-eating, soul-destroying, even democracy-undermining. There’s also a bipartisan backlash against data centers. Plus a widespread conviction that A.I. is going to destroy most jobs. Not to mention dark fears — especially from its very creators — that it could go rogue and lead to the destruction of a large chunk of humanity itself.

So, of course, the knee-jerk contrarian in me now finds myself warming to A.I., thinking it will create more jobs than it will destroy, generate medical and scientific breakthroughs that will save and prolong lives, and allow humanity to discover new skills and achieve previously unimaginable goals.

Help me out, Frank: Which side of my brain is wrong?

Frank Bruni: Medical and scientific advances — absolutely. That side of your brain is working just fine. And I can buy the idea that A.I. won’t be quite the jobs apocalypse that many people fear.

But I see no arithmetic by which it doesn’t diminish the overall number of jobs. And the popular notion among A.I. evangelists that such job elimination will free people in joyless careers to wander rhapsodically through the flowery meadows of creativity — if they don’t need their wages, why aren’t they wandering now? How will they suddenly be able to afford their wandering when a bot has replaced them?

Would you support some version of universal basic income? Because not everybody will get rich off A.I. stocks; according to a Gallup survey last year, more than 40 percent of American adults aren’t in the market at all, and stock ownership is predictably concentrated among the most affluent.

Bret: So far the best economic research doesn’t back up the idea that A.I. is eliminating jobs, even in industries that have been early A.I. adopters. That stands to reason: Productivity-enhancing technologies like A.I. are typically revenue enhancing, and new revenues typically mean more jobs. A lot of types of work will doubtlessly be ended by A.I. — secretarial and paralegal work, for instance, or traditional coding. But many more jobs — whose work might seem even stranger to us now than, say, the description of an airplane mechanic of the 1940s would seem to a train engineer of the 1890s — will come into existence.

As for universal basic income, I think it’s a terrible idea — an invitation for people not to work, which creates a million personal and social problems in its turn. And since we already have $40 trillion in national debt, it would also speed the way to total fiscal collapse.

Frank: Leaving U.B.I. aside for the moment, I have a problem with the idea that the job market will just transition or adapt. Yes, the nimbleness and innovations of private enterprise are remarkable. Yes, there’s a genius to capitalism. But government will get involved — government will have to get involved — and right now that’s petrifying. We have in the Trump administration not only a paragon of rank incompetence (Iran, ICE, the Reflecting Pool, you name it) but also proof that American voters can support — serially — such madness. So moving past President Trump is not the same thing as moving into the clear.

To go back to your opening question of whether A.I. is the Grim Reaper or a keeper, the answer depends utterly, to the point Bill Gates just made in a conversation with our colleague Ezra Klein, on our prudent management and careful planning. Bret, how confident do you feel that today’s America can do prudent management and careful planning?

Bret: Zero confidence. We’re long past the days when the government could manage anything competently, like the Tennessee Valley Authority or the Apollo program. We now live in the era in which it takes government many decades to complete just a few miles of a subway.

But I also think Bill Gates is wrong — or, well, probably wrong. The best regulation for A.I. is self-regulation, which is what OpenAI has done by delaying the release of its newest agent until it is sure it is safe. Also, I was much more impressed with Ezra’s interview of Jensen Huang, the Nvidia C.E.O. Huang’s argument is that the A.I. panic into which we seem to be talking ourselves is wildly overblown, and that the A.I. revolution will look a lot like past technological revolutions: a process that will be far more creative than it is destructive, even if it involves a fair bit of both.

I also think that whatever we choose to do here in the U.S. to impose curbs on A.I. will not make an iota’s difference to what China chooses to do. And I’d rather have America in the lead in the world’s most important technology than to cede the field to an autocratic competitor.

Frank: There is indeed something about the fever pitch of A.I. doomsaying that feels to me like precisely the kind of hysteria we must distrust. The measure of raw emotion in it doesn’t invite wisdom. So I don’t advocate a fast and thorough retreat here — I think Bernie Sanders, for example, is sounding too loud and too showy a note of alarm — but I do think that some kind of pause and some measure of reflection would be sensible and wouldn’t consign us to being economically foolish A.I. laggards. Again, my problem is whether we have the systems and leaders to make proper use of such a pause. This is the epitome of a moment when sage stewardship is everything, but the dawn of A.I. comes at the dusk of American sanity.

Bret: Sage stewardship probably ended around the time of the Eisenhower administration.

Frank: I mean, Trump’s meeting with tech billionaires at the White House on Tuesday was a joke. He told the gathered titans how “very brilliant” they are, clearly reveling in the belief that his proximity to all that brainpower affirmed his own. He prodded them to sign a vague voluntary agreement to do whatever the A.I. equivalent of wearing a seatbelt is. Most impressive of all, he got them to endorse his rebranding of “artificial intelligence” as “super intelligence.” How super! It’s reminiscent of trying to end the Iran war by simply claiming it’s not a war.

Bret: He would have done better to call it Super-Duper-Pooper-Scooper Intelligence, since some days I think the most we can hope for from A.I. is that it might clean up at least some of our messes.

But I’m curious about your views on one more point of A.I. contention: data centers. After years in which liberals and conservatives alike bemoaned the deindustrialization of America — factories shutting down and leaving rust belts in their wake — there is bipartisan opposition to an industry that promises to re-industrialize many of these same places.

Frank: But to re-industrialize them in a highly obnoxious way. To a certain degree, the data center opposition is NIMBYism for the digital age. But it also goes far beyond that, because the centers are mirrors and vessels of so many anxieties, so much bitterness. They’re reminders of how many tech titans far from these communities are accruing more and more wealth that’s not shared, so they’re symbols of the country’s gross — and, I think, unsustainable — economic inequalities.

They create enormous electricity demands at precisely the time when the Trump administration is turning its back on alternative sources of energy — a decision, by the way, that’s clearly going to leave us far behind international competitors in that technology race and that market. All in all, it’s hard to look at a hulking data center on the side of a road near you and feel a tingle about the glories of progress.

Bret: To me, the data center angst is a reminder that Americans of all political stripes always seem to want contrary things: We bemoan the loss of our manufacturing base — and the jobs and communities those manufacturers once supported — then wring our hands over the environmental or aesthetic costs of reacquiring that base. We worry whenever economic growth lags and then become furious that some of the people providing economic growth might be getting an outsize share of the spoils. We want faster cures for diseases, faster access to every conceivable kind of information, faster delivery of our takeout orders, but at the same time convince ourselves that the technology that can help us do all that is going to end humanity as we know it.

The hard truth that too many Americans won’t confront is that you can’t have it both ways. Want to live the truly simple life? It’s probably going to be harder and darker and poorer than the life we have now. And God knows humanity has tried it. Want to live in a world in which technology powers growth and growth takes energy? That’ll have its downsides, too. We just can’t seem to be content with the choices we make.

Frank: We don’t want to make choices, period. Or have anything presented to us as an either/or, plus/minus, benefit/cost decision. With national affluence comes national brattiness, and the greatness of America’s promise — you can be whoever you want, the sky’s the limit, the frontier is endless — is coupled with the inevitability of Americans’ letdown. Much of what we’ve seen over the past decade of American life, especially our political life, are the wages of that disappointment. In a broad historical and international context, we’ve been living the dream. And that turned out to be a font not of satisfaction but of grievance.

Bret: You’ve touched on something really important: There’s a trade-off between the sense — or, I should say, illusion — of limitlessness that is so much a part of the American character and the aimlessness that typifies so much of American life today. So many choices are given to us that every choice we wind up making tends to feel disappointing and dissatisfying. That’s the problem with nearly every society in which freedom is the governing value: It tends to deprive us of a sense of purpose that comes only when we tie ourselves to an ideal or a goal that, in one way or another, limits our freedom.

Frank: There’s an additional — and maybe even bigger — complication or challenge of freedom. It leaves you with responsibility. If you are free to make your own choices, then only you can answer for the way they turn out. That’s a heavy burden that many people can’t bear. The cult of victimhood in modern America is in part a byproduct of freedom. You got in the way of my aspirations. Society blocked my path. Too often, that’s sadly true. But perhaps just as frequently, it’s a dodge. A cop-out. A pretty, self-absolving lie. It feels so much better to rage at others than to train a harsh light on yourself.

Bret: Spoken with the kind of intelligence that, as the Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak reminded us a few months ago, matters most: actual intelligence.

The Times is committed to publishing a diversity of letters to the editor. We’d like to hear what you think about this or any of our articles. Here are some tips. And here’s our email: letters@nytimes.com.
