SUMMARY

Since last month, accusations of rape at Cornell University have caused widespread outrage, renewing a national conversation about sexual assault on college campuses and highlighting the difficulty in achieving justice in such cases. The accusations against seven male students, detailed in a bombshell lawsuit filed by an accuser known as Jane Doe, who was 20 at the time of the encounter, have renewed a national conversation about sexual assault on college campuses. In November 2024, Jane Doe told Cornell police officials that she was “pretty OK” with the two men she had begun the sexual encounter with, but that as more men showed up looking for sex, she came to understand the encounter as rape.

ARTICLE

Why Prosecutors May Face Legal Hurdles in the Cornell Investigation
Experts in sexual assault cases said it may not be easy to win a conviction on the rape allegations that Jane Doe has made against fraternity members.
By Santul Nerkar and Benjamin Weiser
Published 2026-10-02 07:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/nyregion/cornell-investigation-prosecution-challenges.html

Since last month, accusations of rape at Cornell University have caused widespread outrage, renewing a national conversation about sexual assault on college campuses and highlighting the difficulty in achieving justice in such cases.

The accusations against seven male students, detailed in a bombshell lawsuit filed by an accuser known as Jane Doe, who was 20 at the time of the encounter, have renewed a national conversation about sexual assault on college campuses.

The men have not been charged, and it is unclear how long an investigation by the special prosecutor, Letitia James, the New York State attorney general, will take. Prosecuting sex crimes presents inherent challenges, and a potential prosecution of the Cornell students faces distinct and considerable hurdles, legal experts say.

Shifts in the accuser’s account in the days after the encounter — while typical for survivors of sexual assault, experts say — could damage her credibility in front of a potential jury. A report presented by the Cornell Police Department to the Tompkins County, N.Y., district attorney in 2024 left out her claim that she was raped, providing another discrepancy for defense lawyers to seize on.

“Just because a victim’s narrative evolves or changes doesn’t mean it’s untrue,” said Moira Penza, a former federal prosecutor. “But grand juries and trials can’t stop at ‘believe women.’”

Making it harder still are New York’s rape laws, which make it difficult for an intoxicated person to prove they did not consent to a sexual encounter. Supporters of sexual assault victims say that the arc of Jane Doe’s case shows that the process for reporting such crimes is flawed.

“There’s a game of broken telephone that often exists for victims,” said Shulim Leifer, an advocate for sexual assault victims in New York. “I think this could be used as a prime example to show where the gaps are in the system.”

District attorneys sometimes decline to bring charges or abandon cases involving sexual assault, an issue that came to a head early in the #MeToo movement, highlighted by an initial decision not to prosecute Harvey Weinstein. Sometimes, a victim is unwilling to testify, as occurred in the case involving Kobe Bryant, the former N.B.A. star who was accused of rape in 2003 before charges were dropped the following year.

In her lawsuit, Jane Doe says that she was plied with drugs and alcohol and raped by multiple men on Oct. 19, 2024, at the Chi Phi fraternity house near Cornell’s campus. She reported the encounter to Cornell police on Nov. 14, 2024. Using a condensed version of her interviews — which omitted her claim that she was raped — the district attorney declined to bring charges.

In the days after the encounter, Jane Doe messaged one of the men whom she would later accuse of rape — assuring him that “non of the sexual stuff was illegal” — according to documents reviewed by The New York Times. In November 2024, Jane Doe told Cornell police officials that she was “pretty OK” with the two men she had begun the sexual encounter with, but that as more men showed up looking for sex, she came to understand the encounter as rape.

R. Timothy Jansen, a defense lawyer who represented the football player Jameis Winston, who was accused of rape at Florida State University, said that prosecutors would have a hard time proving Jane Doe’s case to a jury. (Prosecutors declined to bring charges against Mr. Winston.) The shifts in the accuser’s accounts, as well as the gap between the time of the alleged assault and when the accuser made her report to Cornell police, would prove to be especially damaging, he said.

“A criminal defense lawyer will destroy her on cross-examination,” Mr. Jansen said. “The whole case is going to be her credibility.”

Jason Goldman, a criminal defense lawyer and former prosecutor in Brooklyn, said the messages Jane Doe sent after the encounter would “be difficult for a jury to square away.” But Ms. Penza said that such inconsistencies were not uncommon for sexual assault victims.

“It’s the norm, not the exception, for a sex crime victim’s initial account to leave out details, describe things non-linearly, and even minimize what happened,” Ms. Penza said.

Mimi Rocah, a former federal prosecutor who also served as the Westchester County, N.Y., district attorney from 2021 to 2024, said that a victim’s statement may initially be contradictory or confusing for many reasons.

“It could be wandering and all over the place because they suffered a trauma, and they don’t know or can’t process or express it,” Ms. Rocah said. She added that prosecutors cannot just sit down and say, “All right, tell me what happened.” District attorney’s offices must have the training and sensitivity to investigate sex crimes.

“This is like 101 of trauma-informed interviewing,” Ms. Rocah said, “and clearly here that did not happen.”

In New York, another challenge lies in the state’s rape laws, which Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins County district attorney, has blamed in part for his decision in 2024 not to prosecute the students who were accused by Jane Doe. (Lawyers for at least three of the men have issued statements denying criminal wrongdoing. In a university investigation in the winter of 2024, the men denied wrongdoing in hours of interviews.)

In her suit filed in September, Jane Doe said she drank copious amounts of alcohol — including, at one point, 10 drinks in a three-hour period — and was pressured by the men into taking ketamine, a powerful anesthetic, making her unable to consent to sex.

Under New York’s law, people who became intoxicated by their own volition cannot claim they were “mentally incapacitated” and thus unable to consent during a sexual encounter, unless they can prove they were physically helpless.

Proposed legislation would allow third-degree rape to be charged in more instances in which a person was intoxicated. Mr. Leifer, the victims’ advocate, supports the new legislation, and said that the current law put an “improper onus” on victims to explain why they were raped.

“There is no manual that anyone gets that says, ‘Here’s what to do when you are raped,’” Mr. Leifer said.

Georgia Gee contributed research.

ai-tech-innovation.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 25  Words: 1530/1590

SUMMARY

The walls are closing in on artificial intelligence: moratoriums on new data center construction, job-loss concerns and rising alarm over safety. Workers whose time was saved can move on to other tasks, also helping the economy expand. Later, innovations such as the telegraph, the telephone, railroads, the internal combustion engine and the commercialization of electricity produced a golden age of productivity growth that carried on into the 20th century.

ARTICLE

Six Charts That Show Just How Much We Need A.I.
All the worry about artificial intelligence should not obscure this key point: If we don’t develop it, we’ll be a lot worse off.
By Steven Rattner
Published 2026-10-02 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/opinion/ai-tech-innovation.html

The walls are closing in on artificial intelligence: moratoriums on new data center construction, job-loss concerns and rising alarm over safety.

All valid worries. But none are sufficient to turn away from one of the greatest technological innovations in history, one with the potential to reinvigorate our slow-growth economy and make it easier to address the country’s increasingly challenging problems. For all the concern about the technology, we need A.I. to deliver.

A quick Economics 101 refresh: Growth — and the increases in incomes and living standards that come with it — is a function of just two things, a larger labor force and how much each worker produces. More workers increase the overall size of the pie. But individuals don’t get a larger share unless each worker produces more.

Greater national income, particularly if it comes from higher productivity, gives the nation more legroom to redistribute wealth fairly among citizens and reduce inequality. It also provides resources to hold down the national debt and fund public services such as health care and education.

On their own, workers generally can’t become more productive. Investment helps, such as by replacing old manufacturing equipment. Training can benefit, too. But the key driver of efficiency is technological innovation. Think robots in factories, self-checkout in a drugstore or automated lawn mowers.

Inventions like these lower the amount of labor required to perform tasks, which reduces companies’ costs and keeps a lid on prices. Workers whose time was saved can move on to other tasks, also helping the economy expand.

For thousands of years, humans suffered from little innovation and saw little change in standards of living. Then, around 1500, productivity started to grow as farming methods became modestly more modern. Beginning in the mid-19th century, the beneficent effects of the Industrial Revolution took hold thanks to extraordinary innovations such as mechanized looms (famously attacked by the Luddites) and steam power.

Later, innovations such as the telegraph, the telephone, railroads, the internal combustion engine and the commercialization of electricity produced a golden age of productivity growth that carried on into the 20th century.

In the early 1970s, productivity growth slowed and has remained depressed for most of the past half-century, with notable exceptions such as the internet boom. Ending the productivity sluggishness should be a top national priority, and using A.I. is the most promising way.

Examples of its power already abound. Siemens uses its A.I. co-pilot to walk technicians through repairs of factory machines, decreasing time spent on unplanned equipment maintenance by 25 percent. Kaiser Permanente has deployed an A.I. scribe to streamline note-taking, cutting documentation time for physicians by nearly 16,000 hours. John Deere has an A.I.-equipped camera system that saved farmers 31 million gallons of herbicide mix in 2025 by spraying the substance only where the system detects weeds.

More will come. History suggests that innovation’s effects on the economy can take years, even decades, to play out. The surge in productivity growth after World War II was driven in part by the continuing deployment of electricity generators and other 19th-century inventions.

Soon after Henry Ford introduced the assembly line in 1913, he famously raised the pay of his workers to $5 a day. Because of his factories’ high productivity, the company’s profits still soared, and the price of a Model T fell to just $260 in 1925 from as much as $600 in 1913.

In 1987, the economist Robert Solow, who would later win a Nobel Prize, said, “You can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics.” He spoke prematurely. Productivity rose sharply in the late 1990s, stimulating growth, adding jobs and leading the federal government under President Bill Clinton to an unusual (and never matched) string of budget surpluses.

Anticipating the unfolding prosperity of his time, John Maynard Keynes wrote in his 1930 essay, “Economic Possibilities for Our Grandchildren,” that within a century, the average worker would toil for only 15 hours a week. Keynes got that wrong, but not for the seemingly obvious reason. Productivity — and accordingly, inflation-adjusted wages — has risen so much since then that Americans could labor just seven hours a week to afford the same lifestyle they enjoyed in 1930. Instead, the average American works 38.3 hours a week, down only 20 percent from 1930. But workers now have more time for leisure and family, and the hours they do spend on the job support bigger incomes and more comfortable lifestyles than their grandparents enjoyed — more goods, bigger houses, pleasure travel and the like.

A.I. has the potential to enhance the way we live in the same way. It saved me and my colleague, Will McGrew, many hours of prowling the internet to research this essay. That left us with time to do other tasks.

Of course there are risks. A.I. will eliminate jobs in some sectors — just like telephone operators disappeared in the last century — even as the productivity gains it generates will create demand for new jobs in others. The historical record has borne this out time and time again. No technological improvement in the history of the world has ultimately failed to create more jobs than it destroyed.

When I started on Wall Street in 1982, we had only hand calculators — no personal computers, no Excel for running models, just pencils and large sheets of paper on which to scribble our calculations. Those “spreadsheets” then had to be typed by a secretarial pool. If my boss found a mistake or wanted a different scenario prepared, we started from scratch. As the technology evolved, lots of those menial tasks disappeared, and yet employment in the financial sector is vastly greater today.

To date, A.I. has killed a limited number of jobs while boosting employment for plumbers, electricians, data scientists and market research analysts. More job losses — and offsetting employment gains — are probably to come, though. The country’s leaders need to anticipate the possibility of an A.I. “rust belt” and create policies to help workers adjust. The government can provide retraining and educational subsidies to younger workers. For older ones, the nation needs to shore up the social safety net, potentially embracing ideas such as wage insurance for those displaced. And securing the solvency of Social Security and Medicare is essential.

The country has dealt with challenges like these before. In 1900, 41 percent of the American work force was on the farm. By 2022, that had dropped to 1.2 percent. The transition succeeded because many workers migrated to cities and the expanding manufacturing sector. Yes, the economies of agricultural states suffered, but we mitigated that with a wide array of government programs aimed at shoring up rural America.

The cost of these government investments should be paid by the beneficiaries of A.I. Thus far, the gains from artificial intelligence have accrued not to workers, but to investors who have reaped soaring profits from the explosive increase in the value of companies in the A.I. industry.

We have many ways to make that right. Some have suggested a “token tax.” (Tokens are a measure of A.I. usage.) The wildly generous tax benefits A.I. companies receive for their capital expenditures — enacted in President Trump’s first term and made permanent in his second — should be curbed, as should the sales and property tax exemptions that many states provide to data centers. And with corporate profits generally booming, Washington should edge the corporate tax rate back up toward the 35 percent that existed before Donald Trump’s presidency.

The more daunting challenge A.I. poses is to ensure that the technology is developed and used safely, a necessity that tech C.E.O.s and independent experts have spoken about with increasing urgency. On this, too, I believe humans can succeed in managing the risk.

The United States and other nations have safely regulated food, medicines, aviation, nuclear energy and many other potentially dangerous items. I remember the widespread fears that the Nuclear Age brought. I participated in air raid drills in the basement of my suburban elementary school, huddled near barrels of emergency rations. Movie thrillers such as “Fail Safe” and “On the Beach” dramatized nuclear catastrophe, and later “The China Syndrome” warned about nuclear power. Yet many nations have continued to develop atomic energy and nuclear weapons with a remarkable record of safety.

As with other powerful technologies, new A.I. products must be tested thoroughly by a governmental entity before they can be deployed. Among other things, governments should consider mandating kill switches in A.I. products, which would provide humans a final defense against models that have gone rogue. Containing the spread of A.I. technology will be more difficult than, say, limiting nuclear proliferation, because A.I. technology is easier to transfer across borders. This is why international cooperation, particularly with China, is critical for global A.I. security. At the same time, powerful models depend on physical inputs — microchips and data centers — and the U.S. lead in the A.I. build-out will therefore be an asset for keeping A.I. under control.

Those calling to stop A.I. development and those insisting that no regulation is necessary are both wrong. As with many promising technologies, the risks of A.I. will never be eliminated. But they should be manageable. And the payoff could be immense.

The Times is committed to publishing a diversity of letters to the editor. We’d like to hear what you think about this or any of our articles. Here are some tips. And here’s our email: letters@nytimes.com.

trump-biden-economic-message.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 21  Words: 957/1030

SUMMARY

When I served in President Joe Biden’s White House, we had good economic news to report: robust job creation, rising wages, low unemployment and a manufacturing jobs revival. The economic indicator that hurt Mr. Biden the most, inflation, is higher today than it was when Mr. Trump returned to office. While I was the press secretary, the Biden White House often operated as if we still had a media ecosystem built for accuracy and process, rather than one built for immediacy and vibes.

ARTICLE

This Mistake Doomed Biden. Trump Is Falling Into the Same Trap.
When leaders ignore people’s lived experience, their political messaging collapses.
By Karine Jean-Pierre
Published 2026-10-02 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/opinion/trump-biden-economic-message.html

When I served in President Joe Biden’s White House, we had good economic news to report: robust job creation, rising wages, low unemployment and a manufacturing jobs revival. Yes, inflation spiked early in his term, but by the time he left office, it had come down considerably.

Mr. Biden wanted his team to highlight his domestic agenda. His policies were working, and he wanted the country to understand what he was doing and why. But the polling was clear: Our economic message didn’t land.

Senior White House advisers, myself included, would meet for hours, day after day, trying to get a handle on the mismatch between the strength of the data and the flagging public confidence. There were differences of opinion and long discussions about the best way to move forward. We pored over the numbers, worked through different messaging options and kept looking for a way to break through.

But Americans weren’t feeling it. Too many people were struggling with the prices of groceries, rent, child care and gas. Their lived experience did not match the encouraging economic news, and that disconnect shaped the entire public conversation.

We believed that if we laid out the evidence clearly enough, people would see what we saw. They didn’t, and we didn’t adjust to meet them where they were.

Some of Mr. Biden’s advisers worried that too much emphasis on the very real challenges people were facing would undermine the case we were making. Others argued that failing to acknowledge those challenges upfront made us sound out of touch. Every day that we failed to reach consensus, the public mood hardened.

The truth is, we had a stale message and outdated models for delivering it. It cost Mr. Biden and, eventually, Vice President Kamala Harris dearly. President Trump is now making a mistake even more damaging.

The economic indicator that hurt Mr. Biden the most, inflation, is higher today than it was when Mr. Trump returned to office. The bond market has been roiled. The Federal Reserve just raised interest rates. Mr. Trump’s trade wars and his war with Iran are hurting the overall economic picture. All of which helps explain his sinking poll numbers.

Mr. Biden repeatedly talked of growing the economy “from the middle out and the bottom up,” but that mantra ultimately didn’t resonate. Mr. Trump’s refrain that we’re the “hottest country anywhere in the world” is a no-sale, both because the facts really aren’t on his side and because he’s barely acknowledging Americans’ legitimate economic worries. By and large, people aren’t buying his assertions that “affordability” is a “fake word” or his insistence that higher gas prices are “a very inexpensive price to pay” for his war aims.

When leaders neglect lived experience, the message collapses.

Why? To start, facts and figures alone no longer carry the weight they once did. There was a time when people would absorb accurate information presented clearly through official channels, like the White House press briefing. They might disagree on what it meant, they might challenge certain points, but it wasn’t automatically treated as spin.

Today, anyone can be a content creator, producing videos, podcasts and memes with subjective, sometimes bogus interpretations of the news. Many Americans now get their news only from outlets that confirm their political leanings. Social media algorithms clearly favor outrage and certainty, not accuracy.

In that environment, official charts and summaries rarely break through. While I was the press secretary, the Biden White House often operated as if we still had a media ecosystem built for accuracy and process, rather than one built for immediacy and vibes.

A TikTok about high prices, filmed with a phone in a grocery store aisle or in front of a gas pump, could garner more attention than anything I said at the daily White House briefings or any interview given by a cabinet secretary on the Sunday morning talk shows. And once a narrative rooted in daily life takes hold, it is almost impossible to dislodge.

We learned that lesson with the economy and again with the debate around Mr. Biden’s age. Looking back, we misread the public mood, thinking the age conversation would fade. At best, my responses from the podium about Mr. Biden’s age failed to put out the fire; at worst, they fueled it.

The Trump White House should realize that over the next two years, there will be only more, not less, scrutiny when the president appears to drift off during meetings, is cagey about the results of his medical exams or goes on one of his erratic, late-night social media screeds. His communications team should know by now that the prices at the pump and the self-checkout line are undefeated.

When people don’t believe what their government says, institutions lose legitimacy. Conspiracy theories flourish. Urgently needed legislation stalls. Elections are lost.

Part of the challenge is that Americans no longer share a single information space: Media fragmentation has created separate realities. And when a government cannot establish shared facts, democratic decision-making becomes harder.

In some ways, Mr. Trump’s style — direct, emotional, repetitive and unmediated — fits the incentives of the current environment. But it has limits. A decade ago, his bluster, so unlike traditional politicians, grabbed ears and eyeballs. Now even many of his fans can see that he’s frequently just seeking attention. Look at just about any poll and you get the sense that voters increasingly don’t trust him.

That tension, the ability to dominate the conversation while struggling to earn trust, defines this moment.

Once people believe their government is not speaking to their reality, it becomes incredibly difficult to earn that trust back. I felt that tension every day in the White House briefing room. I see it happening again now.

Karine Jean-Pierre is the author of “Independent: A Look Inside a Broken White House, Outside the Party Lines.”

ukraine-russia-war-draft.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 19  Words: 1130/1197
================================================================================

SUMMARY

Because bravery has turned into a cliché masking the profound social and economic injustices of this war. Men went to war, he says, because it was more embarrassing not to. Of course, I don’t equate the two sides of this war.

ARTICLE

Please Spare Me Your Talk of Bravery
In the Ukraine war, bravery has turned into a cliché masking profound social and economic injustices.
By Alyona Synenko
Published 2026-10-02 05:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/opinion/ukraine-russia-war-draft.html

A friend of mine is a draft dodger. Everything he does is governed by the unspoken rules of the nationwide hide-and-seek that is playing out between recruitment squads roaming the streets of Ukrainian cities and some two million men wanted for draft evasion.

Buying groceries can be a life-or-death decision. He never steps outside without checking messaging apps where men share information about checkpoints and recruitment raids in our home city, Odesa. These channels count their subscribers in the tens of thousands.

In Odesa, we clock the disappearances — a barista in my favorite coffee shop, an artist who painted cityscapes in the nearby square, a friend’s brother. Coming across a gaping void where a familiar face used to be has become routine.

More of us are taking action. Almost every week, videos appear online of bystanders trying to wrestle men out of conscription vans to rescue them. Last year, 341 clashes between military recruiters and civilians were registered — nearly triple the number in 2024. I used to pause at these videos, dismayed by the brutality of the violence that permeated everyday life. Now I scroll past them, disturbed by my lack of reaction. I’ve grown used to living in this male version of “The Handmaid’s Tale.”

Last autumn, my friend got caught next to his apartment building. It rained that day, and he slipped in the mud running from recruiters. A recovering drug addict who vomited all night and an older man who was picking up his prescription medication were among his fellow captives. “It felt like we were mere bodies there for sale,” my friend said about the day and night he spent at the Territorial Center of Recruitment and Social Support, before he managed to raise the necessary sum and bribe his way out.

Would you accuse him of being a coward? I didn’t. Because bravery has turned into a cliché masking the profound social and economic injustices of this war.

“In fact, this is our brand,” President Volodymyr Zelensky said in the spring of 2022. “To be brave.” He added, “We will spread our courage. We will start a special global campaign.” Billboards in Times Square, a Vogue photo shoot featuring the president’s wife as a “portrait of bravery” and enthusiastic media headlines promoted Ukrainian courage at home and abroad.

Earlier this year, NATO’s secretary general, Mark Rutte, echoed the same theme, describing his interaction with a Ukrainian mine detection dog: “I even looked the dog in the eye, and he told me that he will never give in.”

Even though self-preservation is a basic human instinct, we have been conditioned to despise and mock running from war by millenniums of literature and art. Throughout history, the fear of being labeled a coward has kept soldiers in the fight and sometimes kept wars going against the tide of dissenting public opinion. “If I left that war and let the Communists take over South Vietnam,” President Lyndon B. Johnson said, “then I would be seen as a coward.”

During the Vietnam War, the largest antiwar movement in U.S. history appropriated the insult, rebranding war as moral cowardice. In “The Things They Carried,” by Tim O’Brien, the character of the same name says, “I was a coward. I went to the war.” Men went to war, he says, because it was more embarrassing not to.

Estimates of the number of young Americans who left the country during the Vietnam War to avoid fighting range from 40,000 to 100,000, with Nixon’s speechwriter Pat Buchanan dismissing them as “malingerers, opportunists, criminals and cowards.” When Ukraine loosened exit restrictions for men aged 18 to 22 in August last year, the number of men those ages crossing the border into Poland soared to 1,600 per day over the following two months.

At the same time, hundreds of thousands of young Russians have chosen to leave their country since 2022.

Of course, I don’t equate the two sides of this war. Ukraine was, after all, invaded, and in the days afterward hundreds of thousands of ordinary Ukrainians, men and women, volunteered to join the armed forces. With long lines snaking around enlistment centers, the number of volunteers was so overwhelming, some were sent home. But in the nearly five years of the brutal war, a new kind fear has taken over. We have grown used to drones and explosions in our cities. Now, what scares me and most people I know is the glaring absence of any realistic prospects for peace. We are scared to watch our country bleed its best people and its future.

Many men who refuse to fight are protesting the unequal burden of the war — while some sacrifice their lives, others amass wealth. When Andriy Yermak, Mr. Zelensky’s former chief of staff and, until last year, the second most powerful man in the country, resigned his post mired in a corruption scandal, he told The New York Post that he would go to the front lines. The promise remains unfulfilled, and as a friend of mine said with a chuckle, “All of us will end up at the front before he does.”

So many bright and kind people have been killed. And, every day, Ukrainian soldiers show superhuman levels of selflessness and courage. But their bravery must not be cheapened and paraded as a cardboard cutout to divert attention from growing inequality and corruption. And from the lack of any honest and serious conversation about how we can achieve peace.

Samuel Johnson once said that “mutual cowardice keeps us in peace. Were one-half of mankind brave, and one-half cowards, the brave would be always beating the cowards. Were all brave, they would lead a very uneasy life; all would be continually fighting: but being all cowards, we go on very well.”

I would be happy to live in Johnson’s utopia, populated with cowards who value their lives and the lives of others. And I would take it over this world, where leaders who are supposed to keep us safe though diplomacy and dialogue instead engage in self-important and shallow militaristic discourse.

My grandfather served as a Soviet Navy officer during the Cuban missile crisis, and I have always been disturbed and fascinated by this period in history. Adlai Stevenson, the U.S. ambassador to the U.N. at the time, who advocated diplomacy over military action to avoid escalation, said: “I know that most of those fellows will probably consider me a coward for the rest of my life for what I said today, but perhaps we need a coward in the room when we are talking about nuclear war.”

When I read the news or jump out of bed in the middle of the night during an air raid, I wish there were more diplomats like him in the world today.

Alyona Synenko is a writer from Odesa, Ukraine.

modern-love-i-wanted-to-be-a-good-mormon-but-i-was-gay.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 37  Words: 1479/1576
================================================================================

SUMMARY

My first love convinced me to drink bleach. I was 20, a junior at Brigham Young University in Utah, and already behind by Mormon standards when it came to love and dating. Not because I wanted to die — I knew even a small amount of bleach could be fatal, and I would never actually choose to drink it — but because I felt so repulsed by our actions.

ARTICLE

Nothing Could Purify Me After What I’d Done
Not showering, not praying, not even drinking bleach.
By Gabrielle Shiozawa
Published 2026-10-02 04:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/style/modern-love-i-wanted-to-be-a-good-mormon-but-i-was-gay.html

My first love convinced me to drink bleach.

I was 20, a junior at Brigham Young University in Utah, and already behind by Mormon standards when it came to love and dating. I wasn’t old enough to rent a car or order a drink, yet most of my classmates were dating, engaged or married. We had a children’s playroom in our university library. Classmates brought babies to lectures. It was not a question of if, but when, I would be wed.

Mormon doctrine teaches its followers to marry young, stay sexually abstinent before marriage and have as many children as possible. This is already a tightrope to walk, but I took it even more literally with my then-untreated scrupulosity, a form of obsessive-compulsive disorder characterized by a relentless thought cycle of fear and doubt surrounding morality and religion.

I was consumed by anxiety around everything church related, constantly fearing I had committed a sin I couldn’t remember and that I was unworthy of the blessings my high-demand religion promised. Yet I had never been in any rush to get married before I was inundated with church culture at BYU and felt pressured to check all the boxes.

As a freshman, I had met with my bishop to confess my failures. “All five of my roommates have already gone on dates,” I said. “Also, I haven’t told anyone this, but I’m worried I might be into women.”

“Well, you haven’t acted on those impulses, have you?” he said. “It’s fine to be a lesbian as long as you don’t act on it. You know, I think I understand lesbians, because I, too, am attracted to women.”

His spiritually sanctioned advice was: “Go flirt with boys!”

For two years, I tried. A recently returned missionary took me swing dancing. A too-forward man held my hand, without asking! And a former cop bought me a $50 steak and showed me his gun collection.

I had just about given up on dating when my neighbor, a fellow student, asked me out. I tallied his qualifications as we walked to a bowling alley. He was exactly my height, but his fluffy blond hair made him seem a few inches taller. He laughed endearingly.

I wanted to be a good Mormon girl, to date and marry the way I was supposed to. This man felt safe, so we kept going out. We were each other’s first kiss, at 20 (me) and 22 (him).

“I’ve been waiting to have my first kiss with someone really special,” he said. “I think it’s you.”

Which sounded sweet, but also just seems like something any sexually repressed Mormon would say. And we were two sexually repressed Mormons.

We spent most of our 11 months of dating cooking together in my half-lit apartment kitchen, doing homework on his dingy couch and ignoring how bad we were at kissing. He got me into rock climbing, having no idea he was introducing me to the gayest hobby possible that I would later take up with my future girlfriend.

There were sweet family dinners at his childhood home, a weekend road trip to my Southern Nevada hometown for hiking and camping, and game nights with his high school friends.

I made the mistake of asking my mother what she thought of him after bringing him home like a fish I’d caught, as if to say, “Look! Aren’t you proud?” But she said he was nerdy, and I then made the mistake of telling him that, which went as well as you might expect.

Every time I found myself attracted to a woman, I went to my boyfriend’s apartment to confess. To his credit, he always laughed and said, “You’re probably bisexual,” which felt incredibly progressive. But being a good Mormon meant ignoring that part of me.

I loved that neither of us had any clue what we were doing.

Sure, he convinced me he knew more. He was two years older, and the church’s patriarchal structure convinced me he was the decision maker. He told me not to be clingy, scolded me when I was too prideful. He reminded me that his future wife wouldn’t be someone who struggled with self-harm or lost her temper the way I did.

I felt ashamed. I didn’t trust myself enough to argue. I cried and said I would do better. I grew up being taught that “enduring to the end” was part of being a good Mormon. I believed this meant not only staying true to my religion but also to my first boyfriend. After all, if I could endure dating him, I would never have to kiss another man.

A few months in, he admitted he had never meant to ask me out, but I’d gotten the wrong idea when he asked me to go bowling, and then we just kept hanging out.

Somehow, this revelation didn’t convince either of us to end the relationship.

It wasn’t hard to stay pure. I wanted to cuddle on the couch and go car-camping in the canyons and hike holding hands in the soft morning fog. In the Mormon Church, sexual sin is taught as being almost as bad as murder. My only relief was convincing myself I was more righteous for having no desire to be intimate with a man. I didn’t want his rough hands on my body. I wanted to say no.

But as we lay in the back of my car, he asked for more than I wanted to give. I said, “No, I’m not ready,” and then my voice shook, and I said, “It’s OK.”

His hands on my body. My hands on his.

I remembered what they said at church about women being responsible for maintaining their virtue, for keeping men from temptation, and a sick feeling grew in my stomach.

I drove us home. He said nothing while I hunched over the wheel and sobbed. In a few months, I sold that car, even though I loved it, because every time I looked in the back seat I remembered that I was no longer clean.

As a child, my O.C.D. convinced me the only way to be morally clean was to be physically clean. I drank drops of hand sanitizer in elementary school whenever I didn’t pray the right amount and then wondered why I got stomachaches. As a teenager, I was so ashamed of my first crush on a girl that I washed my hands until they cracked and bled. With no good bacteria left to fight against disease, warts broke out across the backs of my hands. I lived in shame, warts all over my knuckles, and I still couldn’t stop scrubbing them, convinced I would never be clean.

Then I was 20, and I no longer drank drops of hand sanitizer, and I washed my hands a normal amount. But because of what happened in that back seat, I was now dirty again and needed a new salve. I could scrub myself raw in the shower, take medication for the urinary tract infection I got from his hands on my body and pray until my voice grew hoarse, but nothing could fix what I’d done.

So I started obsessing about drinking bleach. Not because I wanted to die — I knew even a small amount of bleach could be fatal, and I would never actually choose to drink it — but because I felt so repulsed by our actions.

I joked about it with my boyfriend. I couldn’t talk about what happened between us, so I joked about drinking bleach.

Then one day he took me to his kitchen and said, “Maybe this will get you to stop talking about it.”

We stood barefoot, afternoon sun streaming in. He held a bottle of bleach in one hand and poured me a capful. Probably a tablespoon. I smelled it before he lifted it to my mouth, sharp and bright.

I didn’t question it. He was just helping me face my fears. Right?

I looked in his eyes and nodded because I thought I loved him. I loved someone who brought poison to my lips and called it a cure. I tipped the liquid back like a shot. Like salty, rancid almond milk. Cold and quick. I wanted to gasp. I swallowed instead. I waited for it to burn, but I felt nothing but nausea.

I wouldn’t tell anyone about this for years, not because I thought he was wrong but because I thought he was right. After all, I did stop talking about bleach after that.

A few weeks later, he came to my apartment to tell me God told him it was time for us to break up. “Your family will never come around to liking me,” he said. “I don’t want to live like that.”

“Anyway,” he said with a laugh, “at least now you know you like men.”

Gabrielle Shiozawa is a writer in Walnut Creek, Calif.

headaches-brain-sag-spinal-fluid-leak.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 17  Words: 1406/1406

SUMMARY

In the early morning light of her home in Dover, Ohio, the 62-year-old woman carefully swung her legs over the side of the bed and stood. But because it is unusual to start getting headaches at this age, and because the patient’s mother had suffered a ruptured brain aneurysm, she sent her for a head CT. The woman’s story was classic for the diagnosis: a headache that responds to posture almost like a light switch, in a way that tension headaches and migraines rarely do.

ARTICLE

The Headaches Disrupted Her Life
The woman’s severe pain seemed to ease only when she was lying down. What would cause such a thing?
By Lisa Sanders, M.D.
Published 2026-10-02 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/02/well/headaches-brain-sag-spinal-fluid-leak.html

In the early morning light of her home in Dover, Ohio, the 62-year-old woman carefully swung her legs over the side of the bed and stood. And there it was: A clamp tightened around the right side of her head. The pain was over her right ear, in her face and down the right side of her neck. She took a deep breath. Another day. Another headache.

She hadn’t been a headache person for most of her life. But that changed early in 2025 with these headaches that hit as soon as she got up in the morning. It was a pressure-like pain, always on the right side, and ibuprofen and acetaminophen barely touched it.

Given the severity of her pain, the nurse practitioner who was the woman’s primary care provider wondered if these were migraines. She prescribed a medication meant to stop this type of headache when taken as soon as the pain starts. But because it is unusual to start getting headaches at this age, and because the patient’s mother had suffered a ruptured brain aneurysm, she sent her for a head CT. It was a relief for the patient to hear that the CT was normal, but she needed to know the cause of her pain. She went to her eye doctor to find out if she needed a new glasses prescription. She did, but that didn’t help. Her boss installed a shade over her desk to cut the glare from the fluorescent light. She was grateful, but the headaches were unrelenting.

Her P.C.P., still wondering if this could be an aneurysm, referred her to a local neurosurgeon. Hearing her story, the physician assistant in the neurosurgery practice agreed that these probably were migraines and prescribed an additional medication, propranolol, to be taken daily. But the possibility of an aneurysm remained, so she also ordered an M.R.I. of her brain and a CT scan of the blood vessels in her brain. The woman had the two studies a couple of weeks later. There was no aneurysm. Her vessels were normal. Her brain, however, was not.

A Worrisome Explanation

When the patient saw the M.R.I. result, she was alarmed. She had, the report said, something called brain sag. She wasn’t sure what that was, but it sounded bad. She left a message for the P.A., and when she didn’t hear back, she got scared. She called her P.C.P. and was referred to another neurosurgeon, this time at the Cleveland Clinic.

The patient’s first thought when she saw Dr. Mohammed Abdulrazzak at the Cleveland Clinic branch in Canton, Ohio, was that he was too young to be a doctor, much less a neurosurgeon. He introduced himself, then sat in the chair across from hers. “I hear you have a headache,” he said. She felt a sense of real interest from him as she told her story. She explained how terrible her headaches were when she was upright, when she laughed or even spoke. When she sneezed, the pain was unbelievable. And recently the headaches seemed to be affecting her memory as well. She had to write things down to keep herself from forgetting. The migraine medications did help, but the only thing that made her headaches almost completely subside was lying down. When she said this, she thought she saw just a hint of excitement in the young doctor’s eyes.

Brain sag, Abdulrazzak explained, was usually caused by the loss of some of the spinal fluid that cushions and supports the brain. When standing, gravity pulls the already-depleted fluid farther downward, stretching the pain-sensitive membranes and structures around the brain. Lying down eases that stretch immediately. The woman’s story was classic for the diagnosis: a headache that responds to posture almost like a light switch, in a way that tension headaches and migraines rarely do.

Abdulrazzak pointed to the black and white curves of her brain on the M.R.I. Even when she was lying down, her cerebellum was so low that it was almost touching the skull near the foramen magnum, the hole through which the spinal column emerged. That’s why her brain appeared to be sagging. He asked the patient if she had had any recent surgery or trauma. She hadn’t. Abdulrazzak wasn’t surprised. Many of these leaks are spontaneous, the cause never discovered.

The hardest part of this disease was finding the leak. In the necessary test, called a myelogram, contrast is injected into the space around the spinal column and a CT scan captures where it leaks out.

The test was awful. The increased pressure caused by the injection of the contrast made her whole head ache. She waited anxiously for the results. No leak was seen. But Abdulrazzak was sure there was one. There was another study, he told her, only recently available, that would give them a better image. They could give her general anesthesia so she wouldn’t feel the pressure from the injected contrast. The woman considered this possibility then shook her head. The headaches were manageable with the medications, she said. She asked if she could just wait and see what happened. Abdulrazzak assured her she could, and told her to come back in a few months.

Another Test

She felt OK for awhile. But just over a year after the headaches started, the medications suddenly stopped working. Getting out of bed in the morning was almost torture, and some days she had to call in sick and spend the entire day in bed.

Her best friend was distressed to see the woman suffer so much. On weekends, the women and their husbands often went to listen to music in the local bars. But the last time they went out, the woman had to leave. The music, the crowd — it was all just too much for her. These days her friend couldn’t help noticing how tired she looked. She was pale. She had dark circles under her eyes. And she was so forgetful. The way she repeated herself reminded the friend of her own grandmother who had Alzheimer’s.

“You’ve got to go back to that doctor and see what he can do,” the friend exclaimed one evening when the woman was in the grips of a really bad headache.

Her friend went with her a few weeks later to see Abdulrazzak, who arranged the second test. In it, the patient lay on her right side. Once she was sedated, a catheter was inserted into the base of the sac containing the spinal cord, and contrast was injected. Then the table was tilted so that the contrast could flow upward, highlighting the entire spinal column. And there it was — the leak. A thin trickle of contrast filled one of the tiny veins leading away from the sac at the level of the 10th thoracic vertebra, just above the bottom of the rib cage.

Two weeks later, Abdulrazzak inserted a tiny catheter into the woman’s thigh. He slowly threaded it up the vein, carefully navigating toward the tiny vessel the spinal fluid was leaking into. He guided his way using a viewable X-ray called a fluoroscope to find the exact spot. Once he was at the site of the leak, he injected a material to completely seal off the vein.

When the patient woke up, Abdulrazzak told her that she would have a headache for a week or so. Her body had increased the amount of spinal fluid it made trying to compensate for the leak. Now that the leak was sealed, her body would have to reduce its spinal fluid output, and that would take a little time.

She went home the next day, and she did have a headache. But as promised, over the next couple of weeks, the pain gradually disappeared. Her memory started to improve. The real test, she knew, would come when she and her friend and their husbands went out. So, some six weeks after her procedure, the two couples struck out for one of their favorite places. She hadn’t had a headache for weeks, and worried the thunderous music would bring it all back. They found a seat as far from the speakers as they could get. Finally the band came out and picked up their instruments. The woman’s heart raced. But once the lead guitarist struck his first chord, quickly followed by bass, drums and keyboard, she sensed that her headaches were gone for good and life could finally return to normal.

protein.html
Source: RenderedHtml  Paragraphs: 36  Words: 1351
================================================================================

SUMMARY

We are living in an era of protein hype. A doughnut with 10 grams of protein is still a doughnut. Peak protein may not last forever.

ARTICLE

Have We Reached Peak PROTEIN?
Protein is everywhere — in chips, candy, cookies, even water. Does that make these products healthy?
By Margot Sanger-Katz and Larry Buchanan
Published 2026-09-28 09:05 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/09/28/upshot/protein.html

In our age of protein, there are now protein candies and cookies:

There’s protein coffee and protein water:

And protein chips and crackers:

New food start-ups have proliferated:

While legacy brands have revamped their most famous offerings:

We are living in an era of protein hype. The macronutrient has become a focus of trendy weight-loss advice. It’s an obsession of weight lifters and longevity biohackers. Doctors have been advising higher protein consumption for patients taking GLP-1 weight loss drugs. And the government’s new dietary guidelines, released last year, boosted the levels of recommended protein by more than 50 percent. The guidelines tell Americans to “prioritize protein foods at every meal.”

The food industry, naturally, has caught on to this nutritional trend. Yogurt and cheese are now being positioned as high-protein foods, which they always have been. Prepackaged salami snacks are called “protein packs.”

But protein is also finding its way into foods that haven’t traditionally contained much of it. You can find protein tortilla chips, granolas, baby food, pudding — even ranch dressing.

Over one week, reporters and editors at The Upshot were asked to snap photos of protein marketing in foods they came across in their daily lives. The folder of images grew rapidly. The protein foods are in bodegas, gas stations, grocery stores, warehouse clubs, coffee shops and chain restaurants.

The trend has puzzled many nutritionists, including experts involved in developing the new protein-enhanced nutritional guidelines.

“A snack food is an indulgent food, and people need to understand it that way,” said Donald Layman, an emeritus professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign who helped inform the protein chapter for the guidelines. He said protein-packed chips and cupcakes are “a bad choice.” A doughnut with 10 grams of protein is still a doughnut.

The guidelines advise Americans to eat less processed food and to focus on foods that are naturally high in protein, including dairy, meat, nuts and beans. Protein added to processed snack foods is not the same thing, he said.

“I refer to it as fairy dust,” Professor Layman said. “Fairy dusting over products that don’t need to have protein in them is useless.”

(We neglected to ask him about his views on several protein-infused vodkas, including one that claims it is “crafted for the wellness-minded and fitness-forward.”)

Protein bars, powders and shakes have been around for a while; they long ago broke out from bodybuilding to the mainstream. They now occupy an expanding share of real estate in grocery stores and gas station convenience stores — in many cases, entire aisles.

But there are now also protein versions of everything else, with a range of claims. Sources of protein and good sources of protein. High PROTEIN, PROTEIN-packed, and sometimes just “PRO.” It is almost always in all caps, and often in the product’s name.

And there are snack categories that appear to exist primarily in the protein universe, like sticks and balls.

Even white-label supermarket brands now offer protein foods.

“If you're not evolving and the consumer is, you’re dead in the water,” said Bonnie Herzog, an equity analyst at Goldman Sachs, who tracks the food and beverage industry. Ms. Herzog, a vegan, said her social media feed was filled with advice to eat more protein and tips on how to do it.

NIQ, which collects detailed data on retail food sales, counts 37,232 products in stores carrying front-of-package protein claims.

It has measured around $90 billion in consumer spending on these products over the last year, including more than $2 billion on protein pizzas and $35 million on protein toaster pastries. (Yes, Protein Pop-Tarts exist.)

“You’ve got the claims sneaking into categories that don’t make a lot of sense,” said Chris Costagli, a vice president at NIQ, who monitors the food and beverage industries. “All of a sudden, you’ve got people that are buying the product just because they see the word.”

Whey, the milk-based protein that is the key ingredient in most protein powders, bars and even ice creams, was once considered a waste product of cheese production. It is now in such demand that prices have doubled in the last five years, according to Ever.Ag, an agricultural risk management firm that closely tracks prices in the dairy industry.

“There were a lot of questions over the last few months of are we at the jump-the-shark moment with some of these new products,” said Kathleen Wolfley, the company’s vice president for insights.

But, she said, “we continue to see further innovation in this marketplace.” She also noted that the protein bonanza had been great news for struggling cheesemakers.

Nearly 90 percent of Americans already get enough protein, according to a recent analysis from the U.S. Department of Agriculture. (If you’re curious how much you should be getting, here’s a calculator.) But consumers still seem hungry for more.

Sales of protein-packed breakfast cereals and granola have increased by 15 percent over the last year, according to NIQ. They are often paired with ultrafiltered high-protein milks. (It is those filtered milks that are used to make the protein foams at your local coffee shop.)

Tortilla chips with protein are also selling at a steady clip, driving PepsiCo’s new launch of Protein Doritos, located on a supermarket endcap near you:

Do protein Doritos taste good? Matt Rosenman, a graphic designer who makes social media content examining food marketing and health, said he had tried nearly all the protein snacks, including tortilla chips that were close to inedible. His verdict on protein Doritos was more positive: “Slightly worse version of Doritos, but they are pretty close.”

In videos, Mr. Rosenman shows some of the common tricks food companies use to make junk foods look like responsible choices. Neutral colors and pictures of farms and mountains signify healthy products. Unregulated words like “plant-based” and “natural” help give foods a virtuous halo. But as the protein arms race has intensified, these subtle techniques have faded. Font size has come to dominate protein claims.

With ubiquitous giant bubbles, companies emphasize protein content, sometimes even when products don’t offer much of it. The Food and Drug Administration, which regulates health claims on foods, has relatively lax rules about how brands use the word “protein” on the front of their packages. While there are rules about claiming a product has “high protein” or is a “good source,” vaguer claims in product names and giant bubbles are almost always unregulated.

“It works, and it works for me,” Mr. Rosenman said. “I saw the giant word ‘protein’ and it stopped me in my tracks.”

Doritos itself is a useful case study. The brightly packaged chips have been around since the 1960s, with reformulations for nearly every major diet trend. The original Doritos emphasized that they were tasty with dips. But nutrition claims started showing up in the 1970s, with the information they contained “no preservatives!”

Since then, there have been versions marketed as cholesterol free, less oil,

Low calorie, low carbohydrate,

“Light” and “naked of dyes.”

Of course, you can protein-max by cooking your own food. There are endless TikToks and Instagram Reels about how to consume more than 150 grams of protein a day, often by sneaking chicken breasts and cottage cheese into just about every meal. (Cottage cheese fatigue has become such an issue that there is now a subcategory of videos on how to make high-protein meals without it.)

But junk food is more fun.

Dariush Mozaffarian, a cardiologist who directs the Food Is Medicine Institute at Tufts University, compared protein chips and protein brownies to SnackWell’s Cookies of yore — products that are no healthier than the highly processed foods they replaced, but sheathed in a patina of virtue.

“It’s a bizarre trend, and not supported by the science,” he said.

As Doritos teaches, nutritional fads come and go. Peak protein may not last forever. (Several industry experts casually mentioned that fiber may be the next big thing.) Around 70 years ago, food scientists at what was then the Kellogg Company teamed with researchers at the Harvard School of Public Health to develop a new cereal, called Special K. Its main selling point? PROTEIN!

ai-chatbots-brain-development-study.html

SUMMARY

Across millions of math sessions by a group that ranged from fifth graders to college students, the researchers compared performance from before 2022, when ChatGPT first came out, with the work that followed its arrival. Researchers found that after 2022, the time students spent mulling over online test questions dropped precipitously on the questions readily handled by chatbots, while their performance improved. But the students who had used A.I. more like a tutor, to explain complex concepts or clarify ideas, not only retained high test scores in the second round, but their essays were higher quality as well.

ARTICLE

Will A.I. Make Your Brain Lazy? Here’s What the New Research Actually Shows.
We’re starting to learn more about how the technology can change us.
By Juliana Castro Varón and Dylan Freedman
Published 2026-09-29 20:34 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/09/29/magazine/ai-chatbots-brain-development-study.html

Machine Learnings

Artificial intelligence is changing the world, and the humans in it, in ways we don’t yet understand. People are increasingly worried that if we rely on chatbots for thinking, our brains will become slower and less engaged. Is A.I. making us stupider? Scientists, too, want to know.

A team of researchers from the University of California, Irvine, and the education company McGraw Hill examined a decade of data from a popular online learning tool by McGraw Hill, starting in 2015. Across millions of math sessions by a group that ranged from fifth graders to college students, the researchers compared performance from before 2022, when ChatGPT first came out, with the work that followed its arrival.

To analyze the results, they split the questions into two types. First: text-based problems that students could easily copy into a chatbot.

And next: visual, interactive or multistep questions that were harder for a chatbot.

Researchers found that after 2022, the time students spent mulling over online test questions dropped precipitously on the questions readily handled by chatbots, while their performance improved.

But when the students were given proctored tests away from their computers, their results were worse than they had been before A.I.

Sina Rismanchian, a Ph.D. candidate at U.C. Irvine and one of the lead authors of the preliminary study, noted that A.I. lets students offload the process required to solve a mathematical problem.

Another multi-institutional study, prepared for the forthcoming Conference on Language Modeling and cited by Rismanchian and his co-authors, shows that when people (in this experiment, adults) become accustomed to skipping the productive struggle of logical and analytical tasks and having the process automated, they are more likely to give up on hard questions that they could otherwise figure out.

A.I. tools condition people to expect immediate responses and deny them the experience of working through challenges, the authors say, which is crucial for skill development and one of the strongest predictors of long-term learning.

“Part of how A.I. is making us dumber,” says Dr. Adam Green, a cognitive neuroscientist at Georgetown University, is “undercutting the development of learning how to think in younger people that now have an alternative.”

Green compares the brain’s tendency to conserve effort to calorie retention.

“Whatever you could do that exerted the least calories but didn’t kill you was the best thing to do evolutionarily,” he says.

But all is not lost. Studies suggest that — for the brain — there are better ways to use A.I.

In July, professors at Middlebury College released a preprint study in which more than 200 undergraduates were asked to write an essay and take a proctored multiple-choice test.

One group of students had access to A.I. to research a topic and write the essay. The other group didn’t. The researchers found that the A.I.-enabled group wrote longer and slightly higher-quality essays. Their test scores were also higher.

A week later, the participants returned for a similar test, but now both groups worked unassisted. The authors broke down the students’ second-round performance based on how A.I. was used in the first round.

The students who relied on A.I. to draft their entire essays in the first round floundered. Their test scores decreased.

But the students who had used A.I. more like a tutor, to explain complex concepts or clarify ideas, not only retained high test scores in the second round, but their essays were higher quality as well.

Experimental evidence suggests that using A.I. not as a full shortcut, but as a means to exercise what they were supposed to learn, allowed them to outperform the remaining participants in the A.I. group and those who hadn’t used A.I. at all.

In other words, these studies so far agree: Artificial intelligence is affecting how people, especially the young, learn and remember. Whether we will be dumber as a result might depend on how — not if — we use A.I.

Latest

Here’s the latest.

One pilot stabbed another at the controls of an Emirati flight to Tel Aviv on Wednesday, causing it to suddenly plunge thousands of feet until passengers and the crew won a fight to regain control of the plane.

Passengers described a terrifying fall during the attack, which ended when some of them stepped into the melee and managed to subdue the aggressive pilot. Overhead bins swung open, parents clung to their children, and videos from inside the plane showed at least one wounded man and others on board covered in blood.

Crew members and passengers made an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, the Israeli prime minister said, and all of the passengers arrived safely in Israel by Wednesday night, after a replacement aircraft was sent to retrieve them by FlyDubai, the airline operating the original flight. As they disembarked, they shared harrowing stories of what happened on board.

A dentist, Shota Musayev, said he was one of the first to reach the cockpit after the attack, finding the injured pilot thrown to the ground there. He said he treated him in midair, including for severe wounds to his head and cuts on his fingers.

Those in the cabin recalled fear racing through them. “In my head, I said, ‘I’m so screwed, I’m so screwed. I don’t deserve to die like this,’” said Peleg Itali, 16, a high school student who was on the plane.

And Asaf Rajuan, one of the passengers who raced to the cockpit, said he and five others “acted on instinct” to restrain the attacker as they realized the plane was out of control.

The plane nose-dived for what felt like 10 to 15 seconds, he said, adding that the passengers’ only hope of rescuing the plane was to work together. Without his fellow passengers, he said, “we’d never have survived.”

One of two other pilots who had been sitting in the row in front of him managed to stabilize the plane, he said, and the pair later landed the aircraft in Saudi Arabia.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a video statement that one pilot had stabbed the other and “apparently attempted to crash the plane with its passengers on board,” nearly all of them Israelis.

He called the pilot who was stabbed, whom he identified as Capt. Smit Machchhar, a hero who saved the lives of 174 people.

“Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker — preventing a catastrophic midair disaster,” he said.

Much about the episode, including the cause of the struggle in the cockpit, remains unclear. The Israeli authorities were investigating whether it was an attempted attack on Israelis or a suicide attempt, among other possible explanations, according to several Israeli officials, all of whom spoke on condition of anonymity in accordance with government protocol.

The aircraft sent distress signals and abruptly reversed course near the Saudi-Jordanian border before making an emergency landing at an airport in Tabuk at about 9:45 a.m. local time. Israeli officials said the plane was carrying 160 to 180 passengers.

The pilot and co-pilot were hospitalized in Saudi Arabia after sustaining injuries, according to a statement from officials at the Tabuk airport. Three Israeli security sources, speaking on the condition of anonymity to comply with government protocol, said the pilot who they believed had carried out the aggression was a citizen of Oman. The Omani foreign ministry declined to immediately comment.

Here’s what else we’re covering:

Passengers describe panic and heroics after the cockpit stabbing.

Passengers on a morning flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv recounted scenes of panic and terror on Wednesday as their aircraft suddenly plunged thousands of feet while screams for help came from behind the cockpit door.

The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said one of the pilots had stabbed the other, Capt. Smit Machchhar, an Indian citizen, and then had tried to crash the plane. The identity of the pilot who attacked Captain Machchhar has not yet been released.

What began as a routine flight became terrifying when the violent altercation broke out inside the cockpit. Passengers, most of them Israelis, described a desperate scramble inside the cabin, as travelers realized the plane was out of control.

A few rushed into the cockpit and tackled the pilot who had stabbed his colleague before two off-duty pilots, who had been traveling in the main cabin, helped land the aircraft safely in Saudi Arabia.

Meital Zoller, who was traveling with her husband and child, said they realized something was wrong when “the plane went up and down.” Then they heard screams, and the plane began diving.

“Within a few minutes, our plane completely lost control, and we felt that this was it — we were about to crash,” one passenger, Miriam Ohayon, told Israel’s I24 News, a television channel. “We heard screams on the plane, and when they opened the cockpit, there was a lot of blood.”

Asaf Rajuan, one of the Israeli passengers who helped subdue the attacker, told reporters that he and five other passengers “acted on instinct” after realizing that the plane was in a steep nosedive. They burst into the cockpit and wrestled with the pilot who had attacked his colleague.

“We neutralized him very quickly,” he said, adding that crew members helped restrain him.

Dr. Shota Musev, a dentist who said he was one of the first to reach the cockpit after the attack, said that he and another passenger tied the attacker’s hands together with headphone cables.

Dr. Musev said he treated the injured pilot for severe wounds to his head and cuts on his fingers. He said the attacker’s body was bloody as well, but it was not immediately clear if the blood was his or someone else’s.

Hila Gaier, who was also on the flight, said that when the plane dived many passengers couldn’t move because of the forces acting on their bodies. “You were sucked downward,” she told Kan, Israel’s public broadcaster. She said she was flying with her partner and two daughters. “I embraced them, told them I loved them, and we tried to practice breathing exercises,” she said.

Flight-tracking data from Flightradar24 showed Flight 1073 descended more than 17,000 feet in less than two minutes. “The plane kept stabilizing and then dropping again for several long seconds,” one passenger, Almog Itali, told Channel 12. The plane landed safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, and the pilots were taken to a hospital.

Adam Polovincik, 40, who was on the flight with his family, described it as an “extreme experience,” even as he tried to remain calm for his children.

Speaking by phone from Saudi Arabia, which has no formal diplomatic relations with Israel, Mr. Polovincik said the circumstances in the Saudi airport were surreal.

“They brought us food and drink, served us coffee,” Mr. Polovincik said. “Yes, there are a lot of soldiers here and government officials, but the atmosphere is very relaxed, pleasant and respectful.”

The passengers were later flown on a replacement plane to Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv, where they were greeted with Israeli flags. Many said they were still reeling from the ordeal. Peleg Itali, a high school student, described his thoughts as he felt the plane start to plummet.

“In my head, I said, ‘I’m so screwed, I’m so screwed. I don’t deserve to die like this,’” he said.

What to know about the clash between pilots on the FlyDubai flight.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel said a pilot tried to seize control of a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday, stabbing the other pilot. Passengers and crew members charged the cockpit and subdued the assailant, with crew members making an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

According to Mr. Netanyahu, one of the pilots attacked the other midair in a possible attempt to crash the plane, FlyDubai Flight 1073. He said a passenger and member of the crew broke into the cockpit to “neutralize” the pilot-assailant, while another crew member stabilized the plane. The flight suddenly plunged thousands of feet and made an emergency landing at an airport in Tabuk, in northwestern Saudi Arabia.

Israeli officials said the plane was carrying between 160 and 180 passengers. FlyDubai said the passengers were all safe and accounted for. The flight’s pilot and co-pilot were treated in a hospital for injuries, according to the airport in Tabuk. The Saudi authorities arrested the suspected assailant, Mr. Netanyahu said.

Much of what happened aboard the flight remained unclear, including the cause of the sudden altitude loss and any possible motive.

What happened?

What have passengers said?

What have the aviation authorities said?

Israel and Saudi Arabia don’t have formal ties, but Israelis have occasionally landed there.

The flight to Israel that was diverted Wednesday morning after a clash in the cockpit landed safely in Saudi Arabia, a country that Israeli citizens rarely set foot in.

The two nations don’t have formal diplomatic, trade or tourism ties, though attempts to forge them have been central to U.S. regional diplomacy in recent years.

Still, their proximity has taken Israelis to Saudi Arabia under exceptional circumstances.

The 1944 Convention on International Civil Aviation, known as the Chicago Convention, laid the foundation for how global civil aviation is governed. It states that all parties to the agreement, which include Israel and Saudi Arabia, should assist aircraft in distress in their territory.

After Wednesday’s emergency landing at the Tabuk airport, a civil-military facility in northwestern Saudi Arabia, the Saudi authorities said that they would provide “necessary care” to passengers. Their statement did not mention the flight’s connection to Israel. The FlyDubai aircraft had been flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv.

In the past few years, at least two other passenger flights en route to Tel Aviv have made emergency landings in Saudi Arabia.

In September 2025, a flight from Dubai landed in the kingdom because of a medical emergency on board, according to a statement by the Israeli Foreign Ministry carried by Israeli news media. The plane then continued on to its destination, according to the statement, which did not say which airline operated the flight or where it landed in Saudi Arabia.

In 2023, an Air Seychelles flight from the Seychelles, an island nation in the Indian Ocean, landed in Jeddah because of a technical malfunction, according to the government-funded Seychelles News Agency. The airport said at the time that roughly 130 passengers were staying at an airport hotel.

In a statement at the time, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel thanked the Saudi authorities for their “good neighborliness” and “warm attitude” toward the Israeli passengers.

FlyDubai operates up to 10 daily flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv.

FlyDubai became the first airline offering commercial flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv in 2020 after Israel and the United Arab Emirates signed an agreement to normalize relations.

The new route meant that Israeli passengers could catch connecting flights in the Persian Gulf, rather than having to go via Europe, significantly cutting down on travel time.

FlyDubai operated the first scheduled commercial flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv in November 2020, after Israel and the Emirates signed the U.S.-brokered Abraham Accords, strengthening economic, political and security relations.

A low-cost carrier, FlyDubai initially offered two daily flights from Dubai International Airport to Tel Aviv and now operates up to 10. One of those flights made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday after what passengers described as a midair altercation between the pilots, which the Israeli authorities were still investigating.

The airline, which began flying in 2009, is wholly owned by Dubai through the Investment Corporation of Dubai, the government’s main investment arm, which also owns Emirates Airlines.

All of the flights between Dubai and Israel travel through Saudi airspace. On Aug. 31, 2020, an El Al jet carrying American and Israeli officials flew to Abu Dhabi along nearly the whole length of Saudi Arabia, the first time Riyadh had allowed an Israeli passenger plane to cross its skies. Two days later, Saudi Arabia said flights from any country to and from the Emirates could fly over its territory, without naming Israel. Saudi Arabia does not have diplomatic relations with Israel.

Most FlyDubai flights fly out of Dubai International Airport’s Terminal 2. Passengers bound for Tel Aviv check in from the much larger Terminal 3, which has heightened security, and can add roughly an hour to the process.

Etihad Airways, Abu Dhabi’s main carrier, added a sixth daily flight to Tel Aviv this summer, making the route its busiest weekly route worldwide.

A passenger describes the chaos of the FlyDubai flight and fears that it would crash.

A passenger on the FlyDubai flight where a clash in the cockpit set off fears of a hijacking Wednesday morning described chaos on board and said that she and others on the plane had thought that it might crash.

The passenger, Miriam Ohayon, spoke to an Israeli television station in one of the first detailed witness accounts to emerge from the plane.

Passengers felt the jet lose control, Ms. Ohayon told Israel’s Channel 24, but some of them intervened to take control. The plane, Flight 1073, which was flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv, landed safely in Saudi Arabia.

“We heard screams on the plane, and when they opened the cockpit, there was a lot of blood,” she said.

Ms. Ohayon’s mother, Yasmin Ohayon, told The New York Times that a woman sitting next to her daughter was among the first to realize something was wrong. The woman saw people fighting inside the cockpit as she was returning from the bathroom and alerted other passengers, Yasmin Ohayon said at Ben Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv, where families were gathering to wait for the passengers.

“Within a few minutes, our plane completely lost control, and we felt that this was it — we were about to crash,” the younger Ms. Ohayon said, adding that she began reciting a Jewish prayer often said in times of distress.

“I’ve already lost my brother; I can’t do this to my mother,” she said she thought. Her brother, Evyatar Ohayon-Abuksis, a soldier, was killed in the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on Israel.

She said that passengers had subdued the attacker and that a nurse and doctor on board provided initial medical care to the pilot.

Asked how the passengers had stopped the attacker, Ms. Ohayon said, “I believe with their bare hands inside the cockpit.”

christa-pike-tennessee-execution.html
