SUMMARY

The death row inmate Christa Pike was in critical condition and receiving medical care, her lawyers said Thursday, a day after Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute her. The failed execution on Wednesday night was the state’s second bungled death penalty attempt this year, and Mr. Lee on Thursday said he was suspending executions — including Ms. Pike’s — to allow an independent review. Christa Pike’s botched execution is the second this year in which Tennessee has failed to execute an inmate using lethal injection drugs.

ARTICLE

Live Updates: Tennessee Inmate in Critical Condition After ‘Torturous’ Botched Execution, Lawyer Says
The inmate, Christa Pike, is “alive right now” after surviving an attempt to execute her by lethal injection, her lawyer said. He called on Gov. Bill Lee to reduce her sentence to life in prison.
By Billy Witz, Emily Cochrane, Jacey Fortin, Maia Spoto, Nicholas Bogel-Burroughs, Benjamin Mueller, Shaila Dewan, Rick Rojas and Yan Zhuang
Published 2026-10-01 14:18 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/10/01/us/christa-pike-tennessee-execution

Latest

Here’s the latest.

The death row inmate Christa Pike was in critical condition and receiving medical care, her lawyers said Thursday, a day after Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute her. They called for Gov. Bill Lee to reduce her sentence to life in prison, calling the botched attempt to end her life with two doses of pentobarbital “cruel and torturous.”

The failed execution on Wednesday night was the state’s second bungled death penalty attempt this year, and Mr. Lee on Thursday said he was suspending executions — including Ms. Pike’s — to allow an independent review.

Lawyers for Ms Pike said that did not go far enough, and urged Mr. Lee to take her off death row. Ms. Pike “has endured punishment greater than any other person in the history of the American death penalty,” said one of her lawyers, Randy Spivey.

Mr. Lee previously denied a similar request and his office did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment. Speaking to reporters earlier Thursday, he said the failed execution “shouldn’t have happened.” He added, “We should find out what happened and make those changes necessary to do what the people of this state want done.”

The governor said it was not immediately clear who would conduct the independent review, but said that the Tennessee Department of Correction appeared to have followed its procedures.

Ms. Pike, 50, was to become the first woman to be executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. It was not clear why the execution attempt failed. Mr. Spivey said it had taken an hour to establish an intravenous line, and that he had counted seven needles used in her left arm alone.

In 1996, Ms. Pike was found guilty of torturing and murdering a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in an attack carried out with her boyfriend and another friend. They slashed at Ms. Slemmer with a box cutter, carved a pentagram into her chest and removed a piece of her skull.

Ms. Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, has long favored Ms. Pike’s execution. “Nobody remembers Colleen,” she told The New York Times last month.

Here’s what we’re covering:

In the final months of his term, Tennessee’s governor confronts another failed execution.

In the waning months of his tenure as Tennessee’s governor, Bill Lee is confronting another uproar over the state’s secretive lethal injection process.

On Thursday, he stopped all remaining executions and ordered an investigation into how Christa Pike, the lone woman on the state’s death row, survived two rounds of lethal drugs being injected into her. But Mr. Lee, who is term-limited, may not be around in office to see the investigation through.

Speaking to reporters a day after the failed execution, Mr. Lee acknowledged that things might change under a new governor. The Republican nominee to replace him as the leader of the deep-red state, Marsha Blackburn, had already called for the return of the electric chair in response.

“What I think should happen, while I’m the governor, is that we should determine the steps forward,” Mr. Lee said. “We should find out what happened and make those changes necessary to do what the people of this state want done.”

Asked about Ms. Blackburn’s comments, he declined to comment. Jerri Green, the Democratic nominee for governor, said she would keep a pause on all executions if elected.

The state’s handling of executions have been a recurring problem. In 2022, during his first term, Mr. Lee paused executions after the drugs used in the lethal injection process had not been tested properly. An independent investigation was conducted, and executions resumed in 2025 under a new protocol.

Then, earlier this year, Mr. Lee granted a temporary reprieve to one death row inmate after prison and medical staff failed to find a vein to inject the lethal drugs. He did not order an investigation or call for a broader pause after that failed execution.

Asked what was different this time, Mr. Lee replied, “We need to find out what happened, and until we find out, there’ll be a stay on executions.”

Most Americans favor the death penalty, but support has declined.

A majority of Americans are in favor of the death penalty for a person convicted of murder, public polling has found, though support has decreased in recent decades.

In the 1990s, about four in five Americans supported capital punishment. But by 2025, 52 percent of Americans favored the death penalty, according to polling by Gallup.

A 2026 survey by the Pew Research Center also found that about 66 percent of Americans favored the death penalty for people convicted of murder, which was about on par with its findings in 2020.

Wide gaps exist in support along partisan lines, with Republicans overwhelmingly in favor and Democrats more split in their opinions, Pew found.

As opposition to the death penalty has risen, a number of states have stopped executions.

Today, 23 states have abolished the death penalty, with Virginia becoming the first Southern state to do so in 2021. The state’s governor, Ralph S. Northam, a Democrat, pointed to racial disparities, noting that a majority of Virginia inmates executed in the 20th century were Black.

Now, executions are mostly conducted by a handful of states. According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Florida has executed 16 inmates so far this year, and Texas has executed six. Alabama, Arizona, Oklahoma and Tennessee have also carried out executions.

The Supreme Court briefly banned the death penalty in 1972 but restored it four years later. Since then, dozens of other countries have abolished capital punishment, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

Gallup found in 2023 that, for the first time since it began asking the question in 2000, more Americans said they believed the death penalty was applied unfairly, rather than fairly.

America’s long history of executions includes many botched ones.

The failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee was the latest in a long string of botched executions in the United States, a history that extends almost as far back as executions themselves.

The failures have varied widely — trouble finding a vein; drugs that didn’t kill, as happened in Tennessee on Wednesday night; and gruesome scenes involving blood or flames. Ms. Pike snored and breathed for an hour before prison officials abandoned the effort to end her life with pentobarbital.

Even as the technology has evolved from ropes to firing squads to modern chemistry, the effort to spare prisoners a protracted, painful death is still far from reliable. While most executions end with the death sentence fulfilled, mistakes can be harrowing.

‘An Awful Sight’

New York carried out the United States’ first execution by electric chair in 1890 when it put William Kemmler to death at a prison in Auburn.

A front-page headline in The Buffalo Evening News said the execution “was an awful sight” and declared “the process a failure.” One doctor involved predicted, wrongly, that “there will never be another electrocution.”

The Evening News article described Mr. Kemmler as the “coolest man in the room” as he adjusted his tie and sat in the electric chair.

The current was turned on and the doctor soon announced that the man was dead. Moments later, in a panic, he asked for the current to be run again.

“This man is not dead,” the doctor cried, according to the Evening News account. “Faces grew white,” the article said.

Mr. Kemmler’s lips dripped, his chest moved, and he made a loud wheezing and groaning sound. Finally, he was again pronounced dead.

“FAR WORSE THAN HANGING,” The New York Times wrote on its front page on Aug. 7, 1890.

Flames and Smoke

One of the more horrific executions took place in 1983 in Alabama, when executioners sent three different jolts of electricity into John Evans III’s body. The first two failed to kill him, but rather sent flames flying from his leg and head.

Mr. Evans’s lawyer called the execution “a barbaric ritual” and said that his client had been “burned alive tonight by the state of Alabama.”

In 1990, a similarly disturbing execution took place in Florida, when fire and smoke emanated from the body of Jessie Tafero as he was put to death.

Unreliable Injections

The Death Penalty Information Center, a research group, says that lethal injection, introduced as a humane alternative to the chair, had the highest botch rate in executions between 1890 and 2010.

In 2018, Alabama prison officials were unable to insert an intravenous line into Doyle Hamm, who was terminally ill, and he became one of a small group to have survived an execution attempt. He died in prison of natural causes three years later.

In Oklahoma, John Grant vomited and shook for several minutes in 2021 during the state’s first execution since 2015, when it had mistakenly used the wrong drug to stop his heart.

The next year, again in Alabama, executioners tried for hours to find the veins of Joe Nathan James in 2022 as he lay in the death chamber. They eventually sliced into one of his arms in what is known as a “cutdown” in order to give him the fatal drugs, according to a private autopsy.

And in 2024, Idaho executioners tried for nearly an hour to insert an intravenous line into the arms, then hands, then legs of Thomas Creech, who was then 73. “I was thinking the whole time that this is really it,” he told The Times several months later. He remains one of eight people on Idaho’s death row.

New Method, New Problems

Alabama pioneered killing prisoners with nitrogen gas in 2024, the first new execution method in decades.

Kenneth Smith, one of three men convicted of murdering Elizabeth Dorlene Sennett, was the first prisoner killed by nitrogen gas. After the execution, the state prison commissioner, John Q. Hamm, said that “nothing was out of the ordinary from what we were expecting.”

But several witnesses told The New York Times that what they saw was disturbing.

“We were told by some people that worked" in the prison system “that he’d take two or three breaths, and he’d be out and gone,” said Mike Sennett, Ms. Sennett’s son. “That ain’t what happened. After about two or three breaths, that’s when the struggling started.”

Mr. Hamm and Mr. Sennett said they believed Mr. Smith might have tried to hold his breath to delay his death.

“With all that struggling and jerking and trying to get off that table, more or less, it’s just something I don’t ever want to see again,” Mr. Sennett said.

Witnesses reported that two other men who were later killed by nitrogen — Alan Miller in 2024 and Anthony Boyd in 2025 — shook and gasped for several minutes before they were pronounced dead. Alabama officials have maintained that the executions had followed protocol.

There are several possibilities for why the Tennessee execution failed.

The execution team went through at least seven needles trying to find a vein suitable for delivering doses of a lethal drug to Tennessee inmate Christa Pike, her lawyers said on Thursday.

Ms. Pike, who survived the botched execution on Wednesday night, was left with blistering and burning around the intravenous insertion sites that the execution team ultimately used to deliver the drug, the lawyers added.

Those details reinforced the sense among outside medical experts that Ms. Pike had survived the procedure because the drug, pentobarbital, probably poured into tissue surrounding the insertion sites instead of entering her bloodstream.

That could have prevented the drug from reaching the levels needed in her circulatory system to stop her breathing.

The drug may nonetheless have lowered her oxygen levels or weakened her circulation enough to cause permanent brain damage. Any leak of the drug into her tissue could also have caused chemical burns.

Ms. Pike’s lawyers said she was in critical condition and receiving lifesaving medical care.

Stephen Ferrell, one of her lawyers, said that while details of the execution attempt were consistent with there having been problems with the intravenous delivery, a number of other factors could have been involved.

The Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement on Wednesday night that it “had followed every step of the state’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the attorney general’s office.” Officials did not answer questions on Thursday about what went wrong with the administration of the drug.

Medical experts said there were signs that the two intravenous catheters, rather than directing the drug into Ms. Pike’s bloodstream, had allowed it to leak into the tissue surrounding the insertion point.

That could have been because of how or where the catheters were inserted, the fragility of Ms. Pike’s veins, or for another reason. Her lawyers said that doctors had always had difficulty finding veins during her blood draws and that Ms. Pike has a blood disorder that exacerbates that problem.

During the execution attempt, they added, Ms. Pike even tried to help the staff place the two IV lines.

“She over and over again said, ‘Please, try up on my shoulder higher, please try here, please try here,’” Randy Spivey, another of her lawyers, said. He added that Ms. Pike thanked them once staff members thought they had established the two lines.

Instances in which intravenous drugs leak into tissue under the skin are known as “IV infiltration,” and have been cited in past botched executions, including ones that caused extensive chemical burns.

Experts said that experienced doctors in a medical setting would typically be able to recognize signs of an IV infiltration as it occurred.

Members of the news media who served as witnesses to the execution attempt said that Ms. Pike at one point described a burning spot in her arm that felt as if it were going to burst and asked if that was normal.

“The pain in her arm should have been a bright red flag that the IV was infiltrating,” said Dr. Mark Heath, an assistant professor of anesthesiology at Columbia University Irving Medical Center.

Dr. Joel Zivot, a professor of anesthesiology at the Emory University School of Medicine who said that he had previously been retained by Ms. Pike’s lawyers as a medical expert, said that such an event would have caused the type of reaction that witnesses described.

The result, he said, could have been a highly alkaline solution leaking into Ms. Pike’s arm. “Essentially, they’ve injected bleach into the tissue of her arm,” Dr. Zivot said.

He added that he was speaking on his own behalf and not for Ms. Pike’s legal team, and that he had no direct knowledge of what happened during the execution attempt.

Having examined Ms. Pike’s medical records before the execution attempt, Dr. Zivot said that she was also susceptible to an IV infiltration. Ms. Pike’s lawyers had previously argued that the procedure could be agonizing for her in part because she has small veins.

“Her venous system was small, and there could be some fragility there,” Dr. Zivot said. “You push a lot of a caustic substance into a small vein like that, under pressure, it’s going to blow.”

He said chemical properties of the lethal drug, pentobarbital, mean that it can burn tissue and skin during executions.

Pentobarbital is a barbiturate that can treat seizures; it works by depressing activity in the nervous system. It is a mainstay drug for euthanizing animals. The drug has also been used in states with legal medical aid in dying.

Its main effect is to shut down electrical activity in the brain, including neurons in the brainstem that control breathing. The body enters a coma-like state, followed by respiratory failure and cardiac arrest.

The federal government adopted single-drug pentobarbital for lethal injections during the first Trump administration.

Under President Biden, the protocol was rescinded after a review by the Justice Department in January 2025 concluded that there remained “significant uncertainty” about whether using the drug for lethal injections “causes unnecessary pain and suffering.”

President Trump’s current administration has reinstated its use, and has said it will also use firing squads.

In Ms. Pike’s case, medical experts said it was also possible that there had been something wrong with the pentobarbital itself.

The primary manufacturer of pentobarbital has restricted the drug’s use in executions, the Justice Department review noted. As a result, states have turned to chemical companies and compounding pharmacies, which are more loosely regulated.

“Is it possible that the pentobarbital itself was somehow not constituted properly?” Dr. Zivot said. “Could it have degraded? Could it have expired? All of those things are possible.”

Almost as soon as lethal injection was first adopted in the United States in the late 1970s as a more medicalized, less painful method of execution, there were prolonged or botched executions.

In part, that was because the injections were often administered by correctional workers with limited medical training. Most doctors and anesthesiologists declined to advise or participate on ethical grounds.

In 2009, the maker of one of the key drugs, sodium thiopental, stopped production in the United States. Other drug companies prohibited the use of their products for executions.

States began scrambling to obtain the drugs, turning to compounding pharmacies and resorting to legally questionable arrangements like loaning the drugs to one another and importing drugs labeled for veterinary use. At one point, the Drug Enforcement Administration even seized Georgia’s supply of lethal injection drugs.

Prisoners argued in court that lethal injection did not eliminate pain and suffering, but only masked it. “It is not the most humane, it is the most humane-looking,” said Corinna Lain, a law professor and the author of “Secrets of the Killing State: the Untold Story of Lethal Injection,” published last year.

In response to the controversies, states shrouded the process in secrecy, passing laws that kept the public from learning details such as how the drugs are obtained and what dosage is used.

Ms. Pike’s lawyers said on Thursday that they hoped records would be preserved that would allow them to learn how her execution had gone wrong. They said they had long warned in court that Ms. Pike’s medical conditions could cause problems, but that those warnings went unheeded.

Mr. Spivey, her lawyer, said that among the at least seven needles used to try to establish an IV line in Ms. Pike’s left arm alone was one that appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her arm after an unsuccessful attempt.

Whatever the reason the execution failed, medical experts said, the possibility that Ms. Pike had suffered the effects of a nonfatal dose of pentobarbital for an extended period created a risk for lasting brain injury.

“She could be facing profound medical complications,” Dr. Zivot said.

Pike said she rued a grisly crime. The victim’s mother wants her dead.

Everything changed for two women when Colleen Slemmer died three decades ago.

Ms. Slemmer, 19, had been studying at a Knoxville, Tenn., education program when three classmates lured her into the woods, tortured her and killed her.

Her mother, May Martinez, had already been uneasy about her daughter traveling hundreds of miles away from Jacksonville, Fla. The loss of her daughter, she said in an interview last month, was devastating.

“I’m not the same person I used to be,” Ms. Martinez said.

Christa Pike was the only person involved in the murder who was sentenced to death. In response to questions from The New York Times, she conceded that initially, she did not feel remorse. But over years of isolation, as a result of being the lone woman on death row, she said she had grown to regret her actions and work to make amends.

“Over years of sitting in here with deep contemplation and reflection, I know and understand the life that I have taken and how much it matters, how much it means, how many effects she could have had on the world, just like the effects I could have on the world,” Ms. Pike said.

Ms. Martinez, who fund-raised the money to drive to witness the execution, said she could not fathom Ms. Pike changing. She and her husband, Raul, remained firmly in support of the execution going forward.

On Wednesday, Ms. Martinez was on the grounds of the prison waiting for the execution. She did not say anything.

Christa Pike’s failed execution echoes another in Tennessee this year.

Christa Pike’s botched execution is the second this year in which Tennessee has failed to execute an inmate using lethal injection drugs.

In May, medical staff members tried to tap into Tony Carruthers’s veins but acknowledged after several attempts that they could not find a “suitable vein” for the drugs, the Tennessee Department of Correction said. Gov. Bill Lee, a Republican, then ordered that any execution of Mr. Carruthers be delayed for a year.

Mr. Carruthers was convicted in connection with three 1994 murders. His lawyer, Maria DeLiberato, later wrote in an opinion essay in The New York Times that she had witnessed her client in “agony” as the execution team tried to insert an intravenous line for over an hour.

Tennessee’s use of lethal injection had come under scrutiny for its effectiveness even before the attempted executions of Ms. Pike and Mr. Carruthers. In 2022, the state paused executions for more than two years after Governor Lee said prison officials had failed to properly test its lethal injection drugs. Inmates have sued the state over its new injection procedure.

Mr. Carruthers represented himself in a 1996 trial over the killings of Marcellos Anderson; his mother, Delois Anderson; and Frederick Taylor. All three were found buried in a Memphis cemetery.

The American Civil Liberties Union argued that Mr. Carruthers was “plainly neither competent to stand trial nor competent to defend himself.” Lawyers who tried to represent him for his trial said they endured personal attacks, which were later connected to Mr. Carruthers’s mental illness.

His case drew attention before the execution attempt because allies and lawyers argued that he had been wrongfully convicted. They said that his mental illness prevented him from understanding his legal situation and the execution.

Multiple judges denied requests for new forensic testing that allies and lawyers said could help prove Mr. Carruthers’s innocence, and the U.S. Supreme Court denied his request to stop the execution.

Critics of the death penalty seized on Mr. Carruthers’s failed execution. Laura Porter, the executive director of the U.S. Campaign to End the Death Penalty, said at the time that “Tennessee has effectively made the case against the death penalty.”

In an interview on Thursday, Ms. DeLiberato said that Mr. Carruthers was still struggling with having full feeling and mobility on one side of his body. She added that his legal team was working to have an outside doctor examine him.

“Having been in that room, knowing exactly where everyone’s standing, what it looks like, what it smells like, what it sounds like, it was a difficult evening for me,” Ms. DeLiberato said, “and I can only imagine it was difficult for Tony.”

An Idaho death row prisoner described living through a botched execution.

Thomas Creech had been imprisoned in Idaho for nearly 50 years, convicted of five murders in three states and suspected of several more, when he was wheeled into an execution chamber in February 2024. For nearly an hour, medical workers at the Idaho Maximum Security Institution struggled to insert an intravenous line to pump a deadly drug into his bloodstream before the proceedings were called off.

Starting with his arms, then his hands and finally his legs, they tried and failed to get a needle into a suitable vein. “The worst ones was when they got down to my ankles,” Mr. Creech said in an interview a few months after his botched execution. “I was thinking the whole time that this is really it. I’m dead. This is my day to die.”

Mr. Creech described what it was like to endure the repeated needle jabs, knowing that any of them — if successful — could mean he would be dead within minutes. He described fear, pain, and his commitment to keeping his focus on his wife, who was sitting just a few feet away in the witness room, behind a glass panel.

Mr. Creech, who is considered a serial killer and is one of the longest-serving death row prisoners in the country, has offered conflicting accounts about his crimes over the years. At one point, he testified that he had killed as many as 42 people, some of them on behalf of a motorcycle gang or as part of a satanic religious ritual. Later, he took back many of those supposed admissions and said he had been put up to the claims by a fame-seeking lawyer.

More recently, and in his interview with The Times, he has said that he believed he had killed seven people. He claimed that he was in the throes of drug abuse at the time and that his victims had all been involved in a gang-rape of his former wife, who later died by suicide.

On the books, though, he has been convicted of five murders, including the fatal beating of a fellow prisoner, David Jensen, in 1981, for which he was sentenced to death.

Mr. Creech described the moments before he was to be executed. He recalled looking over to his current wife through the glass, and trying to tell her that he was sorry. Then he remembered the execution team starting with his right arm and failing to find a usable vein. They moved on to his right hand, his left hand and then his ankles.

The team spent about 42 minutes trying to insert an IV line before the execution was called off, according to Mr. Creech’s lawyers.

When the execution was called off just before 11 a.m., Mr. Creech said, he had trouble believing that he had really survived.

“I thought maybe I might already be in the afterlife,” he said. “Even now, today, I stop and I have to catch myself and think, ‘Am I really dead? I was supposed to be dead on the 28th of February. Am I really dead, and this is part of the afterlife? Continued punishment for my sins that I’ve committed?’”

SUMMARY

Investigators on Thursday were trying to determine what motivated the co-pilot on a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv to stab the pilot, forcing the plane to make an emergency landing after passengers and crew members bravely rushed the cockpit to avert a midair catastrophe. The government of the United Arab Emirates said on Thursday that it would take the lead in the investigation into whether the incident on the FlyDubai flight on Wednesday was linked to terrorism. In an interview with Fox News, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel suggested that the co-pilot, who has not been identified but who Israeli officials have said is an Omani citizen, may have been ideologically motivated.

ARTICLE

Investigators Seek to Establish Motive in FlyDubai Attack
The United Arab Emirates said it would lead the investigation, including into possible links to terrorism. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel said the attacker had undergone “Islamist radical indoctrination,” though he did not elaborate.
By Isabel Kershner, Leo Sands, Heedo Abu Laban, Ismaeel Naar, Johnatan Reiss, Vivian Nereim, Niraj Chokshi, Karla Adam, Somini Sengupta, Suhasini Raj, Mujib Mashal and Pranav Baskar

https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/10/01/world/flydubai-flight-israel-plane-pilots

Latest

Here’s the latest.

Investigators on Thursday were trying to determine what motivated the co-pilot on a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv to stab the pilot, forcing the plane to make an emergency landing after passengers and crew members bravely rushed the cockpit to avert a midair catastrophe.

The government of the United Arab Emirates said on Thursday that it would take the lead in the investigation into whether the incident on the FlyDubai flight on Wednesday was linked to terrorism.

In an interview with Fox News, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel suggested that the co-pilot, who has not been identified but who Israeli officials have said is an Omani citizen, may have been ideologically motivated. “We know that he underwent Islamist radical indoctrination,” Mr. Netanyahu said, adding that investigators had learned this from the man’s “personal information.” He did not provide further details.

Mr. Netanyahu had earlier told Fox News that the attacker was being investigated in Saudi Arabia and would likely be transferred to the Emirates. “And we’ll be following, and possibly also participating in this investigation,” he said.

The pilot, Capt. Smit Machchhar, an Indian citizen who survived the attack, has been airlifted to Abu Dhabi, the Emirati capital, according to two officials familiar with the matter, after receiving treatment in Saudi Arabia. The Indian Embassy in the Emirates said Mr. Machchhar was recovering and in good health. According to witnesses, Israeli passengers helped to subdue the attacker, while a dentist on board performed first aid on Mr. Machchhar. The dentist said he had been bleeding profusely from his injuries.

On Thursday, Israelis expressed pride in the brave actions of the passengers, with newspaper headlines praising them as “Heroes in the Sky” and calling the midair rescue a “Miracle.”

Many questions remained about the attack, including whether the co-pilot had acted alone; what his motives were; and if his intention was to crash the plane or take control of it and land it in a third country. The plane plunged thousands of feet in minutes and was forced to land in Saudi Arabia after the co-pilot stabbed the captain, according to witnesses and officials.

Two reserve pilots on board were credited with stabilizing the plane and landing it safely at Tabuk airport in Saudi Arabia.

Mr. Netanyahu told CNN on Wednesday night that the actions of Mr. Machchhar, the Israeli passengers and the two reserve pilots “managed to prevent a 9/11 disaster,” referring to the terrorist attacks on Sept. 11, 2001.

Four passengers on board also held dual Israeli-American citizenship, according to a U.S. official.

Here’s what we’re covering:

2 passengers who helped thwart the FlyDubai attack add details in a TV interview.

Two Israeli passengers who helped thwart the midair attack on a FlyDubai flight on Wednesday described the ordeal on Israel’s Channel 12 television a day later, recalling the harrowing moments that forced them into action as the aircraft pitched into a sudden dive.

The two men, Tzvika Manes and Asaf Rajuan, described the chaotic scene that began when Mr. Manes’s wife, Tali, screamed while waiting outside the lavatory near the cockpit with their 6-year-old daughter. “He’s stabbing him!” she cried out.

The plane began to lose altitude, and Mr. Manes said his daughters wailed, “Dad, we don’t want to die.” He said, “That was the trigger that made me run inside.” He recalled entering the cockpit, which was splattered with blood.

Mr. Manes and Mr. Rajuan burst into the flight deck, along with another passenger named Yariv and an off-duty pilot who happened to be on board. The flight’s captain had been badly injured by his co-pilot but had still managed to unlock the cockpit door, despite losing blood. Together, the men pulled the wounded pilot to safety, then overpowered his assailant and tied him up. The plane was pulled out of its dive.

Reflecting on the desperate struggle as the airplane full of passengers hurtled toward earth, Mr. Rajuan said that the reality of what they had done was only now setting in. There were 174 passengers and 8 crew on board.

“You don’t think about what you’ve done,” he said, adding: “You just go and do it, almost like a mission. As the days go by, we’ll understand that we managed to save many lives.”

FlyDubai finds itself under scrutiny in Israel.

For almost six years since signing the U.S.-brokered Abraham Accords to normalize relations with Israel, the United Arab Emirates has maintained a steadfast relationship with the country, despite a fierce backlash from some of its Arab neighbors.

Commercial ties were one demonstration of that relationship, and direct flights between the countries became a frequently cited example of their growing links. But the attack in the cockpit of a FlyDubai flight traveling from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday has brought renewed scrutiny of their relationship.

Questions are swirling over what prompted the attack, in which witnesses say the co-pilot stabbed the pilot and passengers and crew members rushed the cockpit to avert a midair catastrophe. The plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

The Emirates has said it is leading the investigation into the attack, including any potential links to terrorism, and FlyDubai has suspended the service between Dubai and Tel Aviv. Israel’s Ministry of Transportation said in a statement on Thursday that the suspension was also a directive from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the recommendation of the head of Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security agency.

Some Israeli officials are also intensifying scrutiny of the airline.

Some Israelis have proved reluctant to fly on the airline after the attack. El Al, Israel’s flagship carrier, said on Thursday that it would start special flights to bring Israelis back from the Emirates.

FlyDubai became the first Emirati airline to fly to Tel Aviv in November 2020, roughly two months after Israel and the United Arab Emirates signed the Abraham Accords. At a ceremony to commemorate the first flight, Mr. Netanyahu of Israel called the inauguration of the route a “pivotal moment.”

By 2024, FlyDubai had become the second-largest foreign carrier operating out of Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion International Airport, carrying more than 500,000 passengers that year, according to Israeli government data. By 2025, the number of passengers had increased to more than 800,000.

FlyDubai’s importance grew this year, as other airlines, including El Al, suspended flights between the Emirates and Israel because of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran in February. It also continued to fly to Tel Aviv during Israel’s war in Gaza, when other regional airlines suspended flights.

Israel’s first ambassador to the United Arab Emirates, Amir Hayek, who served in the position until October 2024, praised FlyDubai on Wednesday and defended the company for continuing to fly to Israel when others stopped or limited service after the start of the Iran war. “The UAE and the airline deserve for us to set aside speculation and allow them to thoroughly investigate what actually happened,” he wrote on social media. “I trust them.”

But Mr. Netanyahu has raised questions about how FlyDubai operates. In an interview with Fox News on Thursday, the prime minister said that the co-pilot was an Omani citizen and asserted that the Israeli authorities prohibited pilots from countries unfriendly to Israel from flying into the country. “We have constraints that say you can’t have pilots from countries that don’t have diplomatic relations with Israel,” he said. Oman and Israel do not have diplomatic relations.

It is unclear what the requirements are for flights between the Emirates and Israel since air travel commenced between the two countries.

FlyDubai’s press office declined to respond to several questions on Thursday. In a statement on Wednesday, it said the motives behind the attack were under investigation. “We urge all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts,” the company said.

Israelis take pride in the brave passengers who saved Flight 1073 from disaster.

Israelis were buoyed on Thursday by the brave actions of several Israeli passengers who, along with crew members, averted a midair disaster aboard a FlyDubai flight to Tel Aviv the day before.

Hebrew newspaper headlines dwelled more on the heroism of the passengers and crew than on the moments of terror after the plane’s co-pilot attacked the pilot in the cockpit, causing the aircraft to plummet nearly 17,000 feet.

Several passengers sprang forward and overpowered the co-pilot, who appeared to be trying to crash the plane, according to witnesses and officials.

“Heroes in the Sky,” read the headlines in two large-circulation morning papers. “Miracle on Flight 1073,” read another.

The dramatic events evoked for some Israelis the days in the 1960s and 1970s when Israel was widely considered to be a small, plucky country that had survived against the odds and took on hijackers.

The Israeli commando raid in 1976 that rescued more than 100 hostages from Entebbe, Uganda, became legendary and spawned several movies. Their Air France flight from Tel Aviv to Paris had been hijacked by Palestinian militants aided by German extremists.

Yonatan (Yoni) Netanyahu, the older brother of Israel’s current prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, led the commandos and was the only Israeli soldier killed in the raid.

Four years earlier, Benjamin Netanyahu, then a young commando himself, took part in a raid that freed hostages held by Palestinian hijackers on a Sabena jet as it sat on the tarmac near Tel Aviv.

But on Wednesday, in the skies above Saudi Arabia between Dubai and Tel Aviv, the saviors were ordinary citizens and crew members, including the injured pilot.

The Israeli passengers who rushed to the cockpit included a man Mr. Netanyahu said was a plumber who led the rescue and a dentist who treated the pilot and helped restrain the assailant.

After the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, civilians stepped up, for example by delivering military equipment and water.

That attack ignited a devastating war in Gaza. Israel’s actions there have drawn international criticism and accusations of war crimes, leaving the country increasingly isolated.

But after the FlyDubai episode, Israeli social media was flooded with memes offering advice to air travelers: In case of emergency, locate the nearest Israeli.

Yair Golan, the leader of Israel’s left-leaning Democrats party and a former deputy military chief, said in a social media post that he was “filled with pride” as details emerged about “the brave Israelis who, in a moment of danger, displayed ingenuity and exceptional courage.”

Mr. Netanyahu told Fox News on Wednesday, after the passengers had returned safely to Tel Aviv, that if you are hijacked, “make sure you have an Israeli sitting next to you.”

The Boeing 737 Max 8 stayed intact despite the enormous stress of its plunge.

The FlyDubai plane whose co-pilot attacked its pilot on Wednesday plunged more than 16,000 feet in 30 seconds, according to data from the tracking site Flightradar24, a descent that an aviation expert said put the jet under substantial structural stress.

Yet, the jet, a Boeing 737 Max 8, stayed largely intact.

“I’m very impressed that the plane held together as much as it did,” said Tony Farina, a specialist in flight projectile design and an adjunct professor at Embry‑Riddle Aeronautical University, a private institution with campuses in Florida and Arizona. “Kudos to Boeing for that design.”

During the unplanned descent, the forces on the jet would have increased dramatically. “As it was speeding up, the forces were going up tremendously,” Dr. Farina said.

President Trump also praised Boeing overnight in a social media post, saying that the plane’s durability was “an amazing show of precise and powerful structural planning and design.”

Noting that only limited information was available, he said that the plane may even have approached the speed of sound. Had it reached that velocity, Dr. Farina said, the plane could have become less stable and harder to control.

But Dr. Farina cautioned that it was difficult to say with certainty what speeds the plane had reached without knowing important details like its angle during the fall, the wind speed and the temperature of air around it. The plane’s flight data recorder should provide a much clearer picture of what happened, he said.

Photos shared on social media of the plane on the tarmac at the Saudi airport where it made an emergency landing show a damaged rudder, but it will probably take some time to understand the full extent of the damage.

“That plane is going to definitely need a full inspection,” he said. “My suspicion is they probably would never use it again.”

Boeing declined to comment.

Investigators seek to answer a central question: How did a weapon enter the cockpit?

The authorities in Israel and the United Arab Emirates were trying to understand on Thursday how a weapon entered the cockpit of the diverted FlyDubai flight to Tel Aviv, as they investigated the co-pilot’s stabbing of the captain.

Many questions remain unanswered about the attack, including the attacker’s motive, his ultimate intention and how he came to have a weapon. As the plane plunged thousands of feet while en route from Dubai on Wednesday morning, passengers and crew members rushed the cockpit and took control of the aircraft, a Boeing 737, and two reserve pilots on board landed it at an airport in Tabuk, in northwestern Saudi Arabia.

The co-pilot, whom Israeli officials identified only as an Omani national, was arrested by the Saudi authorities. The airport in Tabuk said that two pilots were treated for injuries. All the passengers were flown to Israel in another FlyDubai plane.

In an interview with on “Fox & Friends” on Thursday, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that he did not know what weapon the attacker used or how he was able to access it in the cockpit.

The authorities were exploring two possibilities, Mr. Netanyahu said: The co-pilot smuggled the weapon through Dubai’s airport security by evading a metal detector or he used a sharp object that was stored aboard the plane, such as an ax.

“He could have carried a knife or an ax, or he might have gotten an ax from the equipment that might be standard on this airplane,” said Mr. Netanyahu, who cautioned that it was too soon to know for certain.

Marco Chan, a retired airline pilot who teaches aviation operations at Kingston University in London, said on Thursday that Mr. Netanyahu was referring to a “crash ax.”

According to Mr. Chan, who flew for Cathay Pacific and Hong Kong Airlines for 10 years, the cockpits of commercial airliners are typically equipped with axes, which crew members are trained to use to break open the fuselage in emergencies.

On a Boeing 737, as with other models, Mr. Chan said, crash axes are typically stored inside the cockpit directly behind the co-pilot, under a cover but without a lock.

“It’s sharp,” he said. “When we can’t open the door, we would use a crash ax in a location where the external structure of the airplane is slightly weaker, using the ax to break the fuselage open to escape.”

Mr. Chan said that the interior of the cabin is typically marked to show where the wall is slightly weaker, directing crew members where to aim the ax in an emergency evacuation.

The Emirati authorities, who are leading the investigation into the attack, have not provided detailed information on their progress, including any suggestion about the type of weapon that might have been used and how it entered the cockpit.

A spokesman for FlyDubai declined on Thursday to respond to questions about security protocols on its flights to Israel from Dubai.

Israeli politicians use FlyDubai attack to try to score points in this month’s election.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel is in a tight race with a national election approaching, and his supporters and opponents quickly seized on Wednesday’s narrowly averted disaster on a FlyDubai flight to Tel Aviv.

Hours before the mostly Israeli passengers on the plane, Flight 1073 from Dubai, had even made it home, Mr. Netanyahu’s defense minister hinted that he and Mr. Netanyahu had tried to warn of some kind of attack.

“When the prime minister and I sound warnings and security alerts based on intelligence,” the minister, Israel Katz, said in a statement, “it is worth you — our outside enemies and out-of-the-loop formers from within — listening and taking them seriously.” By “formers,” he meant former officials.

On Tuesday, a day before the crisis aboard the FlyDubai flight, Mr. Netanyahu was filmed at an Israeli Air Force base saying, “We have indications that, ahead of the elections, our enemies will try to attack us.”

But neither Mr. Netanyahu nor Mr. Katz provided any specifics with their warnings, leading opponents to dismiss the admonitions as election spinning and fear mongering.

Naftali Bennett, a right-wing political leader who is running to replace Mr. Netanyahu, had criticized the prime minister’s broad warning. On Tuesday, he said on Israeli television that he could get alerts from a phone app and asked what the prime minister was doing to thwart the threats.

On Wednesday’s flight, several passengers and crew members overcame the co-pilot, who was stabbing the captain, according to witnesses and officials. The plane was sent into a nosedive, but two reserve pilots on board the flight have been credited with landing it safely in Saudi Arabia. Investigators have been seeking to determine a motive for the attack.

Yair Lapid, a centrist opposition leader, said in a social media post on Thursday that he had received a security briefing from the prime minister late on Tuesday night. Without going into details about the classified briefing, Mr. Lapid said that from what he heard then, “There was no reason for panic,” adding that the threats Mr. Netanyahu had laid out were nothing new.

“There was no mention of a scenario of a plane hijacking,” Mr. Lapid said. “Not anything like it. Nothing.”

Mr. Netanyahu, Israel’s longest serving prime minister, has been struggling to maintain his reputation as the country’s national security czar, amid reports of the policy, military and intelligence failures leading up to the deadly Hamas assault on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, which ignited a devastating war in Gaza and conflicts across the Middle East.

Much of the campaign for the Oct. 27 general election, which many Israelis and outside observers consider to be the most consequential vote in the country’s history, has focused on what Mr. Netanyahu knew and when.

After nightfall on Wednesday, Mr. Netanyahu went to Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion International Airport to greet the passengers of Flight 1073 when they landed. He spoke on camera with one of the Israelis who had subdued the attacker and credited the courageous actions of passengers and crew members for saving the day.

The Israeli president will honor the passengers who helped to avert the flight disaster.

President Isaac Herzog of Israel on Thursday said that he would recommend five citizens for the country’s highest civilian award for heroism after they intervened to help stop a midair disaster on a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv.

Mr. Herzog said the swift actions of the passengers, who he identified as Yaniv Hayoun, Shota Musayev, Tzvika Manes, his wife Tali Manes, and Asaf Rajuan, helped save the lives of more than 170 people aboard FlyDubai Flight 1073 on Wednesday.

“You put yourselves at risk to save others and prevented a terrible disaster,” Mr. Herzog said in a statement released by his office.

During a violent struggle in the cockpit, the plane’s co-pilot stabbed the Indian pilot, Capt. Smit Machchhar, according to passengers and Israeli officials. Ms. Manes raised the alarm when she heard commotion coming from the cockpit, according to the president’s office. She alerted other passengers and called two off-duty pilots seated in the rear of the cabin to come to the cockpit. The pilots helped to regain control of the aircraft, passengers and officials said.

In a social media post, Mr. Herzog said he offered “warm thanks” to the pilot and the reserve pilots for what he said was their courage and resourcefulness. “The State of Israel extends immense gratitude to you,” he added, addressing Mr. Machchhar.

Mr. Manes forced open the cockpit door along with Mr. Hayoun, a plumber, and Mr. Rajuan, after the captain had managed to unlatch it. The passengers then tackled the assailant.

Mr. Hayoun told Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in a televised conversation on Wednesday that while the other passengers were working to overpower the attacker, he “grabbed the controls and started pulling back the handles,” trying to mimic maneuvers he had seen on television. Mr. Manes said in interviews with Israeli outlets that it took roughly 20 to 25 minutes for the passengers to fully subdue and bind the co-pilot, using corded headphones from the plane’s entertainment system.

Dr. Musayev, a dentist, treated the pilot for what he described as severe wounds to his head and cuts to his fingers, providing what the president’s office described as “lifesaving medical treatment.”

“It was an extraordinary incident. We felt helpless, suspended in midair, and I didn’t know who to turn to,” Mr. Rajuan told the president, according the statement from Mr. Herzog’s office. “But it was all instinct: to survive, to save the family, the people, and the children.”

The Presidential Award for Civilian Heroism was established by Mr. Herzog in the aftermath of the Hamas-led attacks of Oct. 7, 2023, to honor civilians who demonstrated extraordinary bravery to save lives.

How fraught Middle East geopolitics could complicate the FlyDubai investigation.

The government of the United Arab Emirates on Thursday said that it would take the lead in the investigation into the attack aboard the FlyDubai flight traveling from Dubai to Tel Aviv that was forced to land in Saudi Arabia a day earlier.

But as the authorities across the Middle East try to piece together why one pilot attacked another in the cockpit, causing the aircraft to plummet by 17,000 feet in under two minutes, they are tackling a cross-border mystery with dizzying geopolitical complications.

The flight took off from Dubai, the Emirates’ largest city, where the pilots worked for a government-owned carrier. But it made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, where both pilots were hospitalized, and almost all of its passengers were from Israel.

Israel and Saudi Arabia do not have formal diplomatic relations, leaving little precedent for how they might cooperate in a criminal investigation.

Separately, Saudi Arabia and the Emirates are regional rivals with their own political tensions. Both the Saudi and Emirati authorities also operate very opaquely, and typically release minimal information to the public about investigations.

The Emirati government’s announcement that it would lead the investigation offered few details. The comments were published by the country’s state news agency, and said that the attorney general has formed a team to examine the incident, including to determine any motives, whether it had been planned in advance and whether there were any terrorist connections.

The Emirates has jurisdiction to conduct the investigation, even though the incident happened outside its borders, because the plane was registered in the country and flew under its flag, the statement said. It did not say where the pilot who has been accused of carrying out the attack was being held.

Almost all of the information about what happened on the plane has come from Israeli officials and passengers.

On Wednesday, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel said that an attacker had been arrested and “is being interrogated at the moment by Saudi authorities.” He told Fox News that the attacker would be transferred to the Emirates.

The Saudi authorities have said nothing about an arrest or interrogation. On Wednesday, officials at the Saudi airport where the plane landed said in a statement that the plane’s captain and first officer were injured and were taken to a hospital to receive medical care.

The Saudi authorities have also not mentioned Israel at all.

The Saudi government did not respond to a request for comment.

The Indian pilot who was stabbed while fending off his assailant is hailed as a hero.

Capt. Smit Machchhar, the Indian pilot hailed for averting a catastrophe on a FlyDubai flight, had faced a few challenges in the cockpit before. Monsoon rains. Fast-changing wind speeds. And the biggest challenge of all, he recalled on a podcast last year: preparing to land after a passenger went into labor on board.

“There was a sense of urgency,” he said. “In my head, I had zero margin of error.”

None compared to the bloody midair horror he found himself in on Wednesday, when witnesses and officials say a fellow pilot stabbed him in the cockpit of a Dubai to Tel Aviv flight on Wednesday.

Mr. Machchhar, bleeding, managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to overpower the assailant, while two others on board who had flying experience landed the plane in Saudi Arabia.

One passenger said he heard bloodcurdling screams before Mr. Machchhar fell out of the cockpit.

Israeli officials said his co-pilot had apparently tried to crash the plane, with 170 passengers on board. Neither the authorities in the United Arab Emirates, where the flight originated, nor in Saudi Arabia, where the aircraft touched down, have commented on what happened. The Emirati Attorney General’s office on Thursday announced an investigation.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India hailed the captain as a “hero” whose “valor helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy.”

“In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others,” Mr. Modi said on X.

Mr. Machchhar has been airlifted to Abu Dhabi, the Emirati capital, according to two officials familiar with the matter. The Indian Embassy in the Emirates said on social media that the ambassador had visited Mr. Machchhar and his family at the hospital. “Captain Machchhar is in good health and recovering well,” it said.

As Indians rallied around him on Thursday, a portrait emerged of a pilot who found his calling somewhat accidentally, only to end up flying commercial planes for 13 years and later training aspiring pilots at an aviation school.

He grew up in a middle-class suburb of Mumbai, called Ghatkopar, not far from the city’s international airport. Journalists crowded on Thursday near his childhood home in an ordinary neighborhood, its streets lined with auto rickshaws and vegetable carts. A news conference planned with the pilot’s uncle was canceled and a local politician, Parag Shah, said his parents had flown to Dubai in the morning.

Mr. Machchhar attended a neighborhood school, and was set to join the family textiles business. His destiny changed when he attended a seminar on aviation.

“That is where the aviation bug bit me,” he said on the podcast, saying that flying had not been a childhood dream.

He said his mother was nervous.

“You didn’t hear a lot of people becoming pilots, no one had any idea how to do it,” he said. “So first of all, that was something that scared my mom — and of course, the flying bit.”

He enrolled in an 18-month program at a New Zealand-based aviation training school, called Mainland. Its director, Philip Kean, described the program as combining academic rigor and practical training.

“You’ve got to study. You’ve got to fly the plane,” Mr. Kean said. “He was a good student — a good average student. He did his job. He got his commercial license, which he had come here for.”

He began as a first officer, rose to the rank of captain, and according to Dhaval Patel, who knew him from school, soon became a trainer of other pilots at Spice Jet, a private Indian airline that has since folded.

He became a mentor to Mr. Patel, who also worked as a pilot. He was passionate about training other pilots. “He would also ensure that the pilot is confident enough to execute the job well,” said Mr. Patel, who now works in his family’s diamonds business.

“Everything is behind you and you should look ahead,” Mr. Patel recalled him saying many years ago, “because when you are flying, you always look ahead.”

Mr. Machchhar trains aspiring pilots as part of a private aviation school, called Fly By Aviation.

“You should be ready to multitask,” he says in a video directed at aspiring pilots on the school’s Facebook page.

Although the captain does not appear to have much of a public presence on social media, glimpses of his personality and his outlook could be gleaned from interviews. Some of them are striking to read in the aftermath of the FlyDubai incident.

In the hourlong podcast, posted last year, Mr. Machchhar said he avoided “deep discussions” with his colleagues in the cockpit, so as not to be distracted, and said pilots should get plenty of rest so they can perform under challenging situations.

“You have to perform. There’s no alternative,” he said.

Asked to describe his feelings about being a pilot in one word, he replied, “blessed.”

A passenger who helped subdue the attacker describes a bloody scene in the cockpit.

Tzvika Manes, a passenger seated in the front row of FlyDubai Flight 1073 to Tel Aviv on Wednesday, said he heard bloodcurdling screams from the cockpit as the aircraft plunged toward the Saudi desert.

In an interview with The New York Times on Wednesday, Mr. Manes recounted leaping from his seat to retrieve his 6-year-old daughter from the bathroom. The cockpit door was partly open. A pilot, bloodied with stab wounds, had lurched out and was locked in a melee with the plane’s other pilot, he said.

Mr. Manes said he was one of three passengers who subdued the aggressive pilot in a midair struggle, narrowly averting catastrophe. He gave a harrowing account of what happened inside the cockpit, as they wrestled the pilot pressing the attack and landed the plane, in a brief telephone interview.

The compartment itself was disheveled, spattered with blood, he said. The pilot who was attacked — who Mr. Manes said appeared to be Indian — was so badly injured that Mr. Manes said he was amazed that the man had managed to escape from the pilots’ compartment.

“The Indian pilot was struggling — he managed to open the door to get help to save himself,” said Mr. Manes, who added that the bleeding pilot fell out of the cockpit as the other pilot was on top of him, stabbing him.

Then, Mr. Manes said, he and two other passengers “jumped on” the armed pilot and grappled with him to stop the attack. They used the cables from the flight’s headphone sets to tie up the pilot and restrain him, Mr. Manes said.

Meanwhile, passengers on the flight shrieked in terror as the plane quickly lost altitude, with people “flying out of their seats,” before the plane stabilized, Mr. Manes said. He described the scene as traumatic and like a “horror movie.”

After the pilot was restrained, other passengers on the flight with flying experience took control of the aircraft and landed it, Mr. Manes said.

The plane arrived in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, where passengers disembarked, some of them in bloodstained clothing. They waited for a replacement aircraft sent by FlyDubai to continue to Tel Aviv. By Wednesday night, all the passengers had arrived safely in Israel.

Israeli officials said on Wednesday that much about the flight remained unclear, including what motivated the attacking pilot and whether it was specifically an attack on Israelis, as many people in Israel — including some in the government — quickly concluded. The country has been increasingly isolated over the wars in Gaza and Iran and antisemitic attacks are on the rise.

A FlyDubai spokesperson urged all parties “to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts.” The airline later said it was suspending all flights to and from Israel pending an investigation into the episode.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel would later identify the pilot who was stabbed as Capt. Smit Machchhar, an Indian citizen. “Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker — preventing a catastrophic midair disaster,” Mr. Netanyahu said.

The Indian Embassy in Riyadh confirmed the pilot’s identity and said in a statement that he was in a hospital in Tabuk in stable condition.
